10566-the-bequest-ship-s-company-part-6:
W. W. Jacobs built Ship's Company from short comic stories about sailors and small-town life, and "The Bequest" is one of its tales. Robert Clarkson has waited some thirty years for the woman he once courted, while his lifelong rival stood in his way. When the rival dies, a visitor arrives with news that changes what Clarkson may now expect.

Jacobs tells the story through quiet talk by the fire, with dry humor in every exchange. Clarkson weighs patience, loyalty, and hope against the awkward facts of a dead man's wishes. The tale gives readers a gentle, funny look at long waiting, old rivalry, and the surprises that can follow a will.
10786-odd-man-out-sailor-s-knots-part-6:
W. W. Jacobs's "Odd Man Out," the sixth tale in Sailors' Knots from 1909, opens with the night-watchman denouncing friendship as a delusion and a snare. He has had more friendships than most, he says, and nearly all ended suddenly. One friend who once thought he could do no wrong now makes a face at him in the street.

The break came when the friend, uneasy about marrying, asked how his looks would strike the watchman if he were a girl. Honest praise of heart, temper, and purse did not save the friendship. Readers get a funny monologue on truth, vanity, and the odd ways friendships end.
11186-over-the-side-captains-all-book-6:
W. W. Jacobs wrote this short sea tale, Over the Side, sixth in the Captains All series. The narrator argues that seamen are prone to superstition, afloat on black waste waters with vast depths below, where belief in the supernatural comes easier than ashore under cheerful gas-lamps. An incident from his own experience made him chary of calling a man fool or coward for encountering something he cannot explain.

At fifteen, his father refusing to apprentice him to the sea, he shipped before the mast on the brig Endeavour, bound for Riga, and attached himself to Bill Smith. Jem Dadd, a morose man of forty, claimed rats were the souls of drowned sailors and frightened his fellows with supernatural tales. One night a dark figure springs over the side onto the deck, and Bill roars as never before. Jacobs mixes ghost story with shipboard humour.
11364-clarissa-harlowe-or-the-history-of:
Volume six of Samuel Richardson's Clarissa Harlowe, in a nine-volume edition, continues the heroine's story entirely in letters, from letter one through letter seventy-three. Detailed contents show Lovelace writing to Belford about conditional promises to Tomlinson, pleas on their situation, a whimsical contest with his conscience. A meeting with Clarissa in the garden, where her composure and noble conversation refuse him any determination in his favor.

Richardson's epistolary method lets readers follow Clarissa's moral struggle from inside, letter by letter, with Lovelace's self-deception exposed in his own words. This middle volume deepens the novel's central conflict without resolving it. Readers tackling Clarissa will find volume six essential to its tragic arc.
11452-stories-by-american-authors-volume:
Stories by American Authors, volume six from 1891, collects six stories: C. H. White's Village Convict, A. A. Hayes's Denver Express, Lina Redwood Fairfax's Misfortunes of Bro' Thomas Wheatley, L. W. Champney's Heartbreak Cameo, Albert Webster's Miss Eunice's Glove, and Harold Frederic's Brother Sebastian's Friendship. White's opener finds fishermen around a country-store stove discussing Eph, just out of state's prison after burning Eliphalet's barn, having first led the animals out.

Sympathy for Eph, a high-strung boy whose mother Eliphalet foreclosed on in winter, complicates the village's fear. The volume's stories share a regional, character-driven manner. Readers of American local color will find the collection a solid sample of magazine fiction before realism hardened.
11476-husbandry-deep-waters-part-6:
Jacobs's Deep Waters story Husbandry opens with the watchman's comparison: dealing with a man is easy as a teetotaller on a wide pavement. dealing with a woman like the same teetotaller after whiskies trying to climb a step that is not there. A young husband reports his wife's row in stages: cooing and moustache-pulling, temper and remarks about his sister. a banged door felling a vase, four returns with fresh grievances, refusal of food, and a secret supper of loaf, butter, and chops.

The husband's relief at her appetite earns a charge of grudging her food. Jacobs's humor is dated in its gender comedy, but its structure, escalation by anecdote, remains effective. The story is a compact example of his marital farce, told entirely in the watchman's voice.
11956-a-popular-history-of-france-from-t:
Volume 6 of Guizot's History of France, the last of the series, runs from Louis XIV and his court through his death in 1711 to 1715. It then turns to Louis XV, the Regency, and Cardinal Dubois from 1715 to 1723. Later chapters cover the ministry of Cardinal Fleury, France in the colonies from 1745 to 1763, and the Seven Years' War under the Duke of Choiseul.

Guizot closes his long narrative with the monarchy at its height and in decline, as court splendor, ministerial government, colonial rivalry, and European war strained the old regime. The volume's sweep, from Versailles to Canada and India, shows a historian thinking about France as a world power, not merely as a kingdom.
12126-in-the-library-the-lady-of-the-bar:
Two bachelors share a house and a firm in In the Library, a dark short story from W. W. Jacobs Lady of the Barge. Trayton Burleigh and James Fletcher inherited the place from a distant connection, and the partnership has curdled into hatred.

Fletcher, smoking his pipe in the third-floor library, tells Burleigh he must leave house and firm by morning, or face ruin. Burleigh weighs refusal, revenge, and flight through a long, wet night, listening to steps on the stairs and fearing what waits in the dark. Jacobs, usually comic, writes here a tense study of blackmail and pride. The library fire burns low as the two men play out a quiet war of nerves.
12156-the-three-sisters-night-watches-pa:
On a wet autumn evening thirty years before the tale begins, Ursula Mallow dies at Mallett Lodge and makes her sisters promise to lock her room and never open it. That vow drives The Three Sisters, the ghost story in W. W. Jacobs Night Watches.

Tabitha, hard and skeptical, keeps the room shut, while Eunice, the youngest, fears Ursula will return as she promised, to watch over them both. Strange sounds, a locked door, and a cat that cannot explain them wear Eunice down to fainting. Jacobs, master of the comic twist, here writes true unease: the ghost may be real, or may be guilt and grief in an old house. The ending leaves the reader, like Tabitha, unsure what to believe.
12206-breaking-a-spell-odd-craft-part-6:
Claybury folk never took much count of witchcraft, says the old narrator of Breaking a Spell, a comic tale from W. W. Jacobs Odd Craft. The exception is Joe Barlcomb, a newcomer who believes half the old ladies in town are witches and treats them with nervous politeness.

When Barlcomb wife breaks her leg and his luck sours, he seeks a wise woman, Mrs. Prince, for a cure. Her remedy is a midnight riddle: sell six men a ha penny for a shilling, and the man who makes the most fuss is the one who hexed him. Barlcomb midnight rounds turn suspicion into farce. Jacobs uses village superstition to mock fear itself, showing how a man can hex himself with worry.
17726-the-bay-state-monthly-volume-3-no-:
The Bay State Monthly, a Massachusetts magazine, issued this number as volume three, number six, in November 1885. Its opening piece, by Professor William Mathews, profiles Henry W. Paine. Mathews opens by noting that among useful callings, none but medicine has been oftener the butt of vulgar ridicule and abuse than the law, and lawyers and doctors share the joke.

As a monthly number, the magazine mixes Massachusetts biography, history, and literature. Readers get a snapshot of Bay State letters in 1885, through a lawyer's life. The issue suits readers of Massachusetts history and of the legal profession's past.
18762-the-works-of-lord-byron-vol-6:
The sixth volume of Lord Byron's poetical works, in the new revised edition edited by Ernest Hartley Coleridge, appeared in 1903 from John Murray and Scribner's. It carries the text of Don Juan. Its preface records collation with original manuscripts held by Lady Dorchester and John Murray.

For the first time it prints the fragment of a seventeenth canto, fourteen stanzas long. It also rechecks Byron's long quotations from Dalzell's Shipwrecks and Disasters at Sea and Castelnau's history of New Russia. Notes mark variant readings from manuscripts, with the editor's own notes in square brackets. The volume is dedicated, with permission, to Algernon Charles Swinburne.
19378-oriental-encounters-palestine-and-:
Marmaduke Pickthall wrote this travel book on Palestine and Syria in the mid eighteen nineties, published in the late nineteen teens. He rides through hill country, sleeps in towers that once held prisoners, and notes fenced fields, goats, and a blind old woman at a doorway, all in close detail.

The charm is in the encounters: hosts, guides, and villagers met on the road, with Arabic terms kept as heard. Pickthall later became famous as a translator of the Koran. This early book already shows his gift for meeting the East on its own terms rather than as a tourist's backdrop.
21864-journeys-through-bookland-vol-6:
Great poems and tales for young readers fill this sixth volume of Journeys Through Bookland, Charles H. Sylvester's guided tour of the world's best literature for children, in its 1922 edition. Macaulay's Horatius opens the volume, the Roman legend of the bridge retold in ringing verse. Campbell's Lord Ullin's Daughter and The Rainbow follow, then a life of Sir Walter Scott and Scott's own Tournament.

Livingstone meets a lion, Byron destroys Sennacherib, and Tennyson sings Sweet and Low further in. A Kempis, John Brown's Rab and His Friends, and Annie Laurie round out the mix. Sylvester frames each piece for a child reader, with notes and care. The set aimed to walk children into real literature by a pleasant road, volume by volume.
21938-the-works-of-john-knox-volume-1-of:
Scotland's Reformation is told by its fiercest maker in this first volume of the Works of John Knox. David Laing edited it for the Wodrow Society. The editors chose to begin with Knox's History of the Reformation in Scotland, his work of greatest weight. Theodore Beza's Latin greeting heads the volume, calling Knox a kind of apostle of true worship in Scotland. Book one runs from 1494 to 1558, book two through 1559.

Appendices study the Lollards, Patrick Hamilton, and early martyrs under James the Fifth. Knox writes as a participant with a trumpet voice: sermons, plots, and burnings pass in review. The 1895 Edinburgh edition gathers his text with care. As history it is partisan; as a voice of the age, it has no equal in Scotland.
24023-history-of-the-united-states-volum:
E. Benjamin Andrews, chancellor of the University of Nebraska and formerly president of Brown University, wrote History of the United States from the Earliest Discovery of America to the Present Time. Charles Scribner's Sons published the sixth volume in 1912, with 650 illustrations and maps, the last of a set of six.

Volume six opens with the rise of Theodore Roosevelt, pictured at his desk in the White House executive offices. Chapters cover his career, temper, and method, his administration, and reciprocity. Trusts, industrial confederations, and railway, steel, and steamship combinations follow, with the ship subsidy bill, the beef trust, and the steel strike of 1901. It is a contemporary history, written while Roosevelt's age was still fresh.
24943-the-nursery-december-1873-vol-xiv-:
The December 1873 number of The Nursery, Vol. XIV No. 6, mixes winter fun with holiday feeling for young readers. Clear the Coast opens with Albert and Frank racing downhill on Frank's new sled, shouting warnings as a German woman crosses the road with her baskets. A Letter to Santa Claus, The Boy and the Nuts, and Eddy's Thanksgiving carry the seasonal thread through the issue.

What Jessie Cortrell did supplies the number's earnest center. Jessie brings her blind brother Johnny to a doctor who cures him and sends the children home with a sealed envelope for their father. Grandpa's Boots, The Balloon, and verses like The Acorns round out a full monthly. The issue shows the magazine's winter formula at its warmest.
26679-wit-and-mirth-or-pills-to-purge-me:
Thomas D'Urfey edited this fifth volume of Wit and Mirth, or Pills to Purge Melancholy, songs compleat, pleasant and divertive, set to music. The songs are by Dr. John Blow, Henry Purcell, and other excellent masters, with orations spoken on the public stage and prologues and epilogues for D'Urfey's own plays and those of other poets. All are humorous and comical, as the title page promises.

This hosted text follows a 1959 facsimile of an 1876 reprint of the 1719-20 Tonson edition, with modernized typography and music notation. An alphabetical table lists songs from All Christians and Lay-Elders too to Scottish jigs and hornpipes. Readers get Restoration and early Georgian popular song, bawdy, political, and sentimental by turns, with music transcribed for modern use.
27567-aunt-jo-s-scrap-bag-volume-6:
Louisa M. Alcott, author of Little Women, published this sixth volume of Aunt Jo's Scrap-Bag, with Roberts Brothers of Boston. The series holds My Boys, Shawl-Straps, Cupid and Chow-Chow, My Girls, and Jimmy's Cruise in the Pinafore, with this volume of An Old-Fashioned Thanksgiving and other stories.

An illustration for the title story shows Tilly throwing down her axe, flinging open the door, and running straight into the arms of a bear. Another, called How It All Happened, shows Dolly opening a door and starting back in astonishment at a lovely spectacle. Alcott's scrap-bag mixes humor, home life, and surprise for young readers.
27570-buchanan-s-journal-of-man-july-188:
Buchanan's Journal of Man, volume one, number six, dated July 1887, is a periodical of magnetic and psychical science. Its contents list magnetic education and therapeutics, so-called scientific immortality, a review of the new education, and Victoria's half century.

Miscellaneous intelligence covers the Seybert Commission, mesmerism in Paris, medical freedom, and Victoria's jubilee. An outline of anthropology continues with cranioscopy, illustrated. The lead essay, by Dr. Charles Du Prel, treats moral education by magnetism and hypnotic cures. The number gives a vivid sample of fringe science in 1887. Outlook of Diogenes and a bill to destroy the Indians also appear. Medical freedom gets a short note too.
27943-the-home-medical-library-volume-1-:
Kenelm Winslow, formerly assistant professor of comparative therapeutics at Harvard, edited The Home Medical Library in six volumes, published in New York by the Review of Reviews Company in 1907. This first volume covers first aid, family medicines, and the nose, throat, lungs, eye, and ear, among other subjects.

Many medical advising editors and special contributors cooperated, with Albert Warren Ferris as managing editor and specialists on nervous diseases, pregnancy, germ diseases, and the eye and ear. The library aimed to give families reliable medical guidance at home, in the confident style of early twentieth-century popular medicine.
27944-the-home-medical-library-volume-2-:
Kenelm Winslow's Home Medical Library, volume two of six, published in New York by the Review of Reviews Company in 1907, continues the family's medical encyclopedia. The set covers stomach and bowels, tumors and skin diseases, rheumatism, germ diseases, nervous diseases, insanity, and sexual hygiene, among many other subjects.

The same advising editors serve all volumes, with Albert Warren Ferris as managing editor and specialists on nervous diseases, pregnancy, germ diseases, and the eye and ear. Volume two belongs to a series meant to give ordinary households a reliable medical reference before the age of the family doctor's telephone.
27947-the-home-medical-library-volume-5-:
Kenelm Winslow's Home Medical Library, volume five of six, published in New York by the Review of Reviews Company in 1907, continues the family's medical encyclopedia. Like the other volumes, it carries the same roster of advising editors, from managing editor Albert Warren Ferris to specialists on germ diseases and the eye and ear.

The six-volume set ranges across tumors and skin diseases, rheumatism, nervous diseases, insanity, sexual hygiene, woman and child, heart and digestion, diet, sanitation, and pure food. Volume five belongs to a series meant to put a doctor's reference shelf into the ordinary home.
32075-the-galaxy-june-1877-vol-xxiii-jun:
Volume XXIII, number 6, of The Galaxy is the June 1877 issue of the American literary magazine. It opens with Spring Longing, a poem by Emma Lazarus that moves from lilac haze and blossoming orchards to dreams of medieval towns, gypsy flower sellers, and Venetian lagoons. The poem ends with the speaker bound by an iron fate, left to dream and wonder, yearn and sing, while spring passes by.

The issue then turns to serial fiction with A Progressive Baby, presented as Letter III from an address in South Kensington, dated May 28, 1875. Its letter writer tells her friend Susie about life in London, a husband facing a run for Parliament in Ireland, window gardening, and a neglected baby glimpsed in Kensington Gardens. The mix of verse and letter fiction shows the magazine's blend of poetry and contemporary social observation.
32313-the-esperantist-vol-1-no-6:
The Esperantist, number six, April 1904, priced at fourpence net, is the Esperanto gazette for the spreading of the international language. It was edited by H. Bolingbroke Mudie and published by the London Esperanto Club at Outer Temple. Its annual subscription was three shillings. The issue shows a movement organizing itself in print, with notes, science, proverbs, and translations.

Its contents include Editor's Notes, Science Notes, Maltese Proverbs, and Two Fables. They continue with Italian Conscription by Clarence Bicknell, The Green Man by Edward Metcalfe, The Birth of Esperanto continued and translated by John Ellis, and The Tempest continued and translated by A. Motteau. Correspondence Notes, A Visit to the House of Commons by Miss Lawrence, Various Items of Interest, and a Grammatical Synopsis close the issue. Readers get a snapshot of Esperanto in 1904, earnest and international, already translating Shakespeare.
33404-wit-and-mirth-or-pills-to-purge-me:
Thomas D'Urfey's Wit and Mirth, or Pills to Purge Melancholy, volume six of six, gathers songs to cure low spirits, in a 1959 reprint of a classic collection. Its alphabetical table runs from Amoret and Thyrsis lying together to a sailor, a duke's march, and a young man lately in town, with songs of love, drink, and folly. D'Urfey, a Restoration wit, edited the set for singers and merry makers.

The volume suits readers of old songs and social history, offering lyrics that were sung in taverns, theatres, and homes. Its tone is bawdy, funny, and frank, reflecting its age. For students of English song, it is a rich source, preserving tunes and words that might otherwise have been lost to time.
33805-the-mysteries-of-paris-illustrated:
The sixth and last volume of Eugene Sue's Mysteries of Paris closes the Boston edition de luxe, again with etchings. Punishment, Rodolphe and Sarah, love's frenzy, and a hospital stay lead toward a father and daughter, a marriage, and the prison of Bicetre. An epilogue at Gerolstein, with Princess Amelie and a vow, ends the long tale.

Sue resolves fates that have hung since the first volume, rewarding some figures and punishing others. The etchings catch a kneeling figure, a mirror scene, and a church in prayer. The volume gives readers the payoff of a vast serial: justice, reunion, and a final reckoning.
33928-bel-ami-a-ladies-man-the-works-of-:
Guy de Maupassant's Bel Ami, subtitled A Ladies' Man, appears here as volume six of his works, published in New York in 1909. The novel opens with George Duroy leaving a cheap Paris restaurant on June 28, with just three francs and forty centimes to last him to the end of the month. He counts dinners against lunches to make the money stretch.

Duroy, a former soldier with a good bearing and a sweeping glance, watches the women in the restaurant with keen interest. Maupassant follows his climb through Paris society, where charm opens doors that money cannot. The novel remains a sharp, unsparing study of ambition.
3852-memoirs-of-madame-la-marquise-de-mo:
Madame de Montespan's sixth book marks the cooling of the king's favor. Louis, consoled for the death of the Duchesse de Fontanges, no longer returns to the sweet intimacy of eleven or twelve years. He approaches Montespan as one visits an acquaintance, with their children as the only bond. He then sets off on a splendid progress in Picardy and Flanders, and Montespan is not invited to join the boudoir navy.

The king relates the journey's delights to her afterward, while his Chambers of Reunion at Metz and Brisach strip great proprietors of lands once held from Alsace. A later passage shows Madame de Maintenon deftly steering the king on court fashions and a delayed demolition. The volume reads as a farewell to power, told by the woman losing it.
3952-cinq-mars-volume-6:
Alfred de Vigny's sixth volume of Cinq Mars turns to a monk questioned about love. The questioner demands what love is, confessing he knows nothing about it himself. The monk stands astounded, looks on the ground with the stupid eye of some base animal, and after long consideration answers in a drawling nasal voice.

Love must be a kind of malignant fever leading the brain astray, he says, though in truth he has never reflected on it until this moment. He has always been embarrassed speaking to a woman, and wishes women could be omitted from society altogether. Their one use, he says, is to disclose secrets, like the little Duchess or Marion de Lorme, whom he recommends to his Eminence. Readers who like Vigny's irony will find a volume of conspiracy told through comic ignorance.
4106-the-mayflower-and-her-log-july-15-1:
Azel Ames's Mayflower history reaches its sixth volume with the journal of the ship herself, under Master Thomas Jones, from London toward Hudson's River in Virginia. The voyage began at London, as her consort's had at Delfshaven, and the journal tracks wind, weather, and landfall.

Ames sets the log beside the story of the company, noting where the larger ship's fortunes touched the smaller's. The volume gives readers the voyage day by day, in the master's own course. It suits those who want the crossing itself, not only the story around it.
4411-the-ordeal-of-richard-feverel-volum:
Book Six of George Meredith's Ordeal of Richard Feverel opens on a southwestern island in a season of wind and rain, where Lord Mountfalcon still lingers to his friends' disgust. Mount's in for it again, they say among themselves, and the phrase hangs over the book's closing acts. Clare's diary and Austin's return follow.

The chapters promise nature speaking, the magian conflict again, and the last scene, with a letter from Lady Blandish to Austin Wentworth. Richard's ordeal reaches its tragic end here, as his father's system, his marriage, and his loves collide. This final volume completes Meredith's most famous novel of education and its failure.
4418-sandra-belloni-volume-6:
Book Six of George Meredith's Sandra Belloni opens with Emilia stretching out her hand to say goodbye. A hardened girl with dead eyelids does not seem to feel herself at the speaker's mercy, and the farewell carries the weight of the novel's long courtship. Despair, the book's first chapter title, sets the tone.

Later chapters bring Emilia found, the defection of Mr. Pericles from the Brookfield circle, Wilfrid kindling, and the hippogriff in air and on earth. The rape of the black-briony wreath, a call to action, and a further view of sentiment follow. This volume moves Emilia from despair toward a decision, with Meredith's irony intact.
4432-evan-harrington-volume-6:
Book Six of George Meredith's Evan Harrington opens on a summer evening, with dowagers firmly planted on Olympus. Warm colors lie along the grass, reddening pine stems and yellowing aspen leaves. A picnic hangs in doubt after two rude shocks, but happily survives, and the comedy of rank resumes.

The book's chapters promise Evan's light beginning to twinkle again, the hero taking his rank in the orchestra, a pagan sacrifice, and Rose wounded. Before breakfast and the retreat from Beckley follow, with a chapter on seeing in the dark. Evan's fortunes turn here, as love and birth pull him in opposite directions.
4440-vittoria-volume-6:
Book Six of George Meredith's Vittoria turns to episodes of the revolt and the war, opening with the tobacco riots and Rinaldo Guidascarpi. Anna von Lenkenstein, Meredith notes, could wait for vengeance, while Lena acts at once and harms herself most of all. Lena has broken her engagement with Wilfrid, and the cost is plain.

Later chapters tell the five days of Milan, Vittoria disobeying her lover, and the treachery of Pericles, with the white umbrella and the death of Rinaldo Guidascarpi. The book gives the revolution in episodes, mixing street fighting with private betrayals. Vittoria's voice and her choices carry the history.
4449-the-adventures-of-harry-richmond-vo:
Book Six of George Meredith's Adventures of Harry Richmond opens with Harry seeing his father taking the tide, and being carried on it himself. His father's meeting with his grandfather follows, with the commencement of the splendors and perplexities of the grand parade. The Marquis of Edbury and his puppet appear.

Harry becomes one of the chosen of the nation, and his father is miraculously relieved by fortune. The adventurer's schemes reach their height here, with Harry swept along in triumph and doubt. Meredith's comedy of a charming rogue and his loving son turns serious, as fortune's gifts prove double-edged.
4458-beauchamp-s-career-volume-6:
Book Six of George Meredith's Beauchamp's Career turns on two passions in Nevil Beauchamp, and on the Earl of Romfrey and the countess. The earl's nephews show another exhibition of those passions in Beauchamp himself, and a little plot against Cecilia follows. As it might have been foreseen, the plot ends in refusal.

Beauchamp, naval officer turned radical, has fought for principle through elections, newspapers, and love affairs. This volume tests his constancy once more, as family pressure and Cecilia's fate press upon him. Meredith's political novel narrows toward its close, with honor and affection still at odds.
5239-the-confessions-of-harry-lorrequer-:
Charles James Lever's Harry Lorrequer concludes in this sixth volume, covering chapters forty-two through fifty-five. Journeys, a reminiscence of the East, a day in the Phoenix, an adventure in Canada, a courier's passport, a night in Strasbourg, a surprise. Jack Waller's story carries Harry toward the end of his confessions.

The volume holds only this final stretch, and its far-flung episodes show Lever's hero still travelling, still confessing, and still finding trouble. Readers finishing the novel here get its closing adventures, from Canada to the Continent, in the comic voice that carried the whole book.
5813-following-the-equator-a-journey-aro:
Part six of Mark Twain's Following the Equator covers chapters fifty-one through sixty, in India. Chapter fifty-one opens with a Pudd'nhead Wilson maxim about making a nation's superstitions, then declares Benares a big church, a religious hive whose every cell is a temple, shrine, or mosque. Every earthly and heavenly good, Twain jokes, is procurable under one roof.

Twain offers his India at its most vivid: temples, pilgrims, priests, and street life rendered with humor and sharp observation. The part balances wonder at devotion with skepticism about superstition and exploitation. It suits readers who enjoy Twain's Indian chapters, and it offers a memorable, opinionated portrait of Benares and the religious life of a great city.
5823-the-gilded-age-part-6:
Part six of The Gilded Age, by Twain and Warner, covers chapters forty-six through fifty-four, opening on a bright spring morning in Washington. Philip leaves the Capitol walking up Pennsylvania Avenue with Senator Dilworthy, amid soft air, deepening green, pink peach blossom, and the warm south wind. The annual renewal of the city frames a season of lobbying, love, and political maneuver.

Readers see the novel's Washington at its most vivid, as Philip navigates senators, schemes, and personal hopes. The part balances romance with satire, letting spring beauty contrast with the grubby business of influence. It suits readers nearing the novel's climax, since alliances formed on this walk will shape trials and fortunes ahead.
5841-sketches-new-and-old-part-6:
Part six of Mark Twain's Sketches New and Old opens with The Undertaker's Chat, in which an undertaker pats the folded hands of the deceased approvingly. The corpse, he says, was a brick every way you took him, real accommodating, modest-like and simple in his last moments. Friends wanted a metallic burial case, but the dead man's modesty shapes the joke that follows.

Here Twain gives his dark humor at its most characteristic, finding comedy in funerals without cruelty to the dead. The part gathers further sketches where death, business, and human vanity meet in deadpan talk. It suits readers who enjoy Twain's gallows humor, and it shows how a single voice, the undertaker's, can carry a whole sketch.
5859-personal-memoirs-of-p-h-sheridan-vo:
Volume two, part six of Sheridan's Personal Memoirs covers chapters twelve through twenty, on the postwar frontier. Headings treat Fort Leavenworth, the Treaty of Medicine Lodge, going to Fort Dodge, discontented Indians, Indian outrages, a delegation of chiefs, and a terrible raid. The death of Comstock, vast herds of buffalo, a winter campaign, and meeting Buffalo Bill follow.

Readers get Sheridan's account of plains service after the Civil War, with Forsyth's gallant fight and rescue closing the section. The memoir favors operational detail and frontier incident, told in a general's plain prose. Modern readers should note its period language about Native peoples, while historians will value its firsthand view of treaties, raids, and campaigns.
5865-personal-memoirs-of-u-s-grant-part-:
Part six of Grant's Personal Memoirs covers chapters sixty-two through seventy, in the war's final months. Headings treat Sherman's march north, Sheridan ordered to Lynchburg, Canby ordered against Mobile, and movements of Schofield and Thomas. The capture of Columbia, South Carolina, and Sherman in the Carolinas follow, while news of Sherman in possession of Savannah draws statesmen and visitors north.

Grant gives his closing account of coordinated campaigns, as armies converge and the Confederacy's end approaches. The memoir records orders, movements, and meetings with the same plain clarity as earlier volumes. It suits Civil War readers finishing Grant's story, and it offers a commander's view of victory without triumphalism, focused on duty done.
6235-the-battle-of-the-strong-a-romance-:
The bell of the Cohue Royale clatters on the fourth of October for the opening of the Assise d'Heritage. The court fills with governor, bailly, jurats, seigneurs, and avocats learned in Norman custom. The Royal Court and the States will welcome Admiral Prince Philip d'Avranche, Duc de Bercy, and offer a bounty to Jerseymen enlisting under him. The island is en fete, alive with a year of sensations unmatched since the Battle of Jersey.

This final volume brings the long story to its courtroom close, where law, honour, and island custom meet in public. Parker also gives a harrowing climb, fingers gripping rock on a limestone shelf, as a body draws itself up from a granite wall. Ceremony and peril share the stage, and the romance ends with Jersey itself, its courts, its people, and its sea, in full view.
7138-the-great-conspiracy-volume-6:
Logan's sixth part of The Great Conspiracy opens at chapter twenty two, Freedom's Sun Still Rising, after Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation. Friends of freedom saw clearly, none more than Lincoln himself, that until that great act entered the Constitution itself, no real assurance guarded the liberties of the emancipated. Without it, even after rebellion's suppression, a living spark of dissension might at any time fan again into civil war.

At all proper times Lincoln favored and urged congressional action, but definite action began only the following year, and Congress moved slow. In his third annual message Lincoln pledged he would not attempt to retract or modify the proclamation while he remained in his position. Only this sixth part's course is followed here, as emancipation seeks constitutional ground.
7159-the-prince-and-the-pauper-part-6:
Part six of Twain's Prince and the Pauper opens at chapter eighteen, The Prince with the Tramps, as the troop of vagabonds turns out at early dawn. A lowering sky hangs overhead, sloppy ground lies underfoot, and winter chill fills the air, with all gaiety gone from the company. Some stand sullen, some irritable, none gentle humored, all thirsty. The Ruffler puts Jack in Hugo's charge with brief instructions. He commands John Canty to keep away and let him alone, and warns Hugo not to be too rough with the lad.

After a while weather grows milder and clouds lift somewhat. The troop stops shivering as spirits improve. They grow more cheerful, then chaff each other and insult passengers, waking again to life's joys. The dread in which their sort is held shows in how everybody gives them room. Only this part's march is followed here.
7198-the-adventures-of-tom-sawyer-part-6:
Part Six of Mark Twain's Tom Sawyer stirs the sleepy village with the murder trial, which becomes the absorbing topic of all talk at once. Tom cannot escape it, and every mention sends a shudder through him, since his troubled conscience half persuades him that remarks in his hearing are feelers meant to test him. He does not see how he could be suspected, yet comfort eludes him.

Tom takes Huck to a lonely place for a talk, seeking relief in unsealing his tongue for a little while. The trial scenes turn village gossip into a moral pressure chamber, with fear and loyalty pulling the boys in opposite ways. This part holds the trial's opening grip and Tom's private dread.
7247-a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur:
Part Six of Mark Twain's Connecticut Yankee sends the Yankee and the king travelling incognito, and the disguise begins with hair. High classes wear hair banged across the forehead and hanging to the shoulders, low commoners are banged fore and aft, and slaves go bangless with free growth. The Yankee inverts a bowl over the king's head and cuts away all that hangs below it.

Whiskers and moustache follow, trimmed to a villainous half-inch and done inartistically on purpose, so the king can pass as lowly. Twain turns a barber's job into a lesson in rank, showing how much of majesty hangs on a haircut. This part holds the making of the disguise and the road that follows.
736-history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-t:
Edward Gibbon devoted this sixth volume, with notes by H. H. Milman, to the Crusades and their aftermath in the East. It opens with the Crusades themselves, then the Fourth Crusade, which turned its arms against fellow Christians and sacked Constantinople. The partition of the empire by French and Venetians follows.

Gibbon traces how the crusading age weakened the Byzantine state and reshaped trade and power in the Mediterranean. His judgement is cool and ironic, sparing neither popes nor princes. The volume is vital for readers who want the long view of the Crusades, not just battles, but the slow unravelling of an empire.
7755-godolphin-volume-6:
Constance reproaches herself in the final volume of Lytton's Godolphin, after betraying before another man how much she leans on her husband's heart. Her conscience alarms her at the slip, yet she cannot quell delight at Radclyffe's solemn word that Godolphin still loves her.

Radclyffe, austere and sincere, presses her to ask whether she too neglected him in return, and whether softness might have won what pride lost. She turns the question over without rest, weighing her own conduct against his. The closing volume brings a marriage to honest reckoning, where love survives only through plain self-knowledge.
8476-life-on-the-mississippi-part-6:
Part 6 of Life on the Mississippi opens with chapter 26, Under Fire, as talk turns to war. Twain's boat moves down into the upper edge of the former battle stretch, with Columbus just behind, and much is said about the famous battle of Belmont. Several officers aboard had seen active service in the Mississippi war fleet, and their talk fills the chapter.

This section shows the river as a war zone remembered, with veterans' stories correcting romantic notions. Readers get Twain's Civil War river, not as history but as boat talk, with officers who found themselves sadly out of step with glory. It is the book in its reminiscent, slightly skeptical vein.
8706-the-dore-bible-gallery-volume-6:
Gustave Dore's sixth Bible volume tells the early life and ministry of Jesus, passage by passage beside the engravings. It opens with the Nativity: Caesar Augustus decrees a taxing, Joseph travels from Nazareth to Bethlehem, and Mary lays her firstborn in a manger. The star in the East, the flight into Egypt, and the massacre of the innocents follow, then the boy Jesus questioning the doctors in the Temple.

Healing the sick, the Sermon on the Mount, stilling the tempest, and the disciples plucking corn on the Sabbath show the teacher and healer at work. Dore's pictures, even unseen, are suggested by the scale of the chosen scenes. The volume works as a short gospel harmony for family or devotional reading, and as a record of how the nineteenth century pictured the life of Christ.
895-history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-t:
This sixth and final volume of Gibbon's history carries the story to the fall of Constantinople and beyond. It treats the Crusades, the Fourth Crusade's sack of the Christian capital, and the partition of the empire by French and Venetians, then the long Turkish advance that ends the Byzantine state.

Gibbon closes his vast work with a survey of what survived Rome: laws, churches, and cities, and the new nations that rose on Roman ground. Milman's notes complete the edition. The volume is the fitting end to a great history, where the fall that began with Antonines reaches its last, eastern close.
9448-samantha-among-the-brethren-volume-:
A letter from Miss Timson sends Samantha to Loontown in this sixth part of Marietta Holley's Samantha Among the Brethren. Written on the sixth day of a sickness, it brings Josiah and Samantha sailing the next day after it arrives. The sisters of the meeting house counsel her to go, since Sister Bobbet's fall on apple paring halted the papering work.

The interests of Zion, they agree, will not languish for a day or two, and duty calls Samantha plainly. Divisions arise only over which road to take. Holley's dialect comedy carries a serious point about women's work. The part remains a delightful close to the Brethren sequence.
a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur-s-co:
Part 6 cuts King Arthur's hair with a bowl, dresses him in a peasant's coarse brown robe, and sends him travelling incognito with Hank to learn his kingdom at ground level. The king must be drilled to stoop, shuffle, and keep the pride out of his voice, and he fails at nearly every cottage door they try.

On the road they find a smallpox hut where a dying mother curses the lord who jailed her husband, and a manor-house tragedy of lords and priests that destroys a whole family. At Marco's cottage the disguised king hears how his taxes and laws look from below. Twain's comedy darkens here into an indictment of the order Arthur rules.
a-popular-history-of-france-from-the-ear: François Guizot closes his history of France with Louis the Fourteenth and his court, his death, and the long reign of Louis the Fifteenth. The volume passes the Regency and Cardinal Dubois, the ministry of Cardinal Fleury, France in the colonies, the Seven Years' War, and the philosophers. It ends with Louis the Sixteenth, the ministries of Turgot, Necker, and Calonne, the Assembly of Notables, and the convocation of the States-General in 1789.
ante-nicene-fathers-vol-6:
Volume six of the Ante-Nicene Fathers gathers the third century's second rank: Gregory Thaumaturgus, Dionysius the Great, Julius Africanus, Anatolius, and the minor writers, with Methodius and Arnobius. Roberts and Donaldson edited the set in 1885. Several of these names survive in fragments only.

Gregory the wonder-worker was Origen's pupil, and his address of thanks to his teacher is a gem of ancient education. Dionysius of Alexandria writes letters through plague and persecution. Julius Africanus, the first Christian chronographer, tries to date the world. Arnobius, a pagan convert, closes the volume mocking the gods he once served. The volume is a museum of the church's growing mind.
arabian-nights-payne-1883-vol-6:
Volume VI of Payne's Thousand Nights and One Night, from 1883, brings more nights from the Calcutta Arabic text. The unexpurgated Englishing that made John Payne's version the first complete one continues here at full length. Shahrazad's voice, calm under threat of death, frames every marvel that follows.

Readers of the full set prize this sameness-in-variety: the same spell, new wonders each night. Demons, treasures, and sudden reversals of fortune crowd the pages as ever. Volume VI carries the design forward with three volumes left, Burton's famous rival still standing on its claim of completeness.
babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-6:
Volume six of Michael L. Rodkinson's English Babylonian Talmud pairs Tract Yoma with Tract Hagiga. Yoma is the tractate of Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, the holiest day of the Jewish year. Hagiga treats the festival offerings brought by pilgrims to Jerusalem.

Yoma follows the high priest through his long day: his washings, his confessions, the scapegoat sent to the desert, and his entry into the Holy of Holies. Hagiga then weighs who must appear at the feasts and what offerings count. The volume holds the Temple's most solemn rite and its most joyful gatherings side by side. Rodkinson's notes guide readers through both.
bancroft-history-us-vol-6:
Valley Forge and the French alliance mark the sixth volume of Bancroft's History, from 1860. The Revolution's middle years bring hunger, doubt, and then a turning tide. Aid from France lifts the cause when it most needs hope.

Bancroft wrote as America slid toward its own civil war. He found in the old trials a mirror and a warning for his time. Endurance under want becomes his great theme here. The volume shows the Revolution surviving its darkest stretch, held together by Washington's will and the people's refusal to quit a cause they had made their own.
beauchamp-s-career-volume-6:
Volume six of George Meredith's Beauchamp's Career covers chapters forty-two to forty-nine. Two passions, love and family pride, rule the opening. The Earl of Romfrey and his countess confront Nevil's entanglement with Renée, the French wife of his youth. Her boxes, her hotel, and her remembered sentences haunt him.

A little plot against Cecilia Halkett thickens the rivalry between the women. The Earl faces a trial of his own as baronial despotism, the old family tyranny, begins to crumble. Nevil's nephews and cousins expose the Romfrey temper at full stretch. Meredith drives his political novel toward private reckoning. Honour, obstinacy, and affection collide in these chapters, written in his most compressed and glittering style.
breaking-a-spell-odd-craft-part-6:
Breaking a Spell is a comic tale by W W Jacobs, part six of his Odd Craft set, told by an old man of Claybury. Jacobs recalls the last witchcraft scare in the village, some forty years back. Joe Barlcomb, a newcomer, believed in spells with his whole heart.

Joe's politeness to old ladies curdles when they learn he fears half of them as witches. His wife's broken leg, from a chair, reads to him as a spell at work. Mrs Prince sells him a cure: at midnight he must offer six men a ha'penny for a shilling. The fuss that follows names the joker and shames the believer. Claybury laughed, and witch talk died there. Jacobs lets village sense cure village fear.
carlyle-friedrich-vol-6:
Sans Souci and quiet years close Carlyle's vast life of Frederick in this sixth volume, from 1897. The old king rules as an enlightened despot, builds, judges cases, and plays the flute. Death comes at last to the palace he loved best.

Six volumes end with the hero's calm exit from the stage. Carlyle's obsession with his subject never flags across decades of work. Law, farming, and philosophy fill the king's late days here. The set stands complete as the most dogged biography in English letters, a monument to one writer's faith that great men, not forces, make history turn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mary-of-roman: Mary of Romans 16:6 is unknown outside that single verse, where St Paul greets her for having laboured much among the Roman church. Nothing else is recorded of her life, name, or station. Scholars only guess she matches the mother of John Mark, and the verse alone cannot settle the match.
cia-crest-cia-rdp00-01458r000100110004-6:
Federal Register issue for Friday, March 2, 1979, Part IV, adopts questions and answers on the Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures. Five agencies issued it jointly: the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, the Office of Personnel Management, and the Departments of Justice, Labor, and the Treasury. Its stated aim was to clarify the guidelines and give them a common reading.

The notice prints the affected code parts for each agency, from labor rules to fiscal help for state and local governments. The questions then work through practical doubts one by one. One asks where to find people qualified to run validation studies, and points to state psychological associations. Another asks whether a procedure can predict well for a job in one place yet fail for a different job, or the same job elsewhere. The answer is yes, because work behaviours differ, it states.
cia-crest-cia-rdp00-01458r000100130011-6:
Appendix 2, titled The Narrative Report, explains how test results reached hiring units, then judges the write-ups. A candidate outside Washington took PATB I at a field testing site: five thinking tests plus the Strong-Campbell Interest Inventory. Answer sheets went to the Psychological Services Staff in Washington for scoring.

Nothing more happened unless a unit asked for a write-up, the appendix states. Psychologists then gave their reading of the results, never the raw scores. Write-ups with no target job in view tended to be vague, it notes. The reviewers probed what job profiles meant, expecting a full analysis of the skills each post needed. Further checking showed no such analysis stood behind the term, they report. Reliabilities for some battery tests were distressingly low, they warn. No reliability data existed for minorities on any test, nor for women on the work attitude scales, they add.
cia-crest-cia-rdp00m01914r001000030006-6:
Decrypted Soviet cable, issued 8 October 1952 under reference S/NBF/T244, is stamped BRIDE and Top Secret, to be kept under lock and key. It carries traffic from New York to Moscow, numbers 1119 to 1121, dated 4-5 August 1944. Its subject is KOL'TSOV's account of a conversation with a source codenamed JURIST.

The talk took place on 31 July at JURIST's apartment, the cable states. Much of the text never decrypted, and the gaps are marked group by group as unrecovered. What survives touches postwar control of Germany and reparations. JURIST thought a fixed sum in marks should be set, then reviewed and cut if Germany met her obligations, the cable reports. Later parts turn to Poland, where a compromise would shut the most hostile elements out of the government. Finland, it adds, had lost public sympathy in the COUNTRY, a codename left unglossed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01-00569r000100020059-6:
Letter of January 2, 1981 from Martin M. Teasley, Acting Director of the Dwight D. Eisenhower Library in Abilene, Kansas, starts a declassification request. Dr. Jack Holl, Chief Historian at the Department of Energy, wanted a CIA document for an unclassified history of the Atomic Energy Commission. Teasley sent it to the agency's historian for review and release.

The document is a two-page memorandum from Herbert Scoville to the Director of Central Intelligence, dated May 11, 1957, and marked Secret. Its copy, attached here, judges the nuclear test detection system of the day. That system had a very high chance of catching surface tests above twenty kilotons, it states. Certainty fell off below that yield, it adds, and the smallest Soviet test caught so far was about three kilotons. A History Staff note asks for a ruling by 30 January 1981. An Intelligence Branch memo of 16 January carries the request forward.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01-00569r000100030003-6:
Study dated 19 Nov 1981, titled Word Processing Feasibility Study, was prepared for the DCI History Staff. The History Staff had been re-established in November 1980, its introduction states. On 30 October 1981 the agency's Executive Committee approved its long-term program, a copy of which is attached.

The staff's mission is given plainly: preserve the agency's institutional memory and historical records, run a specialised reference service, and write its history. It is also the agency's main contact point with other government history programs, the study states. Its word processing products are listed: classified histories and monographs of 50 to 500 double-spaced pages, a multi-volume general history of the CIA, and oral history transcripts. Typing work fell not only on a support assistant, a later section notes, but on the professional historians themselves. Workload figures rest on less than a year of the new office's experience.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01-00569r000100040093-6:
Two linked letters from Chief Historian J. Kenneth McDonald make up a May 1982 file about a State Department paper on the Cuban crisis. The cover letter, dated 21 May 1982, goes to Suzanne Forbes, an archivist at the John F. Kennedy Library. It thanks her for flagging an interagency agreement on access for official agency historians.

Enclosed is McDonald's letter of 19 May 1982 to the National Security Agency. It releases to that agency a top secret State Department paper titled The Cuban Crisis, 1962, by Frank Sieverts. The paper had been picked out during research at the Kennedy Library. Together the letters show how one agency's historical paper moved between archives under formal release.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01-00569r000100040101-6:
Status of a planned set of histories of former directors is reported to the Director of Central Intelligence in a memorandum dated 29 April 1982. Chief Historian J. Kenneth McDonald writes for information only, through the Executive Secretary. The program would produce studies of individual directors and their time in office, starting with William Colby.

McDonald reports that Colby welcomed the plan and promised his fullest help. Richard Lehman, then nearing retirement from the National Intelligence Council, had agreed to write the Colby study and had drafted a first outline. The memo says Lehman would begin as his council duties wound down. McDonald would steer the scope of the work and decide on editing and review.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01m00147r000100270002-6:
United States policy toward Panama under Noriega after September is laid down in National Security Directive 21, dated 1 September 1989. Routing slips of 5 September 1989 send the paper widely, including to the Latin America offices of analysis and operations. The aim stated is Noriega's departure and a democratic government based on free elections.

The directive says Noriega clearly meant to block the new government due on 1 September. The United States would withhold recognition from any government he controlled. It would state that the Endara slate clearly won the May 7, 1989 elections. Other governments would be pressed to do the same, withdraw ambassadors, and cut contact to a minimum.
cia-crest-cia-rdp02-06298r000900060003-6:
Fisher filter regulators of Type 67F and 67FR are covered in an instruction manual, Form 1692, dated July 1978. A warning head note says the units must be fitted, run, and serviced under federal, state, and local codes, and only by a qualified person. Trouble or venting calls for a technician at once.

The specification panel gives a quarter-inch NPT screwed body and an outlet range of 3 to 100 pounds per square inch across four spring ranges. Maximum inlet pressure is 250 pounds, with temperature limits split between standard and high-temperature elastomers. Installation steps follow, with cautions on overpressure protection and on keeping the spring range label accurate after field changes.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000100240001-6:
Propaganda networks run by Nicaragua's Sandinistas and by Salvadoran guerrillas are the subject of a paper sent to the Director on 5 January 1984. Cover notes from Robert Gates and from the Latin American analysis office show the paper was drafted overnight at the Director's request. The typescript itself is dated the same day.

A summary says the Sandinistas, since taking power in 1979, have pushed a vigorous policy of spreading their message worldwide. The body tracks their diplomacy in world bodies. It reports that Nicaragua took complaints about the United States to the UN Security Council several times and made a like effort in the General Assembly, seeking world attention and support.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000201400001-6:
Succession politics in Taiwan after a Kuomintang plenum are analyzed in a memorandum dated 22 March 1984. The paper reports that President Chiang Ching-kuo strengthened the odds of an orderly succession. His key move was picking Li Teng-hui, an ethnic Taiwanese, for the vice presidency at the party plenum.

Chiang also widened seats on the party Central Standing Committee, giving Taiwan's varied groups a larger stake in the system. The paper reads his gradual renewal and Taiwanization of the party as vital to its hold on power. More personnel shifts are expected after his May reinauguration, likely including a mainlander moderate as premier. Beijing's reaction to the plenum is described as muted.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000302110001-6:
China's construction and housing sector is reviewed in a confidential memorandum dated 9 October 1984. The Development Issues Branch of the China Division prepared the paper. Its opening ties the year's building work to cooperation with the West and to scope for greater American government involvement.

Possible shared work includes bidding and contracting rules for large projects, urban survey work, and state-run building, sale, and financing of housing. Sales openings for American firms include prefabricated housing and housing packages. Reforms announced in April, set out by the construction minister, aim at a more efficient approach to capital building. The paper cautions that deals may yield exchanges more readily than business wins.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000201140001-6:
North Korea's army has been reorganized since 1981, a change fully grasped only this year, in a memorandum dated 17 January 1985. The Korea Branch prepared the paper for an Intelligence Community Staff admiral ahead of a Far East trip. It carries the number EA M 85-10008.

The heart of the change is armor. Mechanized divisions no longer exist as such: each division with armored carriers has split into two mechanized brigades, the paper reports. At least four mechanized corps have been formed to command them, each likely holding five or more brigades. Some units have also shifted forward. Command and control of the new brigades is the reason given for the corps level.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000201690001-6:
China's economy in 1984 is judged in a memorandum dated 6 June 1985, with prospects for reform in 1985. GNP growth of 12 percent made the year's performance the best in the world, the summary states. Farm output rose 14.5 percent under the responsibility system and linked reforms.

Industry was planned to grow 5 percent but rose 14 percent instead. Beijing fears the pace, 18 percent in the fourth quarter, was too hot. Old bottlenecks in energy, raw materials, and transport have worsened. Factory managers used loopholes in the new urban reforms for widespread abuses, feeding inflation. Reformers, the paper notes, have had to show that their October steps did not cause the trouble.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000301860001-6:
Japan's short-term trade policy options are reviewed in a memorandum dated 1 July 1985, EA N 85-10121. The Northeast Asia Division prepared the paper, using information available as of 24 June. Trade officials split their time between two tasks, the summary reports.

One task is a plan to open imports over the next three to five years. The other is a set of quick steps to halt the growth of the trade surplus. Several temporary steps will likely land during the summer. Voluntary export restraints will probably form the core of Tokyo's bid to calm foreign critics, the paper judges. This round of trial balloons is expected to yield bolder action than past rounds.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05c01629r000200360010-6:
Sovereign immunity doctrine is laid out in a legal text excerpt held in Agency files. The passage moves through cases and commentary on when a foreign state may claim immunity in court. A Canadian case, Flota Maritima Browning de Cuba v. The Republic of Cuba, draws extended notes.

The notes stress a modern distinction drawn by Canada's Supreme Court. Acts of a state in its sovereign capacity, aimed at national ends, stand apart from its commercial dealings for profit. Later pages turn to exemptions from territorial jurisdiction. A report of the Inter-American Juridical Committee is quoted on the Brussels Convention of 1926 and its added protocol on the immunity of state ships.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05c01629r000701490001-6:
Legal aspects of export controls for the intelligence community are set out in an outline held in Agency files. The outline is organized as a teaching text. It opens with the Export Administration Act of 1979 and splits its controls into three kinds.

National security controls cover goods and technology that would add greatly to a country's military power at American expense. Foreign policy controls serve stated policy aims, and short supply controls guard the home economy against drains on scarce goods. The Commodity Control List and licensing rules follow. Penalties are listed plainly: generally five years and 50,000 dollars, rising to ten years for willful violations meant to benefit a controlled country. Arms export law comes next.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000200500018-6:
A protest at a Turner speech in Lexington is defended in a pamphlet dated 12 October 1978. The publisher is the Organization of Iranian Moslem Students, with a post office box in Wilmette, Illinois. Its headline calls readers to defend the Lexington 11. The text tells the event from the students' side.

Iranian students stood at the back of the hall with signs and posters exposing the CIA role in Iran, the pamphlet states. The dean tried to clear them before the speech and threatened arrest. Police then arrested three Iranian students and three Americans who spoke up for them. More arrests followed during the speech, and National Guardsmen stayed for the rest of the session.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000300730003-6:
How to manage the improvement of intelligence analysis is tackled in a pair of February 1979 memoranda for the Director. A cover note dated 3 February sends a revised version, toned down so it can circulate without insulting too many people. Details tied to the national foreign assessment center are marked back in on the Director's own copy.

The main memorandum, dated 8 February 1979, warns that the problem is tough and needs patient combing. Its threads: the mental model used to frame the problem, a sorting of symptoms by the functions of intelligence, and a sorting of causes by how the community is organized. Cures must fit the causes. Existing programs are to gain five-year milestones.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000300830002-6:
A charter legislation hearing of 3 August 1978 is reported in a memorandum for the record dated 16 August 1978, OLC 0399/10. The bill is S. 2525. Three former service chiefs testified: General Samuel Wilson, General Russell Dougherty, and Admiral Elmo Zumwalt. Senator Goldwater presided, with Senators Huddleston, Chafee, and Wallop present.

Wilson and Dougherty backed the bill, urging more work on the seam between national and tactical intelligence. Zumwalt was firmly against the very idea of charter legislation. Wilson held that thirty years of experience made a charter timely and helpful. He warned that the bill's reporting duties needed trimming, and that they would spread sensitive information too widely.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000300840001-6:
United States Foreign Intelligence Operational Guidelines is a booklet by Stansfield Turner. Turner was Director of Central Intelligence. The booklet sets out the ethical and legal rules for intelligence work abroad. In his opening letter, Turner describes the grey areas officers face in the field. At times, law and rules run out. Then judgment must guide action. So must democratic ideals, and the standards of the profession itself. He explains why written standards help. They serve new officers and seasoned ones alike.

The guidelines then set out a frame for foreign intelligence work. Numbered rules follow. They cover themes such as taking part in international crime, and human rights. They also cover torture, involuntary detention, and assassination. The booklet draws together the main laws and rules that govern intelligence work. Brief notes explain the values behind them.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000401040007-6:
Monthly Schedules covering 21 August to 23 December 1977 show the Director's engagements in grid form. The Director was the Director of Central Intelligence. One block covers each day, across the autumn months. The entries compress a full official life. They list cabinet and staff meetings. They list presidential pre-briefs and briefings. Policy Review and Special Coordination Committee sessions appear. So do testimony and calls on Capitol Hill. Planning board meetings at the Agency are listed too.

Travel and public duties fill the margins. Turner appeared before the Council on Foreign Relations in New York. He addressed the Atlanta City Forum. A Naval Academy weekend is listed. So is a press tour at Hot Springs with the Business Council. Receptions and lunches appear as well. Times and venues are given in shorthand throughout.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000401180002-6:
Business Council, Homestead, Virginia, 13-14 May 1977 papers open with an aide's memo of 12 May 1977. The file is a second, larger file on the meeting. The memo sets out the trip. The official party was Admiral and Mrs. Turner, with DCI security. Dress rules called for black tie for the Friday dinner. They also called for tennis togs. An hour-by-hour schedule follows. It runs from the National Airport departure through tennis and the black-tie dinner. It covers Saturday's business meeting, and the return.

Thank-you letters follow the memo. On 20 May, Turner wrote to Thomas J. Lennon, president of the Homestead. He recalled his first visit since New Year's 1946. He also wrote to the J. Stanford Smiths, thanking them for their hospitality. Smith's reply of 19 May looks forward to meeting again. A directory of council members fills much of the file.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000501220006-6:
DCI Invitation (Social), Tuesday, 25 September 79 is a scheduling form (79-215) processing an invitation received 27 August 1979. The event is the Veterans of the O.S.S. 1979 dinner, at which the William J. Donovan Award was to be presented to Jacques Chaban-Delmas, with a reception at seven and black-tie dinner at eight in the International Ballroom West of the Washington Hilton, tickets fifty dollars.

The form carries the aide's and executive assistant's recommendation boxes, space for the Director's accept-or-regret decision and whether Mrs. Turner was invited, and routing options to the Deputy Director and others. The printed invitation itself follows, in formal script, naming the Committee of the O.S.S. as host.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000501270001-6:
July 1979 press clippings form a Central Intelligence Agency file from a treaty month. The SALT II pact with the Soviet Union filled the news. A past CIA man wrote to an Illinois paper on the pact. He argued its terms could be checked. The loss of listening posts in Iran did not end that task, he said.

Senate hearings run through the file. Two panels grilled the defense chief at length. They asked what the pact would cap. They asked how checks would work. The volume is a month of print on a hard fight. Spy data, trust and Soviet strength were the core points at stake.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601400041-6:
Executive Order 12036 gets a plain walk-through in this staff note. It is dated 2 February 1978 and numbered 21. President Carter signed the order on 24 January. Turner calls it the frame for all spy work. He picks out three main traits. Each trait bears on how the agency does its job.

Top policy makers will now help set what gets gathered. They will tie that work to funds. They will judge the end work too. A National Security Council panel handles these tasks. Turner chairs it for spy matters. The note also treats curbs on acts at home. It treats links with defense and justice as planned and shared.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601440010-6:
Dallas trip schedule for Monday 21 August fills a single timed sheet. The day starts with a 0645 departure from quarters. The Director of Central Intelligence flies from Andrews Air Force Base to Dallas. At the convention center he receives a VFW award. A luncheon address follows for the Chamber of Commerce and service groups.

A press session and a plant visit fill the afternoon. Notes on the sheet name other award guests that day. Roger Staubach was to get a hall of fame award. Anita Bryant was to get a citizenship award. A senator was set to give a report on veterans. The sheet is a minute-by-minute plan for one working trip.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601470008-6:
Harlan Cleveland wrote to Turner on July 1, 1978 with an invitation. Cleveland directed the Aspen Institute program in international affairs. The letter comes from Princeton, New Jersey. A routing slip from the agency sits at the front of the file.

The ask was to join a workshop that month at Aspen. Secrecy and open rule formed its theme. A list of invited guests sits with the letter. Names from Harvard, Berlin and Bonn appear on it. The file shows the director drawn into a small, high-level talk on secrecy. Such talks shaped how he spoke of his own trade in public that year.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601480025-6:
Economic Club of Detroit announces a national security luncheon in this notice. The date is Thursday noon, April 13, 1978. Cobo Hall in Detroit is the place. Guest of honor and speaker is Admiral Stansfield Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence,. His subject is New Directions in Intelligence.

Joseph L Hudson Jr would preside over the meal. Prices are printed on the notice: members and spouses at one rate, guests a bit higher. Seats would go in the order bookings came in. Held seats would be kept only until 12:20. The notice is a clean piece of club paper, the kind that filled the director's speaking file that spring.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601560080-6:
Herbert E Hetu heads this Central Intelligence Agency file, which holds a Council on Foreign Relations report. The report covers the Committees on Foreign Relations program in its thirty-sixth year. These committees met in cities across the country. Council members led the meetings as discussion chiefs.

Counts in the report sort the year's talks by theme. Energy and resources drew the most meetings, with multinational firms next. National security, arms control and intelligence drew twenty. Trade and money drew seven. Names of the 43 members who led meetings fill a list. The file shows how a private council spread foreign policy debate beyond Washington in that year.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s02015r000100040001-6:
Soviet Land Armaments is an intelligence handbook dated 7 June 1976. The cover marks it secret and gives it copy number 129. Release stamps show it was cleared in part, in sanitized form, in 2012. The handbook comes from the Central Intelligence Agency.

Handbooks of this kind serve as desk references for analysts. They gather what the agency held on a foe's ground-force arms in one place. Tanks, guns and like gear of the Soviet land forces form the subject, as the title states. The file holds the cover and body of a Cold War reference work, kept under tight handling rules in its day.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000100110006-6:
National Security Council Intelligence Directive No 6 treats signals intelligence in this file. It took effect on 17 February 1972 and is marked top secret. Signals intelligence covers two fields, the directive says: communications intelligence and electronics intelligence. Both are national tasks, to be run for the most gain from the means at hand.

The Director of the National Security Agency holds full control of collection and processing, the text states. Mobile platforms stay under military command in the normal case. The directive is a base rule for the listening side of spy work. Its copy in this file was reviewed by the National Security Council and cleared in sanitized form.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200420001-6:
Guido Goldman wrote on March 1, 1977 from the Council on Foreign Relations. He wrote from the Harold Pratt House in New York. The council may take in up to 20 young members each year, he notes. These seats run for five-year terms and cannot be renewed. Members must be under 31 at election.

Goldman chairs a panel charged with finding such candidates. The panel screens the young hopefuls for the membership committee. His letter to Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence, works that task: names, promise and the council's wish to renew itself. The file shows the quiet machinery by which a foreign policy club recruits its next generation.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200560033-6:
William R Kintner wrote on November 2, 1978 from the Foreign Policy Research Institute. His institute sits in Philadelphia. He encloses an article from the fall issue of Orbis. Its title is Central War and Civil Defense. T K Jones and W S Thompson wrote it.

Kintner knows both authors well, he writes. Their grasp of the subject and their integrity impress him. The article takes issue with a report Turner released on civil defense in July 1978. That report ran as a State Department special report. The file is an expert's challenge, sent with respect: a scholarly dispute over how the land would face a central war.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200650015-6:
Your 17 February meeting with the DDS&T panel gets a background memo dated 16 February 1978. A deputy executive secretary writes it for the Director of Central Intelligence. It sums up progress on the chief asks the science and technology panel made. Those asks date from their first session on 1 June 1977.

Two members of the current group sat in that first meeting, the memo notes. The summary is attached for reading before the sitting. The file is marked for internal use only. It shows the advisory system in its follow-up mode: staff panels make asks, the house reports what was done, and the director comes briefed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200660005-6:
Creation of a secretarial and clerical management advisory group is the subject of this routing file. A note on the slip tells the story in short. The idea came from the secretarial and clerical group's own recommendation. It was forwarded to the Director of Central Intelligence for follow-up. The Director approved it.

He urged Mr Blake to share any thoughts on the matter, the note adds. The sender had talked it through with Barbara Cooper. It was routed through Blake's office. As of the 25 November 1977 memo in the file, it sat on hold there. The file is a small paper trail of a staff voice being given a formal seat.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200660023-6:
Reaction to reorganization and DDO cuts fills this memo dated 31 October 1977. It is marked confidential and goes to the Director. At a meeting on 22 September, Turner had asked for reactions in the agency. The reactions were to cover two moves: a reshaping of the analytic arm, and cuts in the operations arm.

A meeting to talk them over was hoped for. The calendar allowed none for months, the writers were told. A written reply would be more timely, it was suggested. So the group writes what staff think of the two decisions. The file is frank feedback, sent up while feeling still ran fresh in the house.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200680003-6:
Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) meeting with the Management Advisory Group for the Intelligence Directorate gets an agenda for 8 June 1977. Four issues structure the hour. Communications with staff take fifteen minutes first. Communications on substantive guidelines take fifteen more. Internal coordination of intelligence takes fifteen. Interagency cooperation takes ten.

General discussion closes with five minutes. More problems are attached, not for talk at this sitting. The first issue is spelled out in the body. Colleagues in the analytic arm worry at gaps in communication, the paper says. The agenda shows analysts bringing the director a house problem of their own: how word moves, or fails to move, inside the building.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200680012-6:
Director of Central Intelligence meeting with the DDO Management Advisory Group gets an agenda for 29 July 1977. The hour runs from 1430 to 1530. The future mission of the operations arm leads, at fifteen minutes. Foreign service cover takes fifteen more.

Voluntary help from citizens and firms takes ten minutes. The operations arm's evaluation and promotion system takes ten. General discussion closes the hour. A discussion paper on the future role of the arm goes with the agenda. It weighs the arm's place within the whole community. The file shows the clandestine staff debating its own future with its chief, months before the cuts fell.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200680021-6:
Secretarial and Clerical Management Advisory Group quarterly report covers July to September 1978. A memo dated 25 October 1978 sends it to the Director and his deputy. The group chairman signs the memo. The group looks forward to more inputs on current issues, it says. An independent look at known concerns comes next.

Inside, the report sorts work as completed or in train. Questions from operations secretaries were answered: ceiling levels, the split of professional and clerical grades, and conversion to officer status. Data on clerical career paths went to the administration arm. A career booklet for the Director of Central Intelligence was in draft. The report shows a staff group with a full plate.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200690011-6:
Last general mailing from the Aspen Institute's Program in International Affairs fills this letter of June 18, 1980. Harlan Cleveland writes to colleagues and friends. He has been appointed the first full-time director of the Hubert H Humphrey Institute of Public Affairs. The post is at the University of Minnesota, from August 1, 1980.

He and his wife Lois will move to the Twin Cities in August, he writes. The program's mailing list and work would pass to other hands. The file, kept by the Central Intelligence Agency, holds more than the letter: Aspen program papers ride with it. The letter marks the end of a run in which a former envoy ran a Princeton-based forum on world affairs.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401180032-6:
An invitation form for the Director of Central Intelligence invitation form 80-280 logs a presidential inaugural celebration for 19 and 20 January 1981. An invitation card brought it, received on 14 November 1980. The celebration honored the inauguration of the President and Vice President. Donation was 135 dollars per person, the form notes. A suspense date of 19 November is marked.

The days named were the hinge of power in Washington. A new President would take the oath on 20 January. Turner, whose term ended with the old one, was asked to the parties as a guest. The file is a small marker of a change of reigns, kept on a staff form with a price and a date.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401300001-6:
Admiral Turner's long range schedule fills this file for the first months of 1981. January lists a Systems Analysis reunion dinner at Fort McNair on the 15th. It is marked as a 1962 to 1968 group. More dinners follow on the 21st and 28th, with a lunch on the 30th. Mrs Turner joins several of the entries.

February and April entries carry marks of doubt in the print. A run of mid-February dates stands out among them. The schedule reaches past the end of Turner's term at the agency. It reads as a past director's forward book: old shipmates, old staff groups and the Washington round, still filling his weeks after office.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000501360004-6:
Press clippings for the week of 21 March carry a file head of their own. Iran, few stories, the head notes. A Christian Science Monitor piece of 19 March 1980 leads the sampled pages. It treats an Iranian woman linked to the Central Intelligence Agency, with a sum of 300 dollars in the tale. The hostage crisis had quieted in print that week.

Other pages return to charters and to the wider cold war. The bundle's own head is the telling part: the clipping desk marked the week by what was missing. Iran had driven the news for months. A week with few Iran stories was worth a note on the file itself.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000501390001-6:
Press clippings for June 1980 open with a New York Times piece of 18 May. Things seem to be slipping out of control, it begins. At least, that is what a lot of Americans are saying, the writer notes. The mood of the country fills the early pages: prices, hostages and a sense of drift.

Later pages range over the campaign year and the cold war. The rescue failure in Iran still echoes in print. The file is a month's bundle from an election summer. It shows the press testing the Carter White House on competence, while the agency kept the cuttings as part of its own record of the season.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000601640020-6:
