Follow-up tasks from a 10 March talk are assigned in a short Agency memo dated 15 March 1977. Executive Secretary B. C. Evans wrote to a set distribution list. The talk was between the Director and Secretary of State Vance, and its record was attached.

Nine numbered items from that record each get an owner in the memo. Most go to the operations or analysis chiefs, with others to the Executive Secretary and aides. Replies were to pass to the deputy director's aide for review with Mr. Knoche before going to Admiral Turner. A second short note dated 14 March 1977 makes the same assignments in brief.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000601820002-6:
Plans to study the Executive Office of the President fill an information packet dated April 1977. The packet names Harrison Wellford and A. D. Frazier, Jr. as project leads at the Office of Management and Budget. Contact phone numbers for public queries are printed on the first page.

Study aims are to fit the office to the President's needs and cut waste. Work runs in four phases, from fact finding through final advice to the President. A history section traces the office from a small budget unit under Franklin D. Roosevelt to 18 units. Twelve of those units arose since 1969, the packet notes.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t02051r000200350069-6:
Arthur H. Dean, lawyer and envoy, is remembered in a New York Times obituary dated 1 December 1987. Dean died of pneumonia at Glen Cove, Long Island, at age 89. He had led talks with China and North Korea at Panmunjom after the Korean War.

Dean rose to senior partner at Sullivan and Cromwell in 1949, the obituary states. He served Presidents Eisenhower, Kennedy, and Johnson as a negotiator and adviser. Work listed includes the 1963 partial test ban talks and help drafting the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. He was born in Ithaca, New York, on 16 October 1898 and trained at Cornell.
cia-crest-cia-rdp07-00617r000100050001-6:
Economic tables for the 1958 handbook are issued as research aid CIA/RR RA-12-R2. The Office of Research and Reports compiled the volume for staff reference use. Front notes cover rounding, the mark for negligible output, and how bloc and NATO totals are built.

One table gives daily food supply per head by country across the 1950s. It sets prewar means against years 1953/54 through 1956/57 in calories per day. United States figures sit near 3,100 calories, while bloc ranges run lower and vary by state. Footnotes mark gaps where no sound figure could be found for a year.
cia-crest-cia-rdp07-00617r000100140001-6:
Copy number 107 of the 1967 handbook, marked RR H 67-1 and dated July 1967, holds economic tables. The Directorate of Intelligence issued the volume as an intelligence handbook. Profile pages give 1966 land mass, people, and gross product by bloc and state, in 1965 prices for most lands.

European NATO gross product is put at 510 billion dollars on the profile pages. The United States figure is 718 billion and Canada is 55 billion for 1966. Tables then track output across 1955, 1960, and 1966 for NATO and Communist states. Side panels give the same three years for smaller NATO lands such as Belgium, Iceland, and Portugal. Footnotes sort out price bases, GDP versus GNP, and years used for each land.
cia-crest-cia-rdp07-00617r000200220001-6:
Marked Confidential on its cover, the 1974 handbook copy number 11 was prepared by the Office of Economic Research. Scope notes give figures for chosen non-Communist lands and all Communist lands. Most tables run from 1965 to 1973. A sources section closes the front matter of the volume.

Totals are rounded to three key digits, and parts may not sum for that reason. The mark N.A. flags missing data and Negl. flags sums too small to count. The metric system is used in all tables throughout the book. One table tracks electric power output in billion kilowatt-hours across 1965 to 1973. OECD output in that table rises from 2,430 to 4,300 over the span. United States output there rises from 1,229.64 to 2,074.10, with hydro power listed apart.
cia-crest-cia-rdp10-00105r000402950001-6:
Raising intelligence work to modern needs is urged in a Soviet article by Major-General Ya. Malakhov. The piece replies to an article by Lieutenant-General M. Kochetkov on lag in field intelligence. Malakhov grants the main points but adds faults of his own.

No single body guides field intelligence in the Soviet army, he argues. That gap leaves means of finding facts far behind means of striking, in his view. Staffing draws sharp words too, with one district cited in detail. In the Belorussian district only 20 percent of intelligence officers held higher schooling, he states. He calls for a full rebuild of officer training for the arm.
cia-crest-cia-rdp10-01569r000100030020-6:
Merging static intelligence work into the Central Intelligence Group is weighed in C.I.G. 13, dated 17 September 1946. The enclosed report comes from the Chief of Naval Intelligence. James S. Lay, Jr. sent it for talk at the next board meeting.

War and Navy studies had each found parts of static work fit for joint effort. Both studies held that joint parts should be housed in one place. The two departments pause their study until the Group's fit for the task is judged. The paper cites the President's letter of 22 January 1946 as the grant for such work. A joint study is urged to settle the point.
cia-crest-cia-rdp10t01930r000200080013-6:
Custody of Senate inquiry records at the National Security Agency is governed by a draft resolution in this file. A covering memo dated 12 January 1976 comes from Alfred Goldberg, OSD Historian. It goes to Mr. S. D. Breckinridge, Chief of the Agency Review Staff.

The draft covers records made or received by the Senate Select Committee on intelligence work. That body was set up under Senate Resolution 21 of the 94th Congress, the text states. Requests for such records must come in writing from the source agency's named officer. That officer must check that proper clearances are held by the person asking. Later clearing down of the records stays with the source agencies under law.
cia-crest-cia-rdp13x00001r000100290007-6:
Letters on a trip through Iceland fill a short file whose inner stamps name a twin record number. Hosted text governs here, and it treats passage via Iceland in wartime. A Donovan letter dated 2 January names a London staff post set to gather and weigh facts for the government.

Men named as proceeding to London via Iceland include Morris Gilbert, Percy Winner, and Theodore Olson. Winfield L. Anshime, Edward B. Harlan, and William F. Tan are also listed in the letter. Donovan asks that the men be let pass through Iceland with due courtesy. A further note treats a man who wishes his talks kept secret from his own office. He would answer a call to a cocktail party at any time, the note states.
cia-crest-cia-rdp13x00001r000100390006-6:
Mixed memos on France, morale, and secret craft fill a 1942 file catalogued under four heads. Heads listed name Japanese intrigue, de Gaulle and the state of France, a plan to weaken civilian morale in Axis lands, and letters on sabotage and a special agent. Early letters are offers of help to the new office.

A letter dated 5 September 1941 from a past comrade seeks a role in Southern California. Donovan replies on 9 December 1941 to a Hollywood address, 6545 Primrose Avenue. He thanks the writer for a wire and states nothing can be done at that time. Later pages turn to Army postal rules for officers bound overseas, dated March 1943 as printed. Mail was to be routed through the New York postmaster under those rules.
cia-crest-cia-rdp13x00001r000100430001-6:
Personnel security work fills the legible core of a wartime file catalogued under bombing and China heads. The catalogue line also names chemical and biological warfare and the censorship office. Scan quality is very rough at the head of the file held here.

Mid-file pages give a Security Office assessment of an employee and his past views. A professor who knew him at Ohio State is quoted on his time in Columbus. The witness doubted he had acted for Communism while there, the assessment reports. He is drawn as a liberal who backed broad federal powers yet opposed Communism. The scan mangles personal names in these pages, so no name is stated here. Early pages hold a Donovan visa plea dated September 1945.
cia-crest-cia-rdp13x00001r000100470007-6:
Joint Intelligence Committee reports from London fill a file catalogued for the London office and European work. Inner stamps in the copy held here name a twin record number, and hosted text governs. A report dated 18 November 1942 tracks the advance against Rommel in Africa.

British forces had reached Tobruk on the 13th, that report states. The port was found near intact and opened for use on the 16th. Enemy forces set to gather at El Agheila are put at 40,000 Germans and 30,000 Italians, with 10,000 support troops. A covering memo dated 7 December 1942 from William L. Langer sends the weekly report to Colonel Donovan. Later pages weigh German air strength against the Russian front.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000100100002-6:
Film handling for Far East AQUATONE flights is set out in a paper dated 22 April 1957. Detachment C is defined as the project unit at Atsugi Naval Air Station, Japan. The paper fixes who must move, process, and report on exposed film abroad.

The detachment chief must ship all exposed film fast for processing and reading. Theatre staff must process film, title all copies kept on site, and draft a first photo report for each flight. That report goes to AQUATONE headquarters at once or at routine speed, as ordered. Reports on flights into Soviet bloc areas are classed as Ode Reports. All AQUATONE goods stay Top Secret CHESS within the TALENT system.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000100430033-6:
A radar absorber test plan is sent to Lincoln Laboratories in a Wright Air Development Center letter. The enclosed report, 57 WCLR-3116, was written by W. F. Bahret of the Center. Charles N. Keller signs the letter as chief of the design branch.

The test, named Passport Visa, gauges absorber cloth built for aircraft skin use. Lab work under Project 6268 had fixed the cloth's traits in small shapes only. Full effect on a whole aircraft can be learned only in flight, the outline states. A T-33 was thus assigned as the flying test bed. Beam angle must shift so hits fall on the beam's nose, the study finds.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000200350103-6:
High altitude air turbulence is measured in NACA Research Memorandum RM L57A11. Gust data come from VGH records taken on Lockheed U-2 research flights. Flights reached 55,000 feet over England and Western Europe, the summary states.

Gust counts and force both fall as height grows, the study finds. The work ran with the Air Weather Service from early 1956. About 22,000 flight miles of data were weighed for this first report. Gust speeds run near three quarters of the older United States figures at like heights. One band, 30,000 to 40,000 feet, breaks the pattern and is flagged as open to doubt.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000300250022-6:
Joint airborne operations are framed in a draft agreement dated 24 February 1967. The two sides would fly photo, electronic, and other special missions together. One side provides the base and its facilities for the project.

The pact runs three years, with talks due three months before it ends. Either side may end it on six months notice, the draft states. The United States side supplies special gear, spares, and upkeep for the work. Both sides plan each mission jointly and share go and no-go calls. United States and third country approvals for each mission rest with the United States side.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400250012-6: Bundle of Project Headquarters document receipt forms and filing slips, sent out on 16 August 1973 under office symbol 344. The slips record numbered papers moving in copies of two. Documents named include 2589-63 of Series B and 1993-62 and 1994-62 of Series D. Filing slips give subjects such as OSA procurement authority and designation of the OSA contracting officer, dated August and September 1962. Each form sends a signed buff copy back to the originator, a green copy to the recipient's file, and a pink copy into suspense.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400380207-6:
Memorandum dated 29 May 1956, addressed to Mr Bissell, lists items on which the writer has taken action. A communications officer is to be sent to a station as soon as possible, so the site is ready to operate by 15 July. A security officer should also visit Adana and the second base, to learn the security picture at first hand.

Ground transport in Turkey is reshaped on local advice: sedans are dropped for jeeps, carryalls, and field ambulances for Adana. A traveller bound for Europe around 6 July is given leave to visit the bases and will be cleared for entry. Other items hold back one man's short trip until a decision lands on how to operate in his area, and reroute engines shipped from the Pratt and Whitney factory straight overseas.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000500070002-6:
Memorandum BH-2753-65 from Jack C. Ledford, Brigadier General and Director of Program B in the NRO, sends the Director of the National Reconnaissance Office a set of briefing outlines. They were prepared for the Dr Land Panel of the President's Scientific Advisory Committee, set to meet on 21 July 1965. Four outlines are attached, covering OXCART, ISINGLASS, and further program matter left redacted.

The OXCART outline, timed at fifteen minutes, lists inlet and electronic inlet control troubles, equipment reliability, and range performance as current problems. A modification program aims to standardise the latest build, adding strength, range, and countermeasures fit, and BLACK SHIELD plans are given their own heading. The ISINGLASS outline allows thirty minutes and works from history and requirement through airframe and engine, with high pressure engine technology given a section of its own.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600040077-6:
Staff duty cover outside work hours is reset in an updated SOP H-20-3, dated 22 February 1973, which replaces an August 1972 version. The Staff Duty Officer acts as the point for choices and actions on weekends, holidays, and other non-working days. He stands in when the detachment commander is not present on the base.

Almost all staff can be given this duty: civilian, military, and technical representatives alike. Communications operators and contract security assistants are the only groups left out. The text gives holiday tour start times, message handling rules, and when the duty officer may go home if no mission alert comes in. Overtime pay or equal time off is provided.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600070001-6:
Base Radiological Defense Plan, dated 2 January 1969, aims to guard staff and aircraft on its station from radiation exposure after a nuclear event. The scan is rough, but the plan's shape is clear. It applies to all military and civilian staff on the station and sets named roles, starting with a Chief Evacuation Officer and a convoy officer for vehicles and gear.

Action runs in phases. Staff are told to take cover in named shelter buildings, among them buildings 120 and 133 to 136 as printed. Section heads report when their people are gathered. Later steps cover securing classified material, locking safes and doors, and an aircraft with a security observer circling while the base stands empty.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600070010-6:
Aircraft fire cover outside emergencies is the subject of standing operating procedure 50-3092-1, dated 26 May 1966. It applies to base staff in air traffic control, aircraft maintenance, and ground support work. The aim is a shared, clear grasp of who does what in the local fire cover program during normal flying.

The control tower tells the base fire department about touch and go landings, low approaches, and any pilot request for extra runway standby cover. Base Operations passes word of unscheduled arrivals and changes. Later pages set strict rules for Teb servicing work, keeping other staff clear of the aircraft's aft section. A real emergency takes priority over all standby duties.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800020004-6:
Memorandum 8998-69, dated 17 July 1969, sends the quarterly reports for OXCART and IDEALIST, 1 April to 30 June 1969, to the Director, CIA Reconnaissance Programs. Donald H. Ross signs as Director of Special Activities. Status notes at the end record aircraft working from Palmdale during runway repair at Edwards Air Force Base, and one U-2R at Lockheed for update.

Inside, an H camera fault is traced to noise spikes from the camera itself, with fixes being tested by the maker and at Detachment G. The drag reduction effort is also redirected: a retrofit path for the U-2R lost too much effect, so the program moved away from retrofit toward a fresh arrangement.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800030003-6:
Quarterly IDEALIST packet dated 11 April 1973 covers 1 January to 31 March 1973, signed by Wendell L. Bevan Jr. Flight totals rise this quarter: 208 flights and 586.3 hours across the four U-2R aircraft listed. The report follows the usual split between an operational summary and a development summary for the Director, CIA Reconnaissance Programs.

The H configuration lens, serial 002, was still at the contractor's plant at quarter's end, after poor flight test results sent it back in December. The B configuration section turns to the first B-3 system with the new apochromatic lens. Training notes include pressure suit chamber flights at Detachment G, with some suits needing factory rework for fit, and Arctic survival training in the Sierra Mountains in January.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800050001-6:
Memorandum 8845-70, dated 13 October 1970, from Harold F. Knowles, forwards the IDEALIST report for 1 July to 30 September 1970. The development summary opens with a T-35 tracker item. Pilot and aircraft status tables at the end place U-2R and older U-2C and U-2G aircraft at Detachment G, Edwards Air Force Base North Base. Further detachments are listed in the same table.

Personnel work takes much of the report. Four officers were weighed for entry into the project during the fall. Interviews were held in Washington by Air Force Surgeon General staff and project doctors. Wives of the officers were interviewed by company psychologists. A 25 September 1970 meeting at Lockheed, Burbank, took up a six-line release proposal for control of parachutes during descent.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800300012-6:
Essay dated 1965, by the Chief, Intelligence Branch, Office of Special Activities, surveys what the U-2 program had achieved. Before the program, the writer argues, the United States relied on classical intelligence sources against the threat of a Soviet surprise attack. Those sources gave much knowledge, but left hard questions about Soviet power, its growth rate, and its aims, all difficult to verify or read with confidence.

U-2 photography then answered set questions. Over a hundred fighter airfields were photographed, showing how the Soviets used fighters for air defense and how fast that system reacted, read against radar intercepts. Surface-to-air defenses are treated next. The file ends with press material quoting former President Eisenhower taking public responsibility for the high altitude spy flights.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800320001-6:
Briefing book on the Office of Special Activities opens with a mission statement and a tabbed index. The mission is printed in full: to develop, attain, and maintain an operational capability to conduct manned covert aerial reconnaissance of denied areas. Tabs that follow cover OSA organization, agreements with the Office of Special Projects, the NRO agreement, policy, program funding, and personnel strength projections for the office.

Papers inside include a 15 September 1965 memorandum on setting up an Office of Special Projects. Contracting and security separation between OSA and OSP is argued in the text. The book closes with the program funding agreement, signed by John A. McCone for CIA on 5 April 1963 and by Roswell Gilpatric for Defense on 4 April 1963, as an appendix to the NRO agreement.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800340018-6:
Progress form on the historical record of OSA, as of 15 March 1968, is a filled-in status sheet for the DDS&T Historical Board. The main report is marked sixty-five percent complete, with a deadline of 1 June 1968. Typed pages total 761, of which 235 are double spaced chronology pages and 526 are annex pages, with a further 235 annexes listed as planned.

An OSA history outline follows, chapter by chapter, from background and the Land Panel recommendation through detachment histories. Chapters cover Detachment C, Detachment G with the Cuban Missile Crisis, and Detachment H with the TACKLE program. A closing note warns the history's author was moved to other tasks, delaying completion by several months.
cia-crest-cia-rdp51-00036a000100050010-6:
Office memorandum dated 20 May 1948, from the Chief, Presentation Division, appraises that division after six months under its present chief. It does not replace a November 1947 study on staffing needs. This appraisal turns instead to the division's mission inside CIA and the problems that mission raises. The basic mission is to provide oral, visual, and graphic intelligence aids for the whole agency.

Responsibility is the central problem, the memo argues, since presentation work touches every branch's material. Later sections propose work for the Situation Room: large portable map and chart studies, six by eight feet, built from branch data and removed each day for safekeeping. Staffing asks close the memo, including one visual information clerk and, if possible, one cartographic engineer.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000100140011-6:
Second copy of a 12 August 1953 memorandum to the Acting Deputy Director for Administration, on the proposal to transfer General Services functions elsewhere. Its argument matches the other copy in this slice: the case for transfer rests on an unproven belief in greater efficiency and savings. The memo's author asks that the case be tested before any decision is taken, rather than assumed from the proposal alone.

Recommendations are set out in order. First, sort out the functions of General Services, Logistics, and the Comptroller with the staff concerned. Next, compare how General Services has performed its present functions with how those functions were performed when other offices held them. The file then repeats the office history, from its 1947 services branch form through the 1952 transfer of garage and trucking work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200030003-6:
Memorandum dated 15 July 1951, from the Chief, Property Control Division, sends a revised draft of proposed agency property regulations. The draft runs to a full code. Its table of contents opens with authority, purpose, and definitions. It then draws a line the whole code rests on. Accountability and responsibility are distinct, and an officer may hold one without the other.

Later sections cover the appointment of accountable officers, transfer of property between accounts, and routine transactions. Loan rules require a signed hand receipt kept in a suspense file until the item returns. Loans to other government agencies must pass through the Property Control Division. Closing pages treat property being repaired and the clearance memoranda that follow staff leaving a station and arriving in Washington.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200030111-6:
CIA regulation on transportation, numbered in the file only by redacted marks, opens with travel orders. Orders are issued by the Transportation Division of the Administrative Services Office. Chiefs of mission abroad may issue orders only inside their own theaters, for staff under them. They may not issue orders for travel to or from the United States, or for a change of station outside the theater.

Requests for orders route through office heads, or through the Personnel Director for changes of station and first postings abroad. Military staff travel is handled by the Military Personnel Division once the Transportation Division approves. The file's last pages are heavily marked by hand and largely illegible, but the printed rules on order authority and routing remain readable throughout the main text.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200030139-6:
Memorandum on allotment account charges for fiscal year 1951 assigns common costs to the accounts that must bear them. Its stated aim is to cut the confusion of the past fiscal year over which account a charge belongs to. Transportation items lead: travel, apart from unvouchered travel, is charged to the branch the traveler belongs to. Freight on goods bought free on board at origin follows the account that paid for the goods themselves.

Postage stamps stocked by the Supply Branch go to the Stock Account. Washington telephone and teletype charges, including switchboard rental and installations, are grouped under their own heading. Standard office furniture and equipment carried in stock also fall to the Stock Account. Special gear, such as printing presses, microfilm machines, and cameras, is charged to the office that asked for it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200050083-6:
General Services Administration Public Buildings Service Circular No. 1, dated 8 March 1950, sets government wide rules for excess and surplus real property. It is issued under the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act of 1949. The circular prescribes how agencies report property held beyond need. It also covers how that property is put to use elsewhere in government. What remains is disposed of as surplus.

Contents run from definitions and basic policy to holding agency duties, records and reports, and exceptions. Leasehold disposal methods are spelled out in the body. They include transfer of the lease interest for fair value, and disposal under existing contract terms. Transfer to the lessor against restoration duties, or disposal for removal from the site, are also listed. A lease clearance form at the end is signed by the administration's authorized official.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200050155-6:
Public Law 585, 79th Congress, is the Atomic Energy Act of 1946, approved 1 August 1946, printed in full. Its declaration of policy states that large scale release of atomic energy is now practical, that the atomic bomb's military weight is evident, and that civilian effects cannot yet be judged. Policy is therefore set toward the public welfare, under the paramount aim of common defense and security, with revision expected as knowledge grows.

The act builds a licensing and control system run by a commission. No license may issue where it would harm the common defense and security, the text states. Byproduct power made while producing fissionable material may be used by the commission, transferred to other agencies, or sold to utilities at reasonable resale prices. International arrangements are defined as treaties or agreements approved by the Senate or Congress.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200100005-6:
Monthly report of operations for the period ending 31 May 1953, from the Chief, Records Management and Distribution Branch. Personnel notes place one records analyst on detail to the Jackson Commission, and one man full time as a courier in the Transportation Division. Nine Mail Control staff and four Records Center staff were on leave of three days or more. Four new applicants were interviewed; Personnel recruited three of them and the branch itself one.

Courier service figures fill much of the report. They cover scheduled trips, and special trips within the agency by foot and vehicle. Trips for other agencies, and trips outside the area, are also counted, with postage expended tabled. File activity counts time spent checking courier receipts and requests for administrative files filled and unfilled. Filming totals since July 1952 pass 1.4 million images, split between flatbed and rotary cameras.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00252a000100020001-6:
Vacancy notice V-2 describes an Instructor, Research post on the Training Staff, Staff Training Division, serving the offices marked OSO and COPS. The instructor works under the Chief of the Staff Training Division, with guidance from the Chief Instructor. Duties open with research: he conducts studies, writes study guides and operational manuals, and keeps up his own knowledge of intelligence work.

Teaching fills the rest of the statement. He prepares and delivers formal lectures on operational topics to students of the Intelligence Officers Course. He gives students individual instruction for overseas operational assignments. He devises practical problems and work-sample situations, and guides student conferences on operational problems and on accounts from the field. Returned field staff are interviewed for their experience and suggestions, and the instructor takes an active role in those talks.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00001a000100050023-6:
Memorandum from the Director of Training to all Assistant Directors sums up discussion of the Social Science Research Council project for training area specialists. Ten agencies met under Bureau of the Budget chairmanship, with the council and the American Council of Learned Societies. The aim is threefold at its head: to add area knowledge to a trade skill, as with an economist who also understands Burma. Joint handling of government needs is called a must.

Positions are recorded agency by agency. Defense would not oppose the plan if others backed it, but would give no funds. It would expect a fair share of students. Army benefit is noted in the text. The file closes with a draft letter for the President, covering better use of staff already in government and a call to cut recruiting of university staff.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00001a000100050041-6:
Second set of summary minutes covers the 22 March 1951 informal meeting on training area specialists, at Room 500 of the Foreign Service Institute. Those present match the other copy in this slice. Hopkins held the chair, with Baird and others for CIA. Staff came from State, the services, the Office of Education, the Budget Bureau, and the two councils. Faculty retention again opens the talks, with the same doubts about a no-recruiting pledge.

This copy adds fuller later items. A survey of laws concludes that a general law is needed, to let agencies send staff to area centers, fund fellowships, and make grants to universities. The meeting adjourned at 5:03 p.m. A first committee meeting was set for 5 April, and Bryce Wood signed the minutes.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00001a000100140014-6:
List of training courses run outside O/TR by offices under the DD/A is a short tabular survey. Inspection and Security shows its opening course on CIA functions and the techniques of its investigators. It runs three weeks, at five week intervals since May 1951. About thirty lecturers serve, and some seventeen students sit in a class. Medical training for technicians bound for the field has a present class of four, taught by a medical officer and a technician.

Finance training is described in fuller prose. Assignments run from one week to three months. One finance officer gives full time to watching over the on-the-job training, and twenty-seven people are in it at the time of writing. The method is learning by doing: reading the rules, discussion, practice work on accounts, and real account work under close watch.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00011a000100070011-6:
Draft memorandum to Training Liaison Officers announces overseas training programs built by the Office of Training. Like the January 1953 notice in this slice, it bars operational work and official contact with Agency staff during training. The programs give area and language training and experience, chiefly for headquarters staff. Other programs can be built on request, the memo adds.

Program A is a two year, full time Near East program. One year of hard area and language study in the United States is followed by a year of study at a United States government facility in the region. Program B is a two year program for area experience and language study in South Asia, the Middle East, and Africa, one person to a country. Program E is a summer seminar for analysts of grades GS-9 to GS-13, with six weeks abroad and about fifteen places.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00110a000100070011-6:
First draft of a statement of management policy for supervisors in CIA, marked Security Information and covering all Agency staff except those in clandestine field work. Its stated aim is a shared grasp of management aims among supervisors, so the Agency might become the best managed body in government. Management is defined as getting work done through people.

Later sections set out who answers for the policy, starting with the Deputy Director of Central Intelligence and the deputy directors below him. Supervision is described as running from unit chief up to the Director. The draft warns that staff picked for skill in a subject often reach charge of others with no past practice in supervising, and that neglect of management duties breaks an organization down.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00071a000100030027-6:
Sanitized Central Intelligence Agency regulation on allowances. It sets the principles for running such payments. Base salary is full pay for the work itself. Pay does not rest on place. Allowances are grants of a different kind. They draw staff to a set overseas place. They also repay costs that home work would not cause. Each job's pay should be fixed first. That fixing rests on the job's own worth.

Allowances need set tests to be met. The facts of a job must meet those tests. Bargaining plays no part in the system. A person cannot bargain with the Agency over them. Bargaining would undo the fairness of average rates. All staff must be treated on the same footing. The kinds of payment are then taken up. Incentive payments come first in the text. The quarters allowance is explained there. It applies when the government cannot supply housing.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000080174-6:
File on a transportation requirement, opening with a memorandum. It went to the Chief, Office of Logistics. Passengers and classified material needed air movement. Daily amounts are estimated in the memo. At least two aircraft should be committed to the work. Those aircraft would fly the trips as analyzed. Timing is tied to late April readiness.

Extra aircraft would be needed on short notice. That need was small at first, the memo states. It would probably grow as operations grew. A meeting in late April closed the discussion. A transportation representative would attend that meeting. Agency contract papers follow in the same file. One names a corporation at Friendship International Airport. That airport sits in Baltimore, Maryland. The contract amount runs to about a million dollars. Advance payment clauses fill the later pages.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000080183-6:
Memorandum from 1956 giving information on insurance. Life and health insurance for Agency project personnel is the subject. Sender and receiver names are redacted in the copy. Life cover could be bought through a named company. An Army and Navy association policy is described. Double indemnity forms part of that cover. Cover runs until age sixty-five in the terms.

A table sets out the life benefit classes. Early classes pay a flat three thousand dollars. Later classes rise to six and nine thousand. The top visible class pays eighteen thousand dollars. Accidental death benefit is listed beside the sums. Monthly premium per thousand is also tabulated. Health cover fills the later pages. Hospital benefits run up to five thousand dollars. Ambulance transfer is capped at fifteen dollars. Other medical service limits are listed too.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000120061-6:
Agency letter contract number CS-100 with Hycon Manufacturing Company. The company sat in Pasadena, California. An order takes effect on 1 April 1956. Services run through 30 June 1956 under it. The contractor must furnish qualified engineers and technicians. Other required personnel are covered by the order too. Those people were picked and trained under an earlier contract.

Services go to places the government designates. Places outside the continental United States are included. Pay rates were settled outside the letter itself. Correspondence and tentative agreements record those rates. Incentive provisions were settled the same way. Direct and indirect cost terms follow that record. A definitive contract was still to be negotiated. Progress payments rest on submitted cost figures meanwhile. Salary rates and indirect costs form that basis. The contractor's own submitted estimates supply the figures.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000130042-6:
Standalone set of general provisions for government contracts. An index lists the provisions in order. Definitions head the list of clauses. Changes, extras, and limitation of claims follow. Federal, state, and local taxes are covered. Default and records duties appear early too. Buy American and convict labor clauses are listed. The eight-hour law of 1912 is named.

Walsh-Healey Act terms appear in the index. Nondiscrimination in employment is covered as well. Officials not to benefit forms one clause. Covenant against contingent fees forms another. Royalties reporting and authorization clauses follow. Patent rights and filing of applications close the list. Disputes and termination provisions end the index. The full text of each provision follows. Patent clauses run long in that text. Payment can be withheld over missing certificates. Invention disclosures drive that withholding rule.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000180074-6:
Negotiated Agency contract number HF-B-5111B, in a very long file. The contractor was an atomic instrument company in Cambridge. Its address was 33 University Road there. Target price reads as 464,627 dollars in the head. Ceiling price reads as 503,027 dollars in the head. The parties executed the contract on 25 July 1956. Inspection point was Cambridge, Massachusetts.

The contractor must furnish facilities under the deal. It must deliver supplies and perform services too. Those duties are set out in the attached schedule. Appendix one forms part of the contract set. In any clash, the schedule controls the outcome. Corporate certification pages follow the signatures. Patent duties run deep in the provisions text. Infringement claims must be reported promptly to the officer. Written detail in reasonable measure is required. Litigation against the government gets its own rule. The contractor must furnish evidence in such cases.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00012a000200090006-6:
Draft memorandum dated 3 August 1948 on technical training. It comes from the covert training arm of the office. Recent conversations with two offices prompted a review. Present programs and future plans were both reviewed. Some training duplicates work done elsewhere, it states. Two other components are named for that overlap. Closer joining with intelligence training is needed.

Past effort went to intelligence training for a year and a half. Agency staff and covert programs were both built then. The coming year shifts the weight of effort. Administration training will get more attention. Language and area studies will get more too. Technical aids to operations get the most weight. Their use is defensive and offensive both. No solid definition of technical exists yet. That lack makes discussion hard, the memo admits. Integrated techniques teaching is argued later. Men who know intelligence and counter-intelligence should teach it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00012a000200090042-6:
Agency memorandum dated 23 January 1953 requesting a forum. Informal discussion of investigative techniques training is sought. Four earlier papers are cited as references. They date from June 1952 to January 1953. One proposed revising the investigative techniques instruction. One was an orientation paper on operational use. Differences of opinion had grown around the program.

One side sees the program as a major training part. The other stresses full commitment before proceeding further. The writer repeats an earlier suggestion in the memo. A skill of this kind grows only through practice. Skiing ability is offered as the comparison. It is actually accomplished through experience alone. A qualified man was requested back in June. He would help develop this program. That request had been repeated on numerous occasions. Nothing had come of it by the memo date. The scan is partly garbled in its later pages.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00012a000600220007-6:
Summary of interviews with consumers and instructors. Training evaluation reports are the subject of the interviews. Most users treat reports as one factor among many. Assignment, transfer, and promotion choices draw on them. Some users weight instructor comments very heavily. Others give those remarks only slight attention. Their subjective nature is the reason given. No user wanted trait ratings eliminated, though.

Limits of basic courses as judging settings are recognized. Few decisions rest on the reports alone. Mental abilities data would be welcome, users said. Behavior and personality data would be welcome too. Agency administration and intelligence supervisors wanted skill appraisal most. Report writing and research skills were their focus. Plans supervisors stressed personality appraisal more heavily. Users wanted course objectives explained in more detail. Precise meanings of grades were also wanted.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100020001-6:
Memorandum for the Director of Central Intelligence. Depletion of the Director's Ceiling Reserve is its subject. It came through the Deputy Director and the Administration deputy. The problem is stated as a plain question. A reservoir of civilian ceiling positions is needed. The Director's reserve for that purpose is shrinking. Facts bearing on the problem follow the question.

Agency civilian ceiling is given as of 31 August 1954. Key figures are redacted in the released copy. Unused ceiling slots sit across six major components. Their spread is fairly equitable, the memo states. A tab traces ceiling against staff on duty. Eleven recent months are covered by that tab. Ceiling rose slightly while staff on duty fell. The gap between them stays fairly constant. Attrition and recruitment problems keep it open. Options include recapturing unused ceiling for the reserve. Casuals' ceiling could also be recaptured.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100090004-6:
Survey report on machine methods and Agency operations. A comprehensive survey was conducted across offices. Present applications of machines are covered first. Projects in development form the second phase. Possible future applications form the third phase. A space plan for staff and machines closes it. Good progress in adapting machines is found. Problems unsolvable by hand were solved that way.

Centralization of machines is common knowledge as best. It is not practical for CIA at this time. Physical spread of offices blocks that step. Security factors block it as well. Six places would hold machine operations under the plan. Compartmenting a machine room could supply security. Wider usage of machines is urged in the findings. Payroll work shows the depth of the survey. Pay elements are computed before journals are prepared. Employee checks and earnings records follow automatically. Cost distribution to stations is balanced against payroll.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100100002-6:
Instructions for transmission and inventory of Top Secret documents. Three objectives open the instruction set. A simple, uniform control system is the first. It covers documents moving between areas and outside agencies. Up-to-date location data is the second objective. The Central Top Secret Control Office holds that data. Accountability for all control numbers is included. Periodic inventories with little time spent come third.

Equipment required is listed after the objectives. A receipt form in quadruplicate is named first. Filing gear for receipts is named second. IBM drawers serve areas with heavy volume. Actions to be discontinued are listed next. One old document receipt form is dropped. Submission of a Top Secret log ends as well. Procedure for receipts is spelled out in steps. The green copy returns to the sender. The yellow copy goes to the central office. That office sits in M Building.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100100011-6:
Report dated 5 April 1952 on Administrative Services. Its area Top Secret control office is the subject. A sub-station is covered in the same report. An Organization and Methods examiner wrote it. Survey dates ran from 1 to 3 April 1952. Compliance with basic Agency regulations was the aim. Uniform operating methods across CIA were the goal.

The records management sub-station was examined in the visit. A reproduction sub-station was examined as well. The travel sub-station was skipped by the examiner. No Top Secret traffic had ever flowed there. Departures from the basic system are listed first. Both alternate control officers are officials, it notes. Neither concerns himself with actual operation of the office. An operating alternate was suggested in reply. Outside processing of material raises a concern later. Such movement outside CIA cannot always be avoided. Strict control of the documents is exercised regardless.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200020019-6:
Memorandum dated 29 August 1950 on a services officer plan. Establishment of one officer for each CIA building is studied. The Audit Section wrote it for the Services Division chief. A conversation of 1 August 1950 prompted the study. Advantages are viewed from an audit standpoint. Better property records lead the list of gains. Accountable officers now serve only part-time in that role.

Their small share of time leaves records poorly kept. A services officer would keep records accurate and current. Better accountability of property follows in the study. Several accounts now sit in each building. Keeping property apart by account is very hard. Eleven accounts in a set of buildings are counted. Requisitions reach accountable officers from many hands. Those officers sign most requests without checking need. Control of Agency property is inadequate as a result. One office was not staffed to perform the function.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200120018-6:
Written supplement on use of punch card gear. Agency use for fiscal year 1953 is tabled. Section XXX carries the summary story. Types of gear are listed with counts used. Interpreters and sorters head the visible table. Collators and reproducing punches appear in it. Percentage of time used is given per machine. Treasury Disbursing Officer gear is listed separately.

Verifiers sit in that second gear table. Accounting machines and collators appear there too. Test scoring machines show a listed share. Facsimile machines close the tabled gear. Remarks follow the gear tables in the text. Higher use of some types is hard to get. Such gear serves more as a research tool. Indexed intelligence data is searched with it. Routine periodic reports are less its product. The Organization and Methods Service reviews this area. Advice on steps in this work falls in its charge.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200150006-6:
Translation of a Soviet article on machine technique. Scientific information is its field of concern. L. I. Gutenmakher is the named author. The journal of the USSR Academy of Sciences carried it. Issue number eight of 1962 holds the piece. A radical change in information methods is promised. Better organization of scientific research would result. Application of advances into the national economy follows.

The problem was set by the Academy's president. A. N. Nesmeyanov framed that basic complex problem. Growth of scientific works created an avalanche. Printed material now entangles scientists and engineers. Total printed output runs to hundreds of millions. Present growth rates drive that accumulation onward. Bibliography alone often fails the inquirer later. Content analysis of articles is what users need. Chemical kinetics material illustrates that need clearly. Data on mechanics of chemical reactions is gathered. Material is collected and arranged per stated problem.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200150015-6:
Part ten of the Agency indexing study covers coding relations between index entries. Many searches raise no doubt about links. Things, acts, and traits combine in them. Their nature permits little uncertainty about interrelation. Oranges are imported to Boston from California. They are never imported the other way around. In general, uncertainty is often probable.

Ways of coding stated links are the subject. Machine searching must capture those links somehow. Giving meaning to listing order is one path. Present machines make that path tangled. Machines likely soon remain unsuited to it. A system of role indicators is more practical. Symbols would carry the link meaning in entries. Other paths receive analysis in the text. One path repeats a symbol for each party. The relation itself gets coded twice thereby. Gives and receives form that worked example. Complexity grows fast in richer situations. Questions of use follow from that growth.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100150074-6:
Memo setting up a Service of Strategic Information. Strategy without reliable information is helpless, it opens. Information aimless toward war purpose is useless. Modern warfare depends upon the economic base. Raw material supply forms part of that base. Factory plant capacity and performance form more. Farm output scope matters to war strength. Signal character and power matter as well.

Strategic reserves determine strength of attack and defense. Steel and gasoline count as such reserves. Men and powder are not the only reserves. Total war commits all national resources together. Moral as well as material resources are committed. Foreseeing enemy calling-up plans is a hard task. A passage from General von Bernhardi is quoted. The service itself would collect fitting information. Existing government departments could also collect for it. Home and abroad collection both fall in scope. Potential enemies are the information targets named.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100150083-6:
Notes for public utterances on Agency functions. Preliminary comments divide the audiences into three. Statements to the general public form the first. Uncleared groups with intelligence training form the second. Cleared groups with considerable knowledge form the third. Basic thoughts hold the same line throughout. The speaker's problems differ sharply by audience though.

With the public it is purely an information problem. The ordinary person has barely heard of the Agency. Reserve type groups want techniques and functions. Highly cleared groups like the War College know much. Specific problems and operations interest those audiences. Any outline must stay completely flexible therefore. These notes approach the uninformed public mainly. An outline rather than a speech results. Statutory provisos receive treatment in the body. No police or subpoena powers are allowed. No law enforcement or internal security functions exist. Police powers that could grow a Gestapo are barred.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100170018-6:
Untitled letter copy reviewing the counsel office. Three days were spent with the Agency's General Counsel. Eric Hager accompanied the writer throughout the visit. The time was necessarily brief overall. Sufficient personnel and sources were consulted anyway. A clear picture of the office emerged. Its relation to other Agency departments was covered.

The better part of three days went to Houston. Other staff members were interviewed at length. Operating department members were talked with briefly. The general nature of their legal problems was sought. The Agency Loyalty Board was investigated at length. Its composition and procedure received that study. Other discharge methods were discussed in the visit. One rests on the National Security Act. Administrative discharge is the second method named. Several actual loyalty cases were discussed in detail. Overall figures on both were obtained there. Official procedures of two boards were read. Recommendations on lawyer placement close the letter.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000200090016-6:
A memorandum for the record dated 26 August 1952 reports a visit by Landrum Bolling and Kay Sisto of the Overseas News Agency. Bolling, once a wartime foreign reporter, had bought the agency with a partner and taken over in May 1952. The agency had been known in the trade as slanted, heavily backed by Zionist funds and closely tied to the Jewish Telegraph Agency. Bolling said he had broken with that past and cleaned up the staff.

The note describes how the agency sold news to about four hundred papers in the United States and relied on stringers abroad. Its money position is called shaky, and Bolling's main effort was winning more subscribers. The record preserves how Agency staff sized up a small news seller that came calling in 1952.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400120001-6:
House Report Number 1976, filed 2 May 1950, reports against a move to kill Reorganization Plan Number 5 of 1950. The Committee on Expenditures in the Executive Departments considered House Resolution 546, which voiced disapproval of the plan. It reported the resolution unfavourably and urged that it not pass. The President had sent the plan to Congress on 13 March 1950.

Had the resolution passed both houses, the plan would never have taken force on 12 May 1950. The report explains that timing under section 6(b)(2) of the Reorganization Act of 1949. A long file follows, printing the plan and the debate around reshaping executive offices. For Agency readers, such plans could shift the bureaus they dealt with across government.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400190013-6:
Executive Order 10000 lays down rules on added pay and credit for certain federal staff serving outside the United States. It rests on section 207 of the Independent Offices Appropriation Act of 1949, as changed later that year. Parts of the Foreign Service Act of 1946 are also cited as authority. Two fields are covered: added compensation for staff employed outside the continental United States or in Alaska, and salary differentials for Foreign Service staff.

The order speaks as the President and prescribes the rules in full. Grades, rates, and the conditions for each payment follow in numbered clauses. Marked as the best copy available, the scan is worn but the structure stays clear. Agency pay offices abroad worked from these rules when they set a posting's extra pay.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500050134-6:
Retired officers serving as part-time consultants are the subject of a memorandum dated 19 July 1951 to the Deputy Director for Administration. CIA wanted the help of certain retired men, whose names are redacted, for consultation on national estimates. Their experience and judgment were sought by the Senior Panel of the Office of National Estimates. They would hold no staff or clerical duties and would serve only when called.

Service was expected to run about ten to twelve days a month. The question is whether any law or rule bars such service. A second question asks whether serving would harm their retired standing or force a hold on retired pay. The memorandum then works through the statutes on retired officers and outside earnings.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500070051-6:
An instruction of the National Security Resources Board, dated 23 August 1948, governs hiring experts and consultants on personal service contract. Its purpose is threefold: cite the laws in play, set terms for pay, leave, and travel, and prescribe the contract form the Board would use. Legal authority rests on section 13 of the Act of 2 August 1946. That clause lets a department head buy short or intermittent expert services by contract.

Such hiring may bypass the civil service and classification laws, the instruction notes. Service is capped at one year where the quoted act applies. Later parts fix rates and the paper trail each contract needs. Kept in Agency files, the Board's sheet shows a sister body solving the same hiring problem in the same summer.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500090004-6:
House Report Number 2162, filed 29 May 1950, reports H.R. 7824 in favour with amendments. Mr. Murray of Tennessee sent it in for the Committee on Post Office and Civil Service. The bill provides for running performance-rating plans for certain federal officers and employees. First among the amendments is a rewritten list of bodies the act would not cover.

The Tennessee Valley Authority, the Post Office field service, and named health staff head that list. The report prints the bill with each change marked, so the House could see the committee's hand. A statement of the bill's purpose and a part-by-part account follow. Together with its Senate twin, the report marks the path of the Performance Rating Act through Congress in 1950.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000700020018-6:
A Signature Record and Cover Sheet is the printed form that travels with a top secret document inside the Central Intelligence Agency. Header boxes record the document number, date, copy number, page count, and attachments. A registry block gives the CIA control number, the date the document arrived, and who logged it. Printed terms state that the sheet stays attached until the document is downgraded, destroyed, or sent outside the Agency.

Access, the form says, is limited to those whose duties touch the material. Each top secret officer, alternate, or assistant who receives or releases the item signs the form. Columns record who has seen the document and the dates of handling. A detachment notice at the foot sends word to central top secret control when the sheet comes off.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000700060113-6:
Comments on a proposed cost-plus-fixed-fee contract form go from the Legal Staff to the Contract Section on 16 March 1950. The form comes back with the letter for talk between the offices. Early notes attack the preamble clauses one by one. In the second clause, the writer offers fresh wording: the government wants the contractor to carry out research and build whatever equipment or articles are later named.

A label in the third clause, actual cost, is called too narrow against Article 5(a), and a plainer facilities wording is proposed. Deleting the fourth clause as needless is urged next. The writer then reworks the fifth clause on the nature of the work. Clause by clause, the letter tightens a form that would bind secret research spending.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000800120007-6:
A memorandum of agreement made on 29 June 1948 binds the United States and an unnamed contractor to a program of secret work. The government wants studies and experimental investigations carried out, plus construction as later specified. The contractor agrees to work on the basis set out in the articles. One recital states that the government's own facilities fall short for the task. Using the contractor is judged good for the national interest.

Much of the material and supplies bought under the deal will be consumed or built into equipment during the work. That fact shapes the property and cost clauses that follow. Authority for the government to sign such an agreement is recited before the promises begin. It is a standard research contract frame, with the subject itself left unnamed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000800170002-6:
Transfer of property between government agencies is ruled on in a General Counsel opinion dated 6 January, answering the Chief of the Services Branch. Property was passing from the Federal Communications Commission to the Central Intelligence Agency. The question is whether the transfer may run without an exchange of funds. Behind it sits a chain of earlier moves: property had passed from the Strategic Services Unit to the wartime successor body, and the Agency's standing as final holder needs settling.

Counsel first gathers the decisions on surplus property moving between recognised departments. Some of those cases concern straight surplus; others grow out of executive reorganisations like this one. The opinion then applies the line of rulings to the Commission's transfer. Title, not payment, is the heart of the answer.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000020005-6:
Counter Intelligence Corps procedures for personnel, administration, and training fill Army Special Regulations Number 380-310-2 of 1 August 1952. Section I covers authority, purpose, mission, and command, plus security from publicity and rules on badges, credentials, and firearms. Section II handles people: how Corps units get their staff, how members are assigned and used, and what happens to those who fail retention tests.

Administration comes next, with channels for letters, classification of routine reports, and the recurring reports owed. Supply sections cover the Corps depot, buying steps, and requisitions beyond set allowances. Training and schools close the scheme. For an Agency that worked beside Army counterintelligence daily, this was the partner service's own rulebook in full.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000040003-6:
H.R. 7430, brought in by Mr. Holifield on 27 February 1950, would add a new title to the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act of 1949. The new title would build a proper traffic management service for the federal government. It went to the Committee on Expenditures in the Executive Departments. First the bill renumbers the old general provisions title in the contents list, pushing it to Title VI.

Sections 601 through 605 of that title are named: use of existing procedures, repeal and saving clauses, funding authority, separability, and effective date. The traffic title itself then sets out how freight and movement business should be run. Shipping was a real cost for every agency, and the bill treats it as a trade needing its own office.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000040012-6:
Part 2 of House Report 670, filed 25 May 1949, is the minority report on H.R. 4754, the Federal Property bill. Mr. Hoffman of Michigan sent it in for members of the Committee on Expenditures in the Executive Departments who dissented. The minority traces the bill's path first. An earlier measure, H.R. 2781 from Mr. Dawson, closely matched a bill the Senate side had favoured in the prior Congress.

A subcommittee of four Democrats and two Republicans held hearings and reported that bill favourably. The full committee added amendments and reported it out on 13 May. A fresh bill, H.R. 4754, was then brought in on 18 May 1949. The minority's objections to the speed and shape of the scheme fill the pages that follow.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000040030-6:
Working relations between the General Accounting Office and the General Services Administration are fixed in a memorandum signed on 17 January 1950. The General Services Administration sent it to heads of departments and independent bodies that same day, over the name of Administrator Jess Larson. Both the Comptroller General and the Administrator executed the paper. It sets how the two offices will handle their linked duties under the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act of 1949.

Audit on one side and supply work on the other had to mesh without friction. Extra copies could be had by calling a named Executive exchange number and extension. For Agency staff, the memorandum showed who would judge their property dealings: the body that supplied them, audited by the body that watched all spending.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000060001-6:
United States Government Salary Tables for the executive branch issue from the General Accounting Office on 6 July 1948 under Table Number 30. They take effect on the first day of the first pay period beginning after 30 June 1948. The tables serve officers who prepare, certify, and pay civilian payrolls and vouchers for staff paid by the year. A forty-hour week is the stated base.

For each salary rate, the table gives the figures for a full two-week pay period. The sums rest on the Federal Employees Pay Acts of 1945 and 1946 and the Federal Employees Salary Act of 1948. Hourly, daily, and overtime rates are shown as well. Payroll clerks worked straight from these pages; a wrong table meant wrong pay across a whole office.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001100020004-6:
House Report Number 2451, ordered printed on 3 July 1952, is the conference report on H.R. 7176, the Interior Department appropriation bill for 1953. Mr. Kirwan sent it in for the committee of conference. The bill makes appropriations for the fiscal year ending 30 June 1953. The report lists, amendment by amendment, how the two houses settled their differences.

The Senate recedes from amendments numbered 2, 15, 28, and a run of others. The House recedes from its disagreement to a longer list and agrees to them. Amendment 6 is taken with a further amendment, spelled out in the text. Such reports are the final wiring of a money bill: dry lists here decide what land, parks, and territory programs actually received.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001100020031-6:
S.J. Res. 122, brought in by Mr. McCarran on 21 January 1952, is a joint resolution to impose limits on executive agreements. It went to the Committee on Foreign Relations. A chain of whereas clauses builds its case. A treaty or executive agreement, the first runs, may be set aside by a later act of Congress. The Supreme Court recognised Congress's right to vacate a treaty early in its history.

Executive agreements made under the President's diplomatic powers are treated as open to the same treatment. A present drift toward using such agreements, rather than sending undertakings to the Senate as the Constitution requires, is then charged. The resolution that follows would fence the practice. The text is the first move in the treaty-power fight of that session.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001100050010-6:
Distribution of an unclassified daily report, whose name is redacted, draws a short memorandum of 21 February 1950 from the Chief of a covert office to the Assistant Director for Operations. Two January papers frame the file: a counsel note of 25 January and a note of 31 January on distribution to newspapers. The writer states plainly that his office is not fitted to read the law on the point.

Three judgements follow. Delaying a decision to seek a formal ruling from the Attorney General would serve no useful purpose, if counsel's view stands. Asking the National Security Council for a policy ruling would not change the risk of going on with distribution. Recipients could not fairly be expected to agree to defend the practice as a group. The memorandum leans toward stopping.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001100070018-6:
A memorandum of 5 February 1951 from Lloyd A. Ray, headed USSR Merchant Marine, Case 6342, lays out facts on Lend-Lease ships. Under the Lend-Lease Agreement, naval and merchant vessels passed to the Soviet Union for its war use. Article V of the Master Agreement calls for return, at the end of the present emergency as the President determines, of defence articles not destroyed, lost, or consumed. Articles the President finds useful for the defence of the United States or the Western Hemisphere are covered.

Despite demands, very few vessels have come back. A further snarl is whether the United States ever agreed to sell the merchant ships outright. Conference transcripts between the two governments are in play on that point. Legal title, the memorandum notes, still rests where the agreement left it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001200030020-6:
Tab A, a confidential proposal on strengthening intelligence activities, states its problem in one line. The Director of Central Intelligence needs ways to make sure the parts of the federal intelligence system get budget support enough for their national security work. Discussion opens with the design of the system itself. The Act and the NSC directives intend the agencies on the Intelligence Advisory Committee to work as one system, linked and leaning on each other.

Each agency still owes its own department its duties, the paper grants. Managed rightly, though, the parts should yield coordinated intelligence. The law's charge that CIA recommend measures to the National Security Council is then quoted as the lever. Budget, in this paper, is where coordination either happens or fails.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001300070007-6:
Soviet Bibliography Number 50, dated 16 January 1950 (the cover reads January 4 in one line), lists fresh writing on the Soviet Union for State Department readers. The Division of Library and Reference Services prepared it, and the Office of Intelligence Research reviewed and distributed it. A note tells authorised readers how to request items, through the Circulation Section in Room 202 of State Annex Number 1, or by a named phone extension.

Agriculture opens the subject sections. Abram Bergson's piece The Yield of the Sickle, from The New Republic of 28 November 1949, is listed first, as a critique of Naum Jasny's book on Soviet farming. Entries give author, title, place, and a one-line note on content. Such lists kept analysts current on open writing about a closed state.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001300360032-6:
Tort claims under the new act are explained in an article from the JAG Journal, the monthly magazine of the Judge Advocate General of the Navy. The piece, by a naval legal officer as the byline is printed, aims at legal forehandedness among staff who run naval law. A front note sets the journal's mission: clear grasp of the basic laws of Navy life and of the rights and duties of naval personnel.

The journal is an unofficial teaching medium, its pages written in an informal style. It warns that its articles are not citable as legal authority in court. Court Martial Orders and the Judge Advocate General's opinions remain the sources that count. Individual views in articles are the authors' own, not the Navy Department's. The article then takes the new tort claims scheme apart for lay readers.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00039a000100050056-6:
Weekly Activities Report number 13, for 23 to 29 March 1955, was sent on 31 March 1955 by the Chief of the Language and External Training School to the Director of Training. Marked confidential in the original, the report's main readable item announces a new round of interviews for full time students in the Washington area. The interviews fall during training, at its end, and six months later.

Other items follow staff and course business in short entries. Students of Indonesian at Yale and Cornell are put forward for a summer graduate program. A place is arranged at lectures on United States foreign policy for senior Agency staff. Pressure from one division for full time intensive Russian training is also noted. The report also records special training in Hungarian for one employee and notice of a short course on parachute technology at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000100100017-6:
Memorandum dated 5 April 1956 asks whether sections 215 to 217 of Title 31, cited from the 1952 code, have been repealed, as code notes suggest. The question matters because the Agency planned to rely on section 215 in a planned rule. The rule would settle claims for damage to private property in a foreign country caused by a federal officer or employee acting within his duties.

The memo traces the older law to Public Law 375 of 1922, which allowed settlement of claims of one thousand dollars or less, with no bar on claims arising abroad. It then sets the 1946 Federal Tort Claims Act beside it, noting that act barred claims arising in a foreign country. Views from Treasury, State, Justice, and other agencies are split, and the memo notes options of asking the Attorney General for an opinion or letting a court case settle the point.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000100300015-6:
House report number 1764, dated 7 June 1954, from the Committee on Interior and Insular Affairs, supports H.R. 8634, a bill to amend section 22 of the Organic Act of Guam. The committee reports the bill with two amendments and urges that it pass as amended, and the report prints the exact wording each amendment would insert.

One amendment concerns terms for government counsel in the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure, in cases under Guam law. It reads them as the Attorney General of Guam or a person named under Guam law. The other adds a clause keeping the rest of the act in force if one part is held invalid. An explanation section traces the Organic Act of 1950, the District Court of Guam, and the reach of the federal civil and criminal rules. Letters from the Departments of the Interior and Justice are included.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000200210005-6:
Business Service Checklist, volume IX, number 47, dated 19 November 1954, is a weekly list issued by the United States Department of Commerce under Secretary Sinclair Weeks. The checklist lists material published by the Department of Commerce and by other agencies, notes that items without a price are free, and gives an order form and field office guidance.

Entries are grouped by office, with page counts and codes. Items include a combined employment and unemployment release from Commerce and Labor. They also include notice of a new Office of Strategic Information set up at the direction of the President on the advice of the National Security Council. An appointment to head the Iron and Steel Division is listed. Later pages list statistical supplements, an airman's guide, NATO work at French airfields, and trade studies on Africa, Bolivia, and Peru.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000300130139-6:
Memorandum for the record on a meeting of the Central Intelligence Agency, the Public Buildings Service, and the architect, held 28 March 1956 in the office of Mr. Otis Foss. Named present are the architect's representative from Harrison and Abramovitz, the chief estimator and supervising architect of the Public Buildings Service, and Agency staff, with one member arriving near the end.

The aim was to go over the proposed contract and let the architect's side raise questions, though all questions tied to the contract. Two items are flagged as most likely to cause dispute: supervision of construction and the architect's fee. The architect would make seven submissions, with the fee paid in six installments and a final payment. Items needed for a presentation to Congress on or after 15 May include site plans, a cost estimate, a block model, and a sketch.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100020023-6:
Compilation titled Restrictions and Limitations Placed on Government Departments and Agencies by Public Laws, 83rd Congress, first session, gathers clauses from appropriations acts that limit how money may be spent. Public Law 179, for the Department of Defense and related agencies, is quoted first, section by section.

Section 605 bars use of Defense travel funds for expenses of attending meetings of technical, scientific, professional, or similar bodies without approval of the Secretary or his designee. Section 608 bars tuition or other payments to schools for training file clerks, stenographers, and typists who are paid below the minimum rate for grade GS-5 under the Classification Act of 1949. A further section allows Defense funds for minor construction, conversion, and improvements at facilities. Later clauses govern transfers between appropriations for annual leave of staff separated in reductions.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100030004-6:
Pamphlet printing remarks of Senator Estes Kefauver of Tennessee on the Internal Security Act, from debate printed in the Congressional Record of 12 September 1950. It was issued by the Government Printing Office in 1950 and marked not printed at government expense. The heading frames the debate as showing need for more effective legislation to control Communists and other subversives.

Kefauver opens by noting a rising public anger against communism and Soviet Russia, with people concerned, alarmed, and some hysterical. He warns that fear drives men to acts they would not consider in calm courage. He argues that, but for the threat of communism and the shadow of a third world war, few would ask Congress to control the thoughts of citizens. Later pages take up proposed amendments, including one limiting unlawful conspiracy to acts by force and violence.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100030013-6:
Department of State outgoing telegram, control T233, dated 23 October 1950, was sent to certain American diplomatic and consular officers. It gives a procedure for Economic Cooperation Administration participants found inadmissible under the Internal Security Act of 1950. References are to earlier telegrams of September and October 1950 on ECA participants and the Act.

Consuls are told to keep processing ECA participants as before, except as noted. A visa applicant who is a prospective ECA participant may be found inadmissible for former membership in a Nazi, Fascist, or Communist party or affiliate. In that case the consul should notify the ECA mission representative abroad. The mission passes the facts to ECA Washington, which may, after a stateside security investigation, ask the Attorney General to invoke the ninth proviso. The State Department will not itself start ninth proviso action in ECA participant cases. Addressee countries listed run from Austria and Belgium to Korea and beyond.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100150092-6:
Memorandum dated 12 April 1946, marked confidential, records questions raised that morning at a Central Intelligence Group Council meeting on a proposed policy for clearance of personnel for duties with the Group. The underlying paper was a memorandum for the Director of Central Intelligence from the Acting Chief of the Central Planning Staff, dated 11 April.

Questions listed are whether responsibility for security clearance should rest with the departments, as a draft directive provided, or with the Group. They also ask whether the directive needed approval of the intelligence advisory body or could issue from the Director alone. A third asks whether exceptions needed department concurrence or could be made by the Director as he saw fit. It was agreed that in any case responsibility for the security of the Group rests with the Director, whatever the arrangement for investigation and clearance of individuals.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100200014-6:
Letter dated 15 June 1956, on Department of State letterhead and marked a copy, answers a letter of 6 June 1956 from Mr. Fountain on behalf of a subcommittee investigating alleged shipments of Commodity Credit Corporation commodities to Soviet bloc countries. The writer assures the subcommittee of the Department's earnest desire to cooperate with its investigation.

A review of correspondence is said to show the Department gave the information requested as far as it could obtain it. One reply was outstanding on points in a letter of 3 May, pending further information from abroad. The letter explains the Department's role in gathering information that Commerce, Agriculture, and other agencies or the subcommittee require: other officials start the requests and the Department transmits them.
