A later passage covers making available copies of reports and letters on possible transshipment of such commodities to Soviet bloc destinations.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100240164-6:
Excerpt from hearings of the Task Force of the Internal Security Subcommittee of the Senate Judiciary Committee, studying the strategy and tactics of world communism, is dated 29 July 1954. It gives testimony by Representative Fred Busbey. Chairman Jenner invites him to speak on why the United States had been ineffective against the Communist situation, through the Central Intelligence Agency among other means.

Busbey states he was on the House subcommittee that heard testimony when the Agency was set up, and that what he says is not top secret. He recounts three fights in that subcommittee. One he won, against incorporating the FBI into the Agency. Two he lost, one for a law that the Agency head be a civilian qualified by experience. Later testimony blames, in his judgment, lack of intelligence training in the individuals employed by the Agency at its start.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200020040-6:
Pages from the Congressional Record, Senate, for 1953, at page 9963, open in debate on a conference report and the safety regulations of the Interstate Commerce Commission. Senator Saltonstall reports talks with Commission representatives and a communication from the General Accounting Office, hoping the House conferees' reading of the report would be clarified before the report was called up.

Senator Maybank, who would have to be absent the next day, states his position in advance. He reports that the chairman of the House subcommittee agreed the report ought to be clarified so the safety program could continue properly. A conference report, he notes, is voted up or down as a whole. Later pages in the file turn to amendments for a telecommunications commission measure. They include inserting the words Governmental use of after the word on, and a new section 9 directing study of the objectives and effectiveness of information programs.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200040002-6:
Copy of the 16 December 1953 memorandum for the Director proposing weekly congressional lunches, in which the Appropriations guests hold the centre. The stated aim is to apprise key members of Congress of pertinent Agency matters, and the schedule begins before Christmas 1953 and runs into February 1954.

For 11 January 1954 the memo invites Congressmen John Taber of New York, Richard B. Wigglesworth of Massachusetts, and Errett P. Scrivner of Kansas, identified as the three Republican members of the House Appropriations Committee who handled the Agency budget for fiscal 1954. The entry before it covers Congressman Vorys and his foreign trade questions as a member of the Randall Commission. The entry after it turns to Senator Saltonstall, who was responsible for Agency legislation in the Senate, and to the Joint Committee proposal before his Armed Services Committee.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200100104-6:
Joint message of November 1956 announces the trip of the Committee of Citizen Advisers on the Mutual Security Program to posts worldwide, from Ankara, Athens, and Bangkok to Taipei, Tehran, and Tokyo. The Department notes the group is not a congressional delegation, and designates the message to identify the party, whose chairman was Mr. Benjamin F. Fairless, with his appointment letter attached.

Members listed, all cleared for top secret, include Benjamin F. Fairless as adviser and chairman, Colgate W. Darden Jr., John L. Lewis, Jesse W. Tapp, and Whittemore Paul as advisers, with an executive director, a staff director, and a military adviser. The group would study the Mutual Security Program. Guidance asks that briefings be limited to two or two and a half hours, ending by mid afternoon, with free time and sightseeing interspersed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200140001-6:
Release from the Senate Internal Security Subcommittee, for release at 8:00 a.m. Friday 21 December 1956, distributes testimony taken 18 December from Yuri Rastvorov. Rastvorov was a former Soviet secret service agent in Japan, Third Secretary of the Soviet Mission when he defected in 1954, and Senator Jenner presided, with Robert Morris as chief counsel.

The hearing is headed Scope of Soviet Activity in the United States. Morris recalls the witness's earlier testimony that he knew Sergei Tikhvinsky as a member of the NKVD. His job, on the witness's direct knowledge, was to recruit Japanese prisoners into the Soviet apparatus and send them back into Japan. Questioning then follows named Soviet officials, including an ambassador to Sweden said to have been forced to leave over espionage activity. A figure who began in the early 1940s in Soviet Navy intelligence is also taken up. The testimony is the witness's own account, under oath.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100240003-6:
House Report number 53, dated 16 February 1955, from the Committee on Armed Services, submits a report by Mr. Durham to accompany H.R. 2123, a bill to repeal Public Law 820 of the 80th Congress. The committee reports the bill favorably without amendment and recommends that it pass, under the title Repealing the Natural Fibers Act.

Public Law 820, at 62 Stat. 1098, provided a revolving fund to purchase natural fibers, including cotton waste, produced in the United States. It also covered materials used in processing them, such as starch, dyestuffs, roller leather, and card clothing, and transport of the fibers to occupied areas for processing. A letter in the report states the proposal would cause no apparent increase in budgetary requirements for the Department of Defense. A closing section prints changes in existing law in parallel columns, as House rules require.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100560008-6:
Senate Report number 1878, dated 30 April 1956, from the Committee on Armed Services, submits a report by Mr. Russell to accompany H.R. 9429, titled Dependents' Medical Care Act. The committee reports the bill favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute and recommends passage.

The bill would make uniform, and expand, medical care for dependents of members of the uniformed services. The term covers the Army, Navy, Air Force, Marine Corps, Coast Guard, and the commissioned corps of the Public Health Service and the Coast and Geodetic Survey. Uniformity is to come from statutory definitions of eligible dependents and of care provided; expansion from contracts with civilian physicians and hospitals. The report estimates about 2.1 million eligible spouses and children in the United States, and quotes a Blue Cross and Blue Shield estimate of 53.2 million dollars for care of forty percent of them.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100670006-6:
Agency file headed Executive Pay Bill gathers material for testimony: notes for the Director's testimony on the executive pay bill, a summary of the legislation at Tab A (S. 2628, H.R. 7619, and the committee analysis), Agency executive positions comparable to assistant secretaries at Tab B, and State and Defense Department hierarchy charts at Tabs C and D.

The testimony notes urge strong support for raising salaries of senior executives in government generally. They then list Agency problems: anonymity is not a very good reward, and good people are lost over schooling children and providing for families. Responsibility is out of proportion to salary, and industry pays more. On the bill itself, the relative positions, not the salaries, of the Director and Deputy Director are of primary concern. A later note welcomes ranging grade GS-18 pay from sixteen thousand to seventeen thousand five hundred dollars, as the Senate bill proposes.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100670015-6:
House Report number 1474, dated 27 July 1955, from the Committee on Post Office and Civil Service, submits a report by Mr. Murray of Tennessee to accompany H.R. 7619 under the title Federal Executive Pay Act of 1955. The committee reports the bill favorably without amendment and recommends passage.

Purpose is a necessary adjustment in pay of officials in the executive branch, almost all of them in posts filled by the President with Senate advice and consent. The report notes the legislation was requested by the President in a letter to the committee chairman, which set out general principles for the adjustment. Tables in the middle give present and proposed salaries post by post. For Veterans Administration medical posts, the Chief Medical Director at sixteen thousand eight hundred dollars would rise to seventeen thousand eight hundred. The deputy chief and assistant chief directors are scaled below.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100670033-6:
Printed bill H.R. 7619, Report number 1474, Union Calendar number 489, was introduced in the House on 26 July 1955 by Mr. Murray of Tennessee, sent to the Committee on Post Office and Civil Service, and ordered printed on 27 July 1955. Title I of the Federal Executives Pay Act of 1955 sets basic compensation for heads of executive departments and other officials.

Department heads and the Secretary of Defense are set at twenty five thousand dollars a year in section 101. Section 102 sets twenty two thousand five hundred dollars for the Deputy Secretary of Defense, Under Secretary of State, Defense Mobilization Director, Comptroller General, and Budget Director. A later schedule names single office holders at a set rate, among them the Director of the Bureau of Prisons and the Commissioners of Public Buildings, Social Security, Reclamation, and Customs.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100690004-6:
Printed bill H.R. 3819 was introduced in the House on 8 February 1955 by Mr. Corbett and sent to the Committee on Post Office and Civil Service. It is the Overseas Allowances Act of 1955, to consolidate and revise the laws on added pay for civilian federal employees stationed outside the continental United States and in Alaska. Its aims include easing recruitment and cutting turnover.

Title I states objectives in section 101. They are to improve and strengthen administration of government activities overseas by codifying into one act the provisions compensating United States citizen employees for extra costs and hardships of overseas assignments. Uniform treatment across agencies is also an aim. A middle transportation passage allows moving an employee's minor dependents to and from the nearest port of entry, one round trip, apart from the parents' home leave. The trips let the children gain an American secondary school education.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100700002-6:
House Report of 22 June 1955, from the Committee on Veterans' Affairs, submits a report by Mr. Teague of Texas to accompany H.R. 5893, under the title Employment of Retired Military Personnel in Federal Civil Service. The committee reports the bill favorably without amendment and recommends passage.

The bill amends paragraph I(a), part I, of Veterans Regulation number 1(a) to cover active service from 27 June 1950 to 1 February 1955. An explanation sets out section 212 of Public Law 212 of the 72d Congress. No holder of a civilian office under the United States or the District of Columbia may receive retired pay as a commissioned officer beyond a set total. The total, with the civilian salary, is more than three thousand dollars, with exceptions then listed. Tables deeper in the report print monthly retired pay rates under the Career Incentive Act of 1955, by grade and years of service.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200070001-6:
Memorandum for the Legislative Counsel comments on H.R. 8486 and H.R. 9220, concerning compensation of personnel paid on the prevailing rate system. Both bills would amend the Act of 1 September 1954, the Fringe Benefits Act, in two ways set out in the memorandum.

First, salaries of new appointees to continuing positions converted from the CPC schedule to the prevailing rate system would be set under the saved rate rule. A comment notes no effect on the Agency, since its conversions did not lower basic rates. Second, agencies would have to give longevity step increases to prevailing rate staff, a benefit not then available to that group. The memorandum recommends support of the longevity provision, as rewarding long and faithful service of the wage board group as General Schedule staff are rewarded. It asks to be kept informed of the bills' progress.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200160001-6:
Memorandum dated 18 March 1955, marked Secret and reviewed by the Office of General Counsel, is addressed to the Assistant to the Deputy Director (Support) on H.R. 687, the Anti-Government Competition Act, 84th Congress, first session. Passage of the bill should not, in the opinion stated, affect the Agency's work or its operations through proprietary business type mechanisms.

Attention is drawn to section 2, which declares it the policy of Congress that the federal government shall not engage in business type operations competitive with private enterprise. An exception covers cases where government performance is shown necessary for legally established national programs. The memorandum holds that all Agency operations must fall in that class. A review of Agency business type activities would show none of them could logically be called competitive with private enterprise. The bill text in the file opens with findings on free competition and national security.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200250001-6:
Memorandum from the Office of Security to the Legislative Counsel concerns Legislative Bill number H.R. 8273. If nothing in the proposed legislation would result in the Agency's credit union having to release the names of its shareholders, the Office of Security raises no point on the bill. The condition is stated as the whole of its interest.

The notice of pending legislation is dated 18 January 1956 and routed to the Comptroller and the Director of Security. A comment in the file states the belief that there is no Agency interest in the bill. The bill would amend the Federal Credit Union Act, among other things on central organizations of credit unions. The bill text defines such an organization as one whose field of membership includes federal credit unions and state or District of Columbia credit unions. It may also include their directors and supervisory committee members.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200340001-6:
Memorandum dated August 1955, for the Office of General Counsel and addressed to Mr. Walter L. Pforzheimer, comments on a proposed amendment to the Foreign Service Act of 1946. The amendment concerns section 921 of that act, on commissary and mess services abroad.

The proposal is found to agree with current Agency policy, as set in a Comptroller memorandum of 15 August 1955. That memorandum covers establishing, equipping, and running personal service and recreational facilities at field installations. It was concurred in by the Director of Logistics, the General Counsel's office, and the Special Support Assistant, and approved by the Deputy Director (Support). No added authority is thought necessary for the Agency to continue in this field. A letter in the file adds that service facilities run with private funds would lower the Agency's cost of operation and greatly improve morale of staff on overseas tours.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200430001-6:
A set of CIA notices of pending legislation, dated June and August 1955, circulates H.R. 7008 for comment inside the Agency. The bill, introduced by Mr. Barrett of Pennsylvania, would amend Public Law 587 to permit federal withholding of certain municipal taxes from employees' wages. The Legislative Counsel's office asks whether the bill interests CIA activities and whether further action is wanted.

The comment sections judge that the bill is not expected to pass, but that it raises security implications worth answering. One note points out that H.R. 7008 closely resembles H.R. 5204, since both bills would extend withholding to political subdivisions. The file preserves the routing forms, the distribution, and the printed text of the bill itself from the 84th Congress.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100040008-6:
A CIA legal paper on redefectors argues that a sovereign must protect the persons of its people. It traces that duty from Mosaic law through tribal custom in western Europe. In modern Anglo-American law, the person is guarded by trespass suits and by the right of self-defence. Threats are punished as well as blows. The paper then turns to Soviet and satellite officials. They work to win back people who fled communist rule.

The paper charges these officials with serious abuses. They used false names and false credentials. They held secret meetings away from their own premises. They lured refugees with false promises of safety, jobs, and family reunion. Those promises proved false more often than true. Once a refugee returned behind the Iron Curtain, he faced force up to murder. The paper cites earlier killings in the United States and Mexico.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100210036-6:
A CIA legal memorandum of 28 August 1955 examines the Crypto Security Law. It was written for the Office of Security. The law sits at section 798 of Title 18. The memo quotes the offence in full. A person commits it by passing guarded facts to an unauthorised person. Publishing such facts, or misusing them, is also an offence. The facts covered concern codes, cipher devices, and intelligence gained from foreign messages.

Much of the memo compares this law with sections 793 and 794. Those are the general espionage provisions. They speak of information relating to the national defence. So a jury must decide whether given material fits that phrase. Section 798 works differently. It points to facts an agency has marked as classified for national security reasons. The memo treats that difference as the law's main strength in court.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100300009-6:
A Director of Central Intelligence directive of 26 March 1954 governs agreed activities. It sets definitions, responsibilities, policy, and procedures. The work falls under NSCID 5. The directive defines two key posts. Commanders lead commands set up by the Joint Chiefs of Staff outside the United States. Senior Representatives are the Director's chief men in their set areas.

Its definitions split espionage from counterespionage. Espionage is the secret gathering of facts on foreign powers. Counterespionage works to uncover and frustrate foreign spying on the United States. Federal espionage supports the national defence worldwide, outside the country. Senior Representatives answer to the Director for all such work in their areas. They must keep local commanders informed of work bearing on their commands. Commanders may in turn offer facilities where they serve the mission better.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200030044-6:
A draft act, with explanatory notes, would raise the Director's pay. The Director is the head of Central Intelligence. Section 1 amends 50 U.S.C. 403. It strikes the figure $16,000 for the Director's salary. A note works out take-home pay on a $20,000 salary. Under 1951 tax rates, a man with one dependent kept $14,178. A general kept $14,566.

Section 2 covers a commissioned officer serving as Director. He would receive the pay and allowances of a general, or the equivalent grade. After four years as Director, he could retire at his own request. His retired pay would be that of a general. This ends the old practice of topping up military pay to the civilian salary. Other sections update a claims reference to chapter 171 of Title 28. They also exempt the Agency from the Performance Rating Act of 1950, and restate home leave.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200030107-6:
A draft bill of 5 February 1948 would provide for the administration of the Central Intelligence Agency, established under section 102 of the National Security Act of 1947. It opens with definitions of the Agency, the Director, a government agency, and the continental United States, then provides for a seal of office of a design the President approves.

Like the other February drafts, it requires an FBI investigation and report on character, associations, and loyalty before anyone is assigned to departmental duty, emergency cases aside. Procurement is handled by applying named sections of the Armed Services Procurement Act then before Congress as H.R. 1366, with 'agency head' read as the Director, Deputy Director, or Executive Director. A death provision lets the Director certify a death as having occurred in connection with Agency service. Later sections take up allowances, including separation support where dangerous or unhealthful post conditions force a family to live elsewhere.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200030116-6: This declassified CIA document is another bill to establish the Central Intelligence Agency. A second founding draft. The paper preserves the text. The file remains. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200070013-6:
An issue of Public Health Reports carries a plan for federal employee health services. It is volume 61, number 40, dated 13 November 1946. A new public law of the 79th Congress opened the way. Heads of departments and agencies may set up employee health programs. They must first consult the United States Public Health Service. The goal is to promote and maintain the physical and mental health of federal staff.

The editorial notes the Service's long record in this field. It had studied industrial and occupational hazards for years. It had advised private industry and agencies alike. Employers found such programs paid off in efficiency and productivity. The plan that follows lists the parts of a preventive medical program. They include promotion of each employee's best health. They include diagnostic and advisory services. They also include the treatment the Act allows, prevention of disease, and study of the program's own statistics.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200270011-6:
A CIA legal memorandum of 15 February 1955 sets out the rights arising from federal employment. It went to the Inspector General. It argues that calls for relief after official mistakes rest partly on wrong ideas. Those ideas concern the government as employer, the nature of public office, and public funds. They also concern the rights and limits that flow from them.

The memo states that government employment involves giving up certain rights. The sovereign may set the terms of its own service. There is little room for court review of administrative discretion in such matters. When the legislature creates rights against the government, it sets its own terms. It may limit people to administrative remedies. Examples follow from the Taft-Hartley Act, which bars strikes by federal staff. The Hatch Act also bars active part in political management or campaigns. Loyalty rules are treated in the same frame.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300220006-6:
A CIA file holds two letters of July 1956 to Loyd Wright. Wright chaired the Commission on Government Security, at 441 G Street in Washington. The first letter, dated 18 July 1956, comes from the Director's office. It sends detailed findings on the security problems that might be designated for study. It offers a full briefing by Agency staff at his convenience. A committee report is enclosed.

The second letter is more personal. It answers Wright on the report of the Special Committee on the Federal Loyalty-Security Program. The writer had now studied the advance copy. CIA, like other sensitive agencies, is exempt from the report's procedural proposals. So those do not affect it. All CIA positions are regarded as sensitive. Every post gives access to classified information. So the general proposals would have little impact on Agency personnel security. The writer still finds merit in some of them.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300280037-6:
A CIA legal memorandum of 15 July 1955 answers a housing question. It went to the Director of Personnel. When Agency employees are assigned to a redacted place, can their dependents be moved there too? Can the dependents be given quarters equal to those of other Agency families at the place? The question arose from a hard factual situation, set out in papers from May and June 1955.

Agency policy rests on section 10(e) of Public Law 110. It lets the Agency spend funds to carry out its functions, including renting buildings. A 1930 act states the general policy that quarters may be furnished free to staff at foreign posts. The cited regulation expects employees and dependents to live together. Dependents are part of the household, with no separate legal entitlement. Emergencies may justify separate quarters for a time. But no law or practice supports a planned move of dependents apart from the employee.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300290054-6:
A CIA legal memo of 17 September answers a claim for shipment of household effects. It went to the Deputy Director (Administration). The claimant's name is redacted. He sought repayment for shipping his effects from Kansas City, Missouri, to Washington, D.C. He had been on duty at Elmendorf Air Force Base, Alaska. At the end of his tour he was transferred to Washington and detailed to the Agency.

The facts rest on the record and a telephone talk. On or about 12 June 1953 a letter reached him at Elmendorf from the Chief of the Military Personnel Division. It spoke of a possible Agency assignment and gave general instructions. One passage warned him not to bring his family. He should make no commitments until fully informed of his duties. Government quarters for families were usually not available in Washington.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300320005-6:
A CIA legal memo of December 1956 interprets the Standardized Government Travel Regulations. It went to the Chief of the Finance Division. The Commercial Staff had asked how TDY travel orders should be written. A staff employee is stationed in Washington, D.C., and lives at Manassas, Virginia. Four questions are posed.

May orders read 'from Manassas' to the TDY destination, if the man does not stop at headquarters? What taxi fare or mileage is allowed from his home to National Airport or Union Station? Is there a set Washington Metropolitan Area, and does Manassas fall inside it? When is mileage allowed on a TDY trip to Baltimore? The answers rest on Comptroller General decisions, volume 20, page 315 among them. Travel between home and office at the start and end of TDY is not repayable.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00050a000100010002-6:
A CIA memorandum sets the procedure for the Clandestine Services in Operation Alert 1955. The exercise ran on 15, 16, and 17 June 1955. It rests on instructions from the Office of Defense Mobilization, dated 28 April 1955. It also rests on the Director's verbal instructions and a meeting of the CIA Emergency Planning Task Force. The procedure is furnished for planning and action.

The purposes are fourfold. The Services would take part with the rest of the Agency and other federal bodies. Members would learn the redeployment plan and the relocation site. Responsible officials would review the vital documents for a sustained alert. Basic facilities would be tested for extended use, from billeting and messing to communications. An exercise would portray simulated situations. Officials would have to act, recommend, and decide as in war. The President had stressed thorough preparation at a Cabinet meeting on 22 April 1955.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00050a000100040009-6:
An article from Science, dated 21 October 1955, examines mechanical translation. Its author is Jacob Ornstein. The article is reprinted in full in this CIA file. Translation of science and technology writings, Ornstein writes, is slow, costly, and still done by hand. Concern over the lag in translating foreign works has turned attention to machines. The electronic computer made the idea seem possible.

Warren Weaver of the Rockefeller Foundation first raised the question. He did so in 1945, and again in a memorandum of 15 July 1949. Reactions among linguists and scientists ran from high optimism to complete skepticism. The article explains how a machine might work. Words carry rule-tags in a glossary. The Russian word for about or of, for example, sends the machine back to search for tags on the noun it follows. The right English rendering is then chosen.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00050a000100070006-6:
Minutes record a Deputy Director (Support) staff meeting of 31 August 1955. The distribution list covers the support components, from General Counsel to the Director of Training. Mr. Lloyd was detained with the Acting DCI. A Management Staff officer outlined the Reports Management Program the DD/S wants put into effect. The first step is a survey of reporting requirements. Material would reach office heads within about a week.

The target date for finishing the surveys was set as 7 October. Figures from Hoover Commission surveys were shared. Benefits from the Records Management Program were already large. The Records Center had saved heavily on file cabinets and folders. Reports Management should bring like gains across the DD/S area. The Comptroller had already begun such a program. Later items covered personnel matters and the undecided site for the Agency's new building.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000100030015-6:
A summary records meetings between team captains and staff of the House Post Office and Civil Service Committee. Agency representatives wanted to give a fuller picture of their status. A voluminous report was avoided. Instead, each agency would submit set information by 24 November 1955. Four items are required. Agencies list their major functions. They describe each function briefly, with its main activities. They give the personnel in each function. They state whether each function is expanding or shrinking, and why.

Personnel must be broken into set categories. Executive Direction and Control covers the offices of secretaries and bureau heads. Administrative Services covers accounting, auditing, budgeting, finance, legal, manpower, personnel, and like work. Later pages pose hard questions, such as whether past cutbacks earn recognition against a new ten percent cut.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000100030042-6:
A CIA worksheet tracks the Davis Committee's duplication findings. Each item names a key officer and an assessment. The first item is personnel record keeping, an internal duplication. The Management Staff has spent about $11,000 of OTR funds on a study. The product so far is only a mass of facts and procedures. The direction taken was misconceived, the note says. The work must go back to the beginning.

A second item asks whether training could move to another agency. The claim that internal language and area instruction is most efficient is to be tested with statistics. The target date is 1 January 1957. Communications duplication draws a flat disagreement from the Director of Communications. Supply record keeping is flagged for study. Later items cover overseas unconventional warfare activities and a loan program being phased out.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000100030079-6:
A CIA memorandum of 25 November 1955 answers the Agency manpower study for the Office of Training. The scan is partly garbled, but the argument can be read. If the DD/S must cut ten percent, each support component would presumably bear its share. The Office of Training could reduce its authorized manpower by ten percent. But the effect on its duties needs serious thought.

Before 15 August, the office's ceiling stood at one figure. After that date it fell to a lower one, including 60 Junior Officer Trainees. That was a 17 percent reduction. A further cut would shrink the office's limited capacity. It provides construction for staff and indirect liaison, and representation for the intelligence community. Other offices, the memo argues, could reduce their present manpower by at least ten percent without doing so. No assurance exists that any such arrangement will materialize.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000100030088-6:
A CIA survey report covers the DDS organization on manpower use and mandatory reduction. It went to the Chairman of the Agency Manpower Survey Committee. Committee representatives asked each component to study itself. Four questions frame the study. What would each Deputy Director do under a ten percent cut? Does any unit duplicate another's work? What requirements exceed present manpower? What desirable tasks have ceilings forced offices to defer?

The report then gives staffing status office by office. Some offices name positions or functions to eliminate. Others would abolish individual positions without ending whole functions. On-duty figures are those recorded in November 1955. Later sections take up the Supply Division and special projects. Deferred work includes career plans for career employees and program analysis.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000100040023-6:
A CIA paper answers the Manpower Utilization Committee's questions for the DD/I area. A ten percent cut, it says, would force thought of a major reorganization. Two principal areas would result. One would join collection and information, merging the Office of Operations and the Office of Central Reference. The other would join production: research, scientific intelligence, estimates, current intelligence, and basic intelligence.

Savings might come from integrating research and scientific intelligence. Current intelligence and estimates could also merge. But disruption, lost key personnel, and confusion might outweigh the savings. The alternative is selective curtailment by priority. A 12 percent reduction in one office would end geographic research on non-Sino-Soviet Bloc countries. Map reference services would shrink sharply. General economic research would also fall. Duplication with military current intelligence publications is also examined.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100410019-6:
A Cartography Division project status list is dated 1 August 1957. The USSR-Satellites Branch leads. Hungary's shipbuilding industry is complete for July. A Moscow city plan appears in first revision. Soviet Bloc sheets locate geomagnetic observatories and selected weather stations. A Saratov airframe plant layout is listed. Eight USSR general summary maps appear as a set.

One project is marked cancelled: USSR railroad work for Central Asia and the western USSR. Several NIS sheets stand at proof. They cover USSR iron ore, alloy deposits, and steel plants, plus Bulgaria relief, soils, and smelters. Later sections list new projects for Cambodia, the Philippines, and Ceylon. Afghanistan's administrative divisions appear as well.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100490002-6:
The NIS Committee held its 236th meeting on 22 January 1956. 236 of 22 January 1956. Members came from State, Army, Navy, and the Air Force. CIA supplied the chairman, vice chairman, and secretary. The Army member announced an appointment. Mr. Andre E. Gerard became ACSI Chapter I coordinator. The committee reviewed Chapter I on NIS 36, Pakistan.

The draft was approved with certain changes. An Army redraft of part of Section 15 was accepted, if State finds it acceptable. The Task Group was asked to review the agencies' detailed comments. Since several sections are completely controlled, the whole chapter was controlled. A Chapter I planning conference schedule for fiscal 1958 follows. Conferences were set at Harriet Lane Hall, from Nationalist China in June 1957 to Japan in April 1958.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100490020-6:
Minutes record NIS Committee Meeting No. 254 of 5 November 1957. The committee reviewed Chapter I on NIS 3, France. The draft was approved with minor changes. The chapter was controlled. Section 12's source comments carried controls, and Sections 17, 18, and 19 were controlled in full. Members received the revised production forecast of 1 November 1957.

State warned on its Near East sections. It has little hope of producing Sections 14, 15, and 16 on Israel, Afghanistan, and the Arabian Peninsula in fiscal 1959. Its few qualified analysts are fully committed elsewhere. A schedule substitution was debated, tied to Hungary's unstable situation and its air forces. The committee also discussed the proposed NIS Annuals at length. A prototype had gone to the agencies for examination.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000200100003-6:
A monthly report covers the Map Library Division for July 1957. The Reference Branch sent out map sheets in answer to 1,225 requests. The request count fell from June's record, while sheets per order rose. A White House request is noted. Some 380 CIA-produced maps were laminated for use in Operation Alert. Demand for coverage of Pennsylvania, Maryland, Virginia, and North Carolina ran heavy.

City plans and special maps were picked for vital storage. They include 128 city plans, 77 maps on Korea and Taiwan, and over 200 city plans of Japan. The Cataloging Section screened all uncataloged maps of Africa. It cancelled 2,953 obsolete maps from the Central Europe holdings. An inventory of the CIA stock collection has begun. A statistical summary of receipts and disbursements follows.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100070001-6:
A House report examines improper use of government equipment and personnel in the Immigration and Naturalization Service. It is House Report No. 2948, 84th Congress, 2d Session. The Committee on Government Operations issued it on 27 July 1956. It is the committee's twenty-sixth intermediate report. William L. Dawson of Illinois chairs the committee. The Legal and Monetary Affairs Subcommittee handled the inquiry.

The report turns on testimony about a seizure of guns. A witness, Mr. Amthor, is reported returning on 5 September with General Swing. All testimony received by 23 July 1956 agreed Amthor was present when the guns were seized that day. If he had in fact left with General Swing, then Swing's own statement is false. The report weighs that contradiction.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100140003-6:
An issue of the Department of State Bulletin fills this file. It is Vol. XXX, No. 771, dated 5 April 1954. The lead item is the twelfth semiannual report on the International Educational Exchange Program. In the past year the program arranged 7,121 exchanges with over 70 countries. Two-thirds of the exchanges brought people to the United States. They came to study, teach, lecture, research, or gain work experience.

Other items fill the issue. Allied efforts to restore freedom of movement in Germany appear, with texts of correspondence. Deputy Under Secretary Murphy writes on Japan's progress and prospects. A Mutual Defense Assistance Agreement with Japan is printed. It rests on the Mutual Security legislation. An item on international copyright protection closes the contents list.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100140030-6:
Guidance on the use of copyrighted material in Department of Defense publications sets out the rules offices were to follow when reprinting protected work. The surviving text opens with unpublished works, directing that questions about notice and protection for them go to the office responsible for patent and copyright matters in each activity.

Later sections cover liability for infringement, defined as using any of the owner's exclusive rights, such as copying, translating, or publishing, without leave. Statutory damages are given as not less than 250 dollars and not more than 5,000 dollars for each violation. The guidance also notes that the United States is not liable for its wrongs unless it allows itself to be sued. Practical steps follow: a license request goes to the owner in duplicate, with a self-addressed return envelope, and no corporate seal is demanded. The copy survives in the Agency's declassified files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100200015-6:
Transmittal Letter No. 1-59 of the General Services Administration, dated June 28, 1955, sends federal agencies a new part of the GSA regulations. The subject is personal property management. The added Part 3 of Chapter V, Title 1, governs interagency motor pools and systems. It tells how they are established and run, under Public Law 766 of the 83rd Congress. Revised and new table of contents pages come with it.

The letter lists the exact page changes to make. It names the regulation sections to remove and insert. It also gives the effective date for the new part. The pool rules that follow cover which vehicles belong in a consolidated pool. They include fire trucks, transit mix trucks, and pole trailers. They also include trucks carrying mounted equipment, such as cranes and snow removal gear. The Agency's copy survives in its declassified files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00538a000100100008-6: A memorandum addressed to the Chief of the General Services Office survives only in badly garbled form. Its subject line cannot be read. The legible fragments record assurances about a transfer of work. Every effort would be made to avoid reductions in grade for the Agency personnel involved. A reproduction workload, described as the present volume, would be kept current. If that volume grew, the writer adds, some way would be found to meet it. Beyond that, the scan allows no confident statement of the document's business.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000100070003-6:
Results of a planning conference held on Friday, May 10, are reported to the Agency's Director of Training. The report is an office memorandum dated May 14, 1957. School and staff chiefs took up three items. They built an agenda for a meeting between the Director of Training and the Director of Personnel. They made plans to meet a possible table-of-organization reduction. They also considered a staff study proposed by the deputy chief.

Suggested agenda topics include the Junior Officer Trainee program. They include the question of overseas slots for its graduates. The conferees also discuss keeping training programs alive when no current requirement exists. The capability, they argue, should be maintained. The School of International Communism and the Operations School, the notes add, share one problem. Both struggle to attract top-flight instructors.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000100090001-6:
A staff study dated August 16, 1957, examines how readable the informal memoranda written in the DD/I offices actually are. The covering note comes from the Chief of Reading Improvement. It is addressed to the Chief of the Intelligence School. The note traces the inquiry to an interview on January 24, 1956. In it, the Director of Central Intelligence asked for suggestions to improve the readability of Agency memoranda.

Comments went to the Director on March 26, 1956. The DD/I in turn recommended firmer principles for better writing. The study then measures current practice. It estimates that ninety percent of the memos sampled have a single addressee. It tabulates where the rest go. Some stay within the writer's own office. Others go to the Director and his deputies, to other DD/I offices, or beyond.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000200040005-6:
An annual report dated July 15, 1957, comes from an officer with about five months in a post. He had served as the Junior Officer Training Program's personnel officer. He warns that the memorandum will not follow the usual annual report style. No history of earlier activity in the post exists. He does not feel he has yet found the full limits of the job.

Instead he lists the functions he performs, with observations. The first function is placement. In 1957, he writes, the JOT personnel officer is doing what Agency placement officers did in the expansion years. Those years ran from 1949 to 1952. He kept statistics on the work from February 18 to July 1, 1957. His own screening of candidates, he concedes, is broader than the deeper probing done by the JOT program officers. Those officers decide finally.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000200060003-6:
A letter dated June 27, 1957, to Matthew Baird encloses a copy of a personal letter its writer, an Agency junior officer trainee, had sent about the JOT program. The covering note responds to a memorandum Baird had circulated to all trainees on June 5 about the future of the program. The writer explains that settling into a new job had delayed his answer.

The enclosed letter praises the program staff who had helped him: they were always ready to assist, he writes, and dissolved the bureaucratic fog that gathers around even simple problems. He adds that any program so closely tied to one man takes on that man's character, and he counts the staff's qualities as the direct result of Baird's influence over them.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000200100017-6:
Weekly Activity Report number 41, dated October 12, 1956, goes from the Chief of the Plans and Policy Staff to the Director of Training. It leads with the Foreign Language Development Program. On October 10, staff met with Mr. Karamessines. They discussed the DD/P position paper on the program. It was agreed that regulation instruments were needed. They would put a Career Council decision into effect.

It was also agreed that the DD/P paper was not a useful basis for revising those regulations. DD/P would instead supply a paper of its own. That paper would name the specific change it wanted in each regulation. Other items report training course proposals reviewed and approved. They also report an article planned for the November OTR Bulletin. The article would explain new procedures for selecting Agency candidates for the senior defense schools.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300030005-6:
Weekly Activities Report number 39, dated October 2, 1958, from the Chief of the Agency's Language and Area School, reports a staffing gain in prospect. Informal arrangements with the Far East division were expected to bring a native speaker of Korean to the school on detail. He would completely redo the school's Korean tapes and help with any Korean class that developed, though talk in the division of a part-time class had quieted for the moment.

An attached report from the Deputy for Language Training covers a Saturday morning briefing in the R&S auditorium. Forty-five instructors, new and old, from the Voluntary Language Training Program attended, to have the program's methods explained and demonstrated to them.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300030014-6:
Weekly Activities Report number 30, dated July 31, 1958, from the Chief of the Language and Area School, reports on the monthly language training roundtable of the intelligence community. It met on July 24 and 25, with the Navy, Air Force, National Security Agency, State Department, and CIA represented. The report praises the format: a leisurely setting that allows long hours of informal professional talk alongside the formal business.

Testing numbers dominate the rest. In the past two weeks 135 oral examinations had been given in ten languages, from French and German to Chinese and Japanese, bringing the total since June 1 to 602. Of the original group of 850 people to be tested, about 125 remained, most of them away on vacation.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300030023-6:
Weekly Activities Report number 21, dated May 29, 1958, comes from the Chief of the Agency's Language and Area School. It mixes personnel errands with course news. A specialist could report for temporary duty on May 27. He would gladly review a case again in September. By accident, the school found itself passing an individual to another office. That office wanted him for an operational assignment.

Two teaching losses are noted with regret. The SR division asked to pull one of the best students from the intensive Russian course on June 13. The Far East division recalled a student two days before his course ended. On the brighter side, a young man was engaged to give extra drill hours to Greek students. A course in Japanese grass writing, the most cursive hand, was planned for January. It would have forty-eight class hours.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300050030-6:
Weekly Activity Report number 13 of the Registrar's office covers March 26 to April 1, 1958. It opens with a clipping from Lovejoy's College Digest, an article titled Electronic Computers Stimulate Need for Corps of College-Trained Experts. The article surveys twenty-three colleges and universities with automatic computers on campus and predicts 10,000 electronic computers in use in the United States by 1966, requiring a trained force to run them.

A harder item follows: a USIA employee was excluded from a course because the future assignments and cover of two Agency students ruled out their attending alongside him. The decision, reached after checking that the division's position was genuine, was to be passed to USIA with understandable reluctance, since the course had been announced openly.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300070001-6:
Weekly Activities Report number 43 comes from the Agency's School of International Communism and the USSR. It covers October 24 to 30, 1958. Its significant item is a success story from the National War College. A student from the school had lately won acclaim there. He was chairman of the winning committee in the first student problem. He reports, modestly, on his own part. His committee's contributions were so poor that he tore them up. He wrote the brief himself, on leadership in the rise of Soviet power and the decline of Western influence.

Other items are working arrangements. Material requested by the NEA division was made available to it. An ORR lecturer would address the Mid-Career Officers Course at the Foreign Service Institute. The school agreed to supply a lecture on Soviet intelligence. It was for a proposed chief of stations course.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300110006-6:
Weekly Report number 7 of the Assessment and Evaluation Staff covers February 5 to 11, 1958, and is addressed to the Director of Training. Its significant item is a profile of the people the Agency was testing. Against a reported rise of interest in scientific matters, the report lists the major college subjects of candidates tested between December 1955 and May 1956. Social sciences, including area studies, dominate with 142 candidates, followed by the humanities with 38.

Business and commerce, earth sciences, engineering, and mathematics trail far behind, and the physical and biological sciences record none at all in this count. The week's other business includes an assessment conducted on February 7 and 8, and an argument over course length: anything beyond the minimally essential period, one paper holds, is gravy.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000400030083-6:
The Agency's Intelligence School Weekly Report number 4 covers January 23 to 30, 1958. It reports no significant items. A tentative schedule had been prepared for a forthcoming course. A formal request had been received from the Office of Communications. It asked for a Supervision Special. A draft answer accepting it was prepared for the Director of Training's signature.

An experimental Introduction to Supervision course was announced. It covered grades GS-9 to GS-11 and ran from February 17 to 21. By the Registrar's figures, it was already oversubscribed. Demand for supervision training, the report notes, is plainly large. The grade range for the course may have to widen. Clerical figures follow. Of two people tested in shorthand that week, none qualified. All four tested in typewriting qualified.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000400090005-6:
Weekly Activity Report number 47 comes from the Agency's Junior Officer Training Program. It covers November 19 to 25, 1958. The Security Office had no objection to a Christmas party. The trainees of the Integrated Program would hold it at Bolling Air Force Base on the evening of December 18. Two conditions applied. Proper decorum was to be kept, and each man's assigned cover was to be maintained. The party would be held in the Billy Mitchell Room. It would start at half past eight or nine. A trainee was in charge of the project.

Another item takes up assignments in the NEA division. An officer had been asked to examine one question. It was the use of Negro personnel there, in the report's own wording. His opinion was narrow. They could be used effectively only in certain types of work. The conditions were tied to the specific job rather than to the geographical area.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000200040001-6:
The Commission on Organization of the Executive Branch of the Government sends Congress its report on intelligence activities in June 1955. The letter of transmittal is dated June 30, 1955. It rests on Public Law 103 of the 83rd Congress, approved July 10, 1953. The investigation behind the report was performed by a task force. Its chairman was General Mark W. Clark, then president of The Citadel. The report ranges across the intelligence machinery of the whole government.

Its pages weigh how each service organizes its intelligence work. One passage faults the Air Force arrangement. In it, the intelligence chief answers to a deputy chief of staff. He does not answer to the Chief of Staff himself. The report says this layering hurts the efficiency of staff operations. The copy survives in the Agency's declassified files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000200070008-6:
An address reviews the Office of Training as its fourth year draws to a close, in what the speaker calls a kind of State of the Union message about the office. Achievements, relations with the rest of the Agency and with the intelligence community, and the road ahead are its themes. The year just past earns a nickname: the Year of Inspections. The office was examined in turn by the Inspector General, by the Management Staff, by the Doolittle Group, and finally by the Clark Committee, which was not through with it yet.

Plans fill the later pages. One course would be offered twice a year until the need for it was met. Reading work was expanding on several fronts, with an Advanced Reading Improvement Course, a French Reading Improvement Course, and a reading analysis program grown out of them.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000300100006-6: Minutes of the first meeting of the Professional Selection Panel, held August 22, 1952, record the panel organizing itself. A temporary chairman was chosen and secretarial help arranged. Voting membership was settled. Advisory representation, including a medical voice, was discussed. The Career Service Program still awaited the Agency Director's approval. The panel could not yet discharge the whole of its business. Cases before it were for information rather than final action. The scan is heavily garbled. Names and several decisions cannot be read with confidence.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000300100015-6:
Remarks by General Walter B. Smith to the Eighth Agency Orientation Course take up the career service in the CIA. His answers to questions follow. Smith tells the new officers that questions about a career service are always with the Agency. People, he says, want to see themselves in a settled relation. They want a place in the overall business of the Agency, alongside their own narrower careers. He asks the audience's indulgence as he works through the subject.

He stresses the standing the Agency's people had already won. They held key positions through professional competence. He calls the quality of its citizens the key to effective operations. A question on personnel turnover draws a measured answer. Turnover is relatively small, though still a concern at the Agency's size. The scan is garbled in places, so some passages cannot be followed closely.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000400140001-6:
Staffing work on the conclusions of a survey of overseas training follows the survey team from station to station. Language training dominates the findings. Stations, the report says, afford their personnel the chance to study foreign languages. The study is at Agency expense. A number of staff employees have taken that chance. Some of them went on to intensive language training after arrival. One station is praised for a well-planned program. It provides proficiency testing.

Against that stand wide differences among stations. The differences lie in how their language programs are carried out. The staffing paper works through what the conclusions require. The file opens with a routing slip. It carries the survey's recommendations into the machinery of assignment and support. There, training conclusions become billets, funds, and orders.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100060005-6:
A survey of the CIA Budget Staff is reported on March 16, 1950. It sets its purpose plainly. The team was to judge whether budgeting methods in the Agency are sound and accurate. It was to judge whether they are as simple as they can be made. It was to judge whether budget and fiscal operations have been separated as far as possible. The surveyors assume their readers already know something. The Agency has a good budget program run by capable people. The team therefore hunts only for further improvement and simplification.

One fault they find is procedural. Project submissions were prepared by the operating activity. They went straight to the reviewing committee. The Agency Budget Officer sat on that committee, but at a handicap. He first saw the papers there. The survey holds it would be far better for him to review every project before the committee met.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100080003-6:
A statement dated September 3, 1957, fixes the mission and functions of the Office of Security. Its mission is twofold: to prepare and execute the Agency's security program, and to perform security inspection functions. The functions begin with policy: the office recommends Agency security policies and builds the procedures that carry them out.

The office also stands at the gate of employment. Through investigation, technical interrogation, and liaison contact it obtains and weighs information about people proposed for employment, assignment, or association with the Agency, and it approves or disapproves them on security grounds. It keeps current records of the security acceptability of overt and semi-covert staff, and it controls certain outside activities and official actions of Agency employees from the security side.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100080012-6:
Proposed statements of functions for the Security Office set out what each of its staffs should do. The Policy Staff's draft covers four fields. They are joint and interdepartmental work, finished intelligence, and advice on the security side of Agency activities. They include service as security adviser to the Agency's honor awards board. The Inspection Staff would make special security inspections. They would cover Agency installations at home and abroad, and contractors' facilities. The staff would judge the security suitability of outside training arrangements.

A third staff handles people. It runs security investigations of overt and semi-covert personnel. It appraises the reports for adequacy of coverage and pertinence. It approves or recommends against the employment of staff, consultants, and contractors. Those judgments are made on security grounds. The statements are drafts. They are meant to fix in writing who in the office does what.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100090011-6:
Recruitment for the former Government Printing Office plant is the subject of a February 1957 memorandum. It goes to the Deputy Director (Support). A January 30 memorandum had told the Office of Logistics of a change. The Agency's personnel ceiling had been increased. The increase provided for the transfer of the printing plant. The memorandum asked two things. It asked for justification for filling any of the plant's vacant positions. It asked for a report of the savings expected from the transfer.

The reply describes a deliberate pause. The office's original plan was to weigh the plant's true personnel needs first. It would use several months of operating experience before deciding anything. Only then would it act. It would either cut the number of slots, or recruit to fill the vacancies. The vacancies counted would be those real work had shown to be necessary.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100090020-6:
A staff study asks one question about the Administration Building printing plant. Can its workload problem be eased by adjusting the demands laid on it? Requirements on the plant fall into three classes. They are the National Intelligence Survey program, the Agency's own non-survey work, and work for other agencies. The workload problem, the study says, is directly tied to one thing. It is the size of the staff available to meet those demands. The survey program accounts for the largest block of plant manhours.

Relief is sought from the users. The largest single Agency user outside the survey program is named. The Chief of the Cartographic Division undertakes to hold back some work. He would hold re-runs of published maps and other non-priority map printing. That work could be done in the plant's slack time. Recommendations go to the Deputy Director (Support) for approval.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100170003-6:
A study of the Agency's Technical Accounting Staff opens with its problem. The team was to judge the staff's mission, functions, and procedures. It was to judge its delegations of authority and its staffing needs. The test was propriety and adequacy. The staff had been established by the Comptroller. Authority was delegated to it by him, to help him carry out his mission. Judging how effectively its individual projects worked was expressly outside the study's scope.

The facts build a picture of overload. An analysis covers the projects taken up in the period ending June 30, 1956. It counts projects begun, completed, and left unfinished in each fiscal year. The count points to a rising workload. The staff, the study finds, was taking on more work than could be finished promptly. Its target dates were unrealistic.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100210008-6:
A recommendation for installing Flexowriter machines in the Agency's Office of Logistics transmits the results of a study. The study was made jointly by two groups. They were the Business Machines Service of the Management Staff and members of the office's own Supply and Procurement Division. The machines would prepare certain operating documents. Those documents are needed to replenish stock items. The writer concurs in the study's recommendations. He offers the Business Machines Service's help with the installation, if the office agrees.

The waste the machines would cure is retyping. As the attached report describes the flow, a requisition is typed in the division and forwarded. The same item name is then typed by hand onto an invitation to bid or a purchase order. The full name is typed yet again on the purchase order once a bid succeeds.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100220007-6:
A staff paper on the Printing and Reproduction Division of the Logistics Office finds the present arrangement sound. Photography, printing, and the attendant service functions sit in a services branch, an assignment the paper calls simple and workable. The proposed structure changes it in only one respect, the transfer of a single function between sections. Four separate proposals in the wider study would, however, affect the division's personnel ceiling.

The justification counts the division's people by the same manhour method used elsewhere in the study. Its plant description is concrete: rolls of paper, an automatic processor that fixes, washes, and dries in one continuous run, and electronically controlled trimming devices. The division also keeps photostat and ozalid facilities for the Agency's textual material, maps, and charts.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100230015-6:
Recommendations on clerical training are reviewed for the Deputy Director (Support). The review follows a survey of the Clerical Training Program. With two exceptions, the Agency's Office of Training concurs in the survey's findings and recommendations. It does not concur in two of them. One would offer the Clerical Reference Course from September to June only. The other would delete two positions from the present staff strength of the clerical training unit.

The office's view is that the first recommendation is unwise. It is unwise for the program as it runs. The argument that follows weighs the demand on the school. It weighs the increased calls on the higher courses. It weighs the aggregate of special activities laid on the unit. It weighs the instructor hours its staff actually carries. Those points are set out in the tables attached to the review.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200100018-6:
Flow charts titled Present Flow of EDAC-IWG map one journey. An economic intelligence request moves through the committee system to a finished product. The first chart traces the path from the requesting body. It runs through research divisions and other government agency members. It enters substantive production, then consolidation, review, and editing. It reaches dissemination, and finally returns to the requester.

A second chart follows the same journey for the Economic Intelligence Committee. It begins with a sub-committee's determination of the need for economic intelligence. It begins with its terms of reference. Text attached to the charts states the coordinating rule behind them. A Coordination Staff is charged with coordinating foreign economic intelligence production. It is charged with its development, implementation, and control. The office's responsibilities in the intelligence field would then be met.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200100027-6:
A formal statement describes the functions of the CIA Office of Research and Reports, known as ORR. The office worked under its Assistant Director, with support from an Administrative Staff and a Requirements and Control Staff. Its work was split into three broad fields: economic research, geographic research, and coordination. An organization chart is attached, and each staff and division is named with its duties.

Sections that follow spell out branch-level work in detail. Economic units covered fields such as aircraft, shipbuilding, weapons, and industrial projects, along with production rates, stocks, plants, and investment. Services branches dealt with trade, finance, transport, power, labor, and consumer goods. The statement gives a clear map of how the office divided research tasks.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200110026-6:
An office memo dated 30 September 1949, from the Management Officer to the Executive, reviews plans to reorganize the Office of Reports and Estimates. The plans sent in were judged basically sound, but the memo urges several refinements. The Estimates Production Board should stand as the top production coordination body. The Publications Group should sit at division level as a support element. Requirements work should gain separate staff status because it is substantive, not clerical.

Other changes join the Global Survey and International Organization groups into one division under a single chief. Administrative work in personnel, services, information control, and presentation would be grouped to cut the number of staff chiefs reporting direct to the Assistant Director. All division and staff chiefs would report through the Deputy Assistant Director, and revised charts are attached.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200150004-6:
A March 1956 memorandum for the record, headed Further Interviews under Project 6-24, records talks with CIA finance and personnel offices about how staff clear through the Agency. The Fiscal Division notes that everyone on the vouchered payroll clears through it, and that its only advances are for travel under travel orders, including shipment of effects. Where time is short, a traveler might be sent to Finance for an advance instead.

Other interviews cover separation and return. Payroll staff said clearing a person took ten to fifteen hours of work, and a problem raised more than once was late notice of separations. A central processing branch handled staff going to or returning from overseas duty, staff agents at times included, and returnees who planned to resign were sent on to their own office. The notes show routine procedure in unusual detail.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200170002-6:
Tab I of a 1956 personnel records survey lists where every copy of five chosen forms went inside the CIA intelligence and plans directorates and the Department of State. The forms are the Request for Personnel Action, Notice of Personnel Action, Personal History Statement, Fitness Report, and Profile or qualifications summary. Tables mark each office that received a copy, and a separate mark shows copies that were noted and passed on to another office.

Notes explain how the tables should be read and compare CIA practice with State Department practice. In State, an officer's copy flow could reach many offices, with copies posted and then passed along. A March 1956 check of unofficial files in the two directorates found wide extra copying. The tab makes record duplication visible office by office.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000100020011-6:
A progress report for the Geography Division, dated November 1958, opens with a list of finished work. Production that month included two reports in the CIA/RR-GR series, one GM report, a contribution to a National Intelligence Survey annual, and six support jobs. Named items include Civil Divisions of the World, Part V on the Western Hemisphere, and a GM report on Macedonia, called a perennial bone of contention.

Support jobs served named requesters, from the Department of State to the armed services and internal offices, and covered Siberian transportation, population concentrations, and observation areas for missile indicators. Later sections track outside meetings, including talks on United States mapping requirements and a Working Group on Antarctica preparing a report for higher bodies. Coordination work with other offices fills much of the report.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000100180014-6:
Minutes of the Intelligence Advisory Committee's Ad Hoc Committee on Exchanges record a meeting on 26 August 1958, with the secretary acting as chairman in the chairman's absence. Members listed come from State, the Army, the Navy, the Air Force, the Joint Staff side, and the information agency, among others. The minutes of the 16 July meeting were approved before business began.

Business opened with the widening of committee work to cover exchanges of materiel with Bloc countries, as set out in a status report and an amended paper of 12 August 1958. The Townsend proposal was named as a matter the committee should now take up. Later items weigh placing briefed officers or sources in the USSR for short periods, a point that drew no firm interest. They also weigh the yield of a thrift institutions exchange, where talks on investment policy were expected.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000200110001-6:
A memorandum dated 2 September 1958 sends members the minutes of a National Intelligence Survey Chapter IX Subcommittee meeting held at half past nine on 29 August 1958. Named members and alternates came from air and navy charting and oceanography offices, the Office of Civil Defense side, and CIA, which held the chair. The meeting took up an Army proposal on scheduling.

The Army proposed dropping one Chapter IX from the fiscal 1960 schedule so that the twelve Section 19 portions of the Chapter I Annuals could be finished during fiscal 1959. Discussion of that trade fills the minutes. A later schedule list names countries and target dates, running from Costa Rica and French West Africa to Egypt, Nigeria, Nationalist China, and the USSR, the last carrying five credits. Forecast lists for fiscal 1961 appear as well.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000200220009-6:
An earlier draft memorandum dated 22 August 1958, from the Geography Division side to the Deputy Director for Intelligence, is headed Probable Location of Chinese Sputnik Launching Site. Recent reports from Warsaw and elsewhere were the latest signs, the draft says, that the Soviet Union had decided to work with Communist China on launching an earth satellite. Geographic research then under way on guided missile ranges in China made a geographic estimate of the likely locale possible.

Soviet cooperation would likely require Soviet personnel, missiles, launching gear, and support gear, with the Chinese share expected to be limited. A transplanted Sputnik would fly as the three earlier Sputniks had from Tyura Tam. A supporting map is mentioned. On terrain, narrow river valleys fail the test, while the steppes of Inner Mongolia north of Peiping, level to rolling grass plains, meet the stated needs.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000100110007-6:
A Fifth Annual Progress Report of the Economic Defense Intelligence Committee covers 1 July 1956 to 30 June 1957. Contents list an introduction, a summary of activities, the committee program, and future activities, with tabs for completed reports, other documents sent to members, and cases pending and completed. The program section names planning for economic warfare and an edited transcript of a propellants seminar held in June 1956.

The report notes a growing tendency for the economic defense community, under operational pressure, to deal direct with single intelligence components rather than through the committee. That trend is weighed against a current government review of joint trade control policies and expected talks in the control bodies that autumn. State and Commerce review notes appear on the cover, and the report is marked Secret throughout.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000200030005-6:
A revised memorandum from the Office of National Estimates, dated 17 November 1959, reviews the situation in the Caribbean for the Director. After discussion with Intelligence Board representatives, its general conclusion is that events since estimate SNIE 80-59 have not much changed that estimate's validity. It recommends moving the next Caribbean estimate forward, from March to early January 1960. Short assessments then follow for each country the estimate covered.

On Cuba, adverse trends set out in June had grown much stronger. Castro's radical advisers and the Communists kept gaining ground at the expense of moderates, though final power still seemed to rest with Fidel Castro himself. On the Dominican Republic, the memo sees Trujillo's latent opposition only slowly surfacing. He keeps wide support among the lower classes and peasants, and full backing from the military, the mainstay of his rule.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000300050002-6:
A second copy of paper IAC-D-103/6 carries the Third Semi-Annual Report of the Intelligence Advisory Committee's Ad Hoc Committee on Exchanges, dated 11 February 1958. The cover note again says the report would be placed on the agenda of an early committee meeting for noting. Authorization and organization match the companion copy: a committee set up on 28 February 1956 to gain the most intelligence value from East-West delegation exchanges.

Members again span State, Army, Navy, Air Force, the Joint Staff, CIA, and the Atomic Energy Commission. The information agency attended, and CIA supplied chairman and secretariat. An annex repeats the medical exchange case. An American party brought back vaccine samples, medical literature, and substantial information on Soviet medical research, while the Soviet party probably gained something from visiting American research institutes.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000300050011-6:
Paper IAC-D-101/4, dated 23 April 1957, forwards a report by the Ad Hoc Prisoners Information Support Committee for noting and action on its recommendations. A transmittal memorandum from the Office of the Secretary of Defense, dated 16 April 1957, explains the group's origin. It was created by the Intelligence Advisory Committee in April 1956. Its task was to study the need for an organization to collect, judge, and spread intelligence in support of recovering United States nationals held in Communist countries. All members of the subcommittee concurred in the report.

Passages inside review what machinery already existed for judging and sorting information so the support tasks could be met. They recall that the parent committee had approved two prisoner officers' recommendations in April 1956. It had also agreed to set up the ad hoc working group. The report closes the study the 1956 papers in this band began.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000300090026-6:
Minutes numbered IAC-M-348 record a short committee meeting at a quarter to eleven on 17 June 1958. Director Allen W. Dulles and Deputy Director for Intelligence Robert Amory, Jr. are both marked as presiding for parts of the meeting. Members present match the standing list for State, the services, the Joint Staff, the Atomic Energy Commission, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

Items are recorded in brief. One passage concerns military and political developments in Indonesia, in a section partly removed in this sanitized copy. Estimate NIE 75-58, on conditions and trends in French Tropical Africa, is recorded as approved. The file is the shortest of the June and July minutes in this band, and its brevity reflects how little of some discussions the released copy retains.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000200010042-6:
A sanitized project file consists largely of shipping and receiving forms, with project and personal names removed. Form fields can be read throughout: receiving officer's voucher number, storekeeper, postings, stock or part numbers, dates shipped, and inspection and transport officer blocks. One legible passage names a Westinghouse unit at Friendship International Airport, Baltimore, Maryland, in connection with shipping work.

Other forms in the middle carry repair and shipment entries, with fields for weight, cube, and attachments. Because the forms are fragmentary and heavily redacted, they show the paperwork path of project materiel rather than any single transaction in full. Dates and most figures are not legible enough to quote. The file is best used as evidence of how project shipping was documented, form by form, at the time.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000200130175-6:
An index to general provisions, followed by the full provisions text, runs past one hundred pages. The index lists thirty-eight articles, starting with definitions, changes, extras, variation in quantity, inspection, and responsibility for supplies. Payments, assignment of claims, added bond security, and federal, state, and local taxes follow. Disputes and an article on Soviet controlled areas come next.

Labor articles cover the Eight-Hour Law, here dated 1913 in the index, and the Walsh-Healey Public Contracts Act. Nondiscrimination in employment, officials not to benefit, and contingent fees are also covered. Termination for convenience of the government, patent filing and rights, royalty reporting, and rights in data marked unlimited all appear. Military security requirements and use of small business concerns complete the list. A patent passage in the body requires written disclosure of each subject invention promptly after conception, with a statement whether a patent application will be filed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000300040066-6: A semi-annual cost detail print lists voucher rows by date, voucher number, description, and amount. The vendor name that recurs through the rows is Hycon Manufacturing Company, rendered HYCON MFG CO, beside a BC 200 code. Many rows are adjustment vouchers, marked ADJ VO with differing numbers, rather than fresh charges.
