The sheet is a raw cost listing for that vendor's account, with no narrative text and some digits garbled in the scan.

July 1956 Agency allotment ledger for fiscal year 1957, marked Secret, is headed 07 56 Allot Ledger in the evidence title. Accounts include 7-1004-10-001, 7-1004-30-010, and several 7-1004-50 accounts, one of them labelled Aquatone. cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00900a000100020003-6:
Personnel notice dated 4 June 1958, expiring 1 January 1959, announces a survey of overseas service. The Agency was weighing a better retirement program tied in part to overseas duty, and it lacked central records of past service. Staff were asked for the kind of service, the country, the start and end dates, and the government component served.

Form 1451, Record of Overseas Service, was to go to all vouchered employees, who would fill in their own cards. Staff paid from confidential funds and staff agents were covered by separate return routes, some marked Eyes Only. Forms were due back to the Office of Personnel by 30 June 1958, or 30 July for staff overseas.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00900a000100130010-6:
Untitled numbered advice for a Budget and Fiscal Section opens with Headquarters posting of debts. Daily posting of each debt to its cost centre would stop. In its place, staff would post monthly sums of debts paid off and debts still open. The change breaks with the Agency Handbook, so the Comptroller must agree to it first. A draft request for that agreement goes with the paper.

The case for the change is waste. Daily posting, the paper says, repeats facts already held on the source papers and in section files. Later fixes to those postings waste still more staff time. Later items take up notices for late accountings, sent on a stamped routing slip in place of retyped lists. One more item gives replies to dispatches a higher priority, with room for cases that need more time.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00910a000100020002-6:
Untitled Agency report lists the most significant Management Staff contributions from 1 October 1960 through 31 March 1961. The Records Management Staff had won disposal agreements from six intelligence community agencies, covering Army, Navy, Air Force, the Atomic Energy Commission, State, and the FBI. Those agreements allowed prompt destruction of 1,000 cubic feet of reference material and 3,000 cubic feet more on a continuing basis.

Other work kept shelf filing in use to avoid buying cabinets and safes, and a study of FE Support Staff procedures produced thirty-six recommendations, most of them accepted. The staff also set minimum security accountability records for classified documents in the DD/P, with a standard log and control procedure for Area Divisions and Staffs.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00910a000100020110-6:
Semi-annual report material for the President's Board of Consultants on Foreign Intelligence Activities covers Management Staff work. The period runs from 1 November 1956 to 1 May 1957. Most of the effort went to help Agency components tighten their office practice. Control of posts was pushed down to Deputy Directors through Tables of Organization. That let manpower needs be judged closer to the work itself.

Other items include a new format for Agency regulations and work on clearing a backlog. A study of space moves for the DD/P area is also listed. A check on unvouchered funds found no abuse of that pay route. As a result, 105 employees were moved from the unvouchered payroll to the vouchered payroll.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100020199-6:
Submission dated 28 March 1956 gives economic needs for the Agency's OCI Periodic Requirements List. The list runs from 1 May to 31 July 1956. A new item on the USSR asks for facts on changes at the top of the Council of Ministers. It asks for changes in both people and structure. First deputy chairmen and deputy chairmen are to be named. Their likely duties and special fields are to be given. Most items on the home economy are kept as they stand.

One added item follows the Soviet drive for automation. It cites a new Ministry of Instruments and Means of Automation. It also cites a State Committee for New Techniques. More steps of that kind are asked for. A revised item covers civil defence progress in the Soviet Bloc since 1950. A matching Eastern Europe item asks about shelter building and training for atomic defence.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100050033-6:
Revision of needs for the reading panels of the Agency's Construction Branch goes from the Chief, S/CST, through the Chief, D/S. The branch mission is stated in short form. The branch made all-source economic reports on the building of fixed sites in the Sino-Soviet Bloc. It reported on the making of building supplies. Its scope covers building groups, costs, methods, and design standards. It covers the making and the spread of building supplies.

Interest is mainly in the Bloc and lands near it. Strong interest is shown in deals between any country and a Bloc member. The deal counts when it involves building work, or the supply or receipt of building supplies and gear. Military building classes run from camps and barracks through storage depots, forts, and naval bases, to shelters, training areas, airfields, and guided missile launching sites.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100110027-6:
Memo dated 3 May 1956 reports a visit to Harvard on 24 to 27 April 1956. The report goes to the Assistant Director for Research and Reports. Three aims are listed for the trip. The first was to reassure recruits in processing that the Agency still wanted them. Their patience was asked for as well. The second was to renew contact with faculty members. The third was to judge the job market the Agency had to compete in for trained staff. Appendices list the students and faculty.

All students first approached the past fall still wanted Agency work. One case stands apart from the rest. That student, due an M.A. in June from the Soviet Union program, had taken a post elsewhere at 5,500 dollars a year. No firm Agency offer had come by 1 April, though a lower Agency figure had pleased the student before that. Faculty were found courteous and highly cooperative.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180002-6:
Confidential memo in the Agency's files, dated 21 November 1957, is numbered ED/EC D-126/4. It goes from the Chairman of Working Group I to the Chairman of the Executive Committee. It comments on reports of the EC Ad Hoc Subcommittee on List Review. The reports are ED/EC D-126, 126/1, and 126/2. Working Group I had taken up the first three reports in a run of meetings. The group weighed what they meant for the strategic trade control system as a whole, and their advice on single changes to the COCOM lists.

The first head concerns a new test in ED/EC D-126/1. Questions arose over how that test would work in practice. Later points take up the timing of list changes, with a view that decisions could be made much faster than at present. A yearly review of List III, by majority vote of COCOM members, is also put forward.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180011-6:
Secret paper dated 24 September 1956 comments on the Defense Department's sector approach to strategic trade controls. It is Project No. 11.162 of the Agency's Economic Defense Division, ORR. That approach had moved through joint committees for about a year. It was first tied to a Defense plan for judging a Japanese bid to relax the China differential, and to a mobilisation base concept. An October 1955 Defense paper on the British thermonuclear warfare concept picked out electric power as a vital sector.

The comments warn against one habit of thought. An item should not be called strategic just because it is of direct use to the military, or enters the last stage of making military goods. The sector plan is judged unworkable in part. The Bloc made many of the goods and gear such sectors needed. It leaned only slightly on imports for them.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180020-6:
Statistical Review of East-West Trade 1956-57, kept in the Agency's files, forms part of a report to Congress. It is part of the Eleventh Report under the Mutual Defense Assistance Control Act of 1951, the Battle Act. The Department of State issued it as Publication 6684. It is General Foreign Policy Series 132, released in July 1958. The Government Printing Office printed it. A letter of transmittal sends Congress the eleventh half-year report on work under the Act. That work ran from 1 July to 31 December 1957.

Sections by country describe how allied governments ran strategic trade controls. Italy, for one, used a joint committee of ministries for the task. The committee screened import and export licence requests for controlled goods. Italy ran import certificate and delivery check procedures as well. It made end-use checks on strategic exports where such checks seemed fit.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180039-6:
Minutes ED/EC M-252 record a meeting at 2:00 p.m. on 9 July 1957, in Room 1213, Maiatico. They were issued on 15 July 1957. Mr. Hale chaired the meeting. The Agency, Commerce, Defense, ICA, State, and Treasury sat at the table. An opening note takes up a Paris cable of 8 July. Numbered items cover Working Group I advice on List II quotas. They cover the NSC and CFEP task to review economic defense policy.

The Paris cable was a request from the United States delegation for guidance. Points were due to come up when the CHINCOM talks opened on 16 July. The State member went through the questions and the draft replies. Talk on quotas brought out one clear view. The delegation should have wide room to move. Full use should be made of two-way talks, to win a better reaction from partner countries.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180093-6:
Official Use Only memorandum in the Agency's files, dated 10 February 1958, from Mr. Metzger of the Legal Adviser's office to Admiral DeLany deals with Eximbank credits for exports from the United States and the Battle Act. It answers a February 6 memorandum enclosing an Eximbank letter of December 1957. The live question was whether Eximbank credit to private Finnish importers was barred by the Act.

Two sales frame the problem. An Ohio firm wanted Eximbank help to finance two power shovels for use on hydro-power plant construction and waterway cleaning in Finland. Another exporter held an order for machinery worth 75,000 dollars. Finnish buyers would pay 20 percent in cash and wanted two years of credit on the rest, with the American exporters carrying part of that credit themselves.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180138-6: This declassified CIA classified proposal on US economic defense policy went to the NSC. The hidden doctrine. The file holds what remains. The record stays. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180165-6:
Memorandum in the Agency's files to Admiral W. S. DeLany, Deputy Director for Mutual Defense Assistance Control, forwards comments on the first draft of the Eighth Battle Act Report, issued 14 July 1956. A few staff had reviewed the draft, and their comments are sent for whatever use he sees fit. As in past years, the reviewers limited their attention to statements about Sino-Soviet Bloc economic activities.

Chapter I edits are given line by line. One change makes a sentence read that imports from the USSR showed the greatest absolute increase, and from Communist China the next. Another corrects a sentence so Communist China, as a single country of the Bloc, had a distribution of trade. Later notes add the word approximately before an expenditure figure of about 30 million dollars, given uncertainty over its exact size.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200080011-6:
Agency requirements memo takes up congestion in the Shanghai port area. The scan is partly garbled, but the shape of the paper is clear. Congestion at Shanghai had been reported for years, in varying degree, and a 1956 report raised it once more. The causes were not fully clear. The tie-up was traced in part to the rate at which goods arrived, and to a shortage of labour. Poor harbour management, limits in port sites and storage space, and limits in output plans are named too.

The needs were written for a source able to weigh each factor. Detailed questions follow in the memo. They ask about the labour force in set areas of the port. They ask about storage areas and how long goods sat in them. They ask whether wharf areas were full. They ask how cargo was handled in each area, by type of goods.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200090038-6:
Paper dated 8 January 1958 for Working Group I of the Economic Defense Advisory Committee gives the Agency member's intelligence. The subject is the Soviet Bloc position in rolling mills, presses, and gear making machinery. Growth in the steel industry has slowed across the Bloc since 1955. The slowdown is sharpest in the Soviet Union. It is traced to a failure to supply the capital gear needed for the first goals. That gear had to come from Bloc resources.

Rolling and finishing gear had long been neglected in the Bloc. The Soviet Ministry of Ferrous Metallurgy had put its spending on primary iron and steel making plant. The Fifth Five Year Plan goal for new iron ore mining capacity fell short by 26 million tons. Press sections then count types built by rated pressure. They list mechanical presses, and hydraulic forging and bending presses. They list extrusion presses from about 1,300 tons up to 6,000 tons.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200120007-6:
Agency Current Support Memorandum No. 620, dated 24 November 1958, reports Chinese Communist ship chartering since mid-1958. SINOFRACHT is the Chinese ship chartering body. In past years it had secured many vessels through a British registered company. In recent months it was dealing openly for the first time. It had chartered more ships than before on the open market.

By September the Chinese had placed 108 ships under time charters. About 65 were for less than one year. About 33 were for more than one year. The paper sets out the gains China drew from the switch. A depressed world charter market offered the lowest prices in many years. Locking ships in for long spans at those prices guarded China against a later rise. Owners' refusal to grant options underlined that point.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200120016-6:
Agency Current Support Memorandum No. 599, dated 20 August 1958, reports congestion on Yangtze River transport. The Leap Forward had brought the tie-up, the paper says. The difficulties flowed from increased output under the current Leap Forward program. Fairly severe congestion had been reported on the Yangtze in 1956. That was the last year with a speed-up in economic growth. The Chinese had then worked on port sites. They had cut the problem to minor size by 1957.

Timing marks the change between the two years. Congestion in 1956 came late in the year. It peaked in the fourth quarter. In 1958 it arrived earlier in the year. The new output push drove it. The river system did not yet have the port and handling capacity for the extra cargo. The campaign was generating that cargo at the time.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200130051-6:
Russian-language technical text with drawings, kept in the Agency's files, describes a solid-type air raid shelter. It is set against the layer-type shelter in the same manual. Much of the file is given to a plan of a basement shelter. It is given to a schematic drawing, numbered figure 31 in the text. It shows the filter and ventilation installation for such a shelter. Parts named in the legible text include air intake chambers, industrial filters, air ducts, sealed doors, filter absorbers, and ventilators with motor and hand drive.

The copy is a scanned section of a Soviet civil defence manual, kept in Russian. Its value sits in the engineering detail it holds. It shows how a basement was fitted as a shelter, how air was drawn in and cleaned, and how the gear was arranged in the space available.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200140014-6:
Paper in the Agency's files takes up the contest for control of Yemen. The scan is partly garbled, but its subject and main lines are legible. Yemen had become a field of Bloc attention at the time. Credits of 25 million dollars to Yemen are named in the text. Bloc military assistance ran alongside the economic offers. The contest is framed as part of a wider Bloc drive in the area. The drive used aid and arms to gain a footing on the Red Sea coast.

Details in the legible parts include an airfield near Hodeida. Soviet technicians are reported in connection with its building from September of the year discussed. Arms deliveries were arranged through third parties. The paper weighs one question above the rest. What would a Bloc foothold in Yemen mean for the states backing the rival side? That side was the other party in the Yemeni contest.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200180010-6:
Minutes TSC-M-54, dated 7 August 1958, record a Subcommittee on Transportation meeting held 29 July 1958. The meeting sat in Room 1121, M Building, convened at 1000 hours. An Army chairman presided. Members came from the services, the Joint Chiefs, OSD, State, Commerce, and the Agency. The chairman reported that he and the secretary had attended the Economic Intelligence Committee meeting of 7 June 1958. The parent committee there reviewed the subcommittee's work for fiscal year 1958.

Praise from that review is recorded in the minutes. The EIC chairman said the subcommittee should be commended for fine work. Its members had shown eagerness to grapple with intelligence problems in their field. They had shown eagerness to resolve those problems as well. The EIC also asked the subcommittee to review priority research gaps. A capabilities group chairman then reported on the Baltic to the Alps paper. Its final draft was already prepared, he said.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000400070003-6:
Secret compilation on implementation of the Killian Report works through NSC Action 1430 item by item, in the same series as the panel implementation papers in this file group. On peripheral war, the study of techniques and weapons technology is noted as running through the Weapons Systems Evaluation Group and an Agency contract. Specific Recommendation C.4 follows, on examining intelligence data more broadly, or inventing a new technique, for discovery of hoaxes, with a National Intelligence Estimate as the first step.

Specific Recommendation C.3, on aerial reconnaissance, is treated at length in later pages. The Navy Department had under study the use of high altitude photography from rockets fired vertically, among other work in the services and inside the Agency. The compilation, dated August in the scan with the year in the mid-1950s, lists the more promising of the efforts then under study or development.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000400080084-6:
Secret Agency message dated 10 November 1956, routed through SA/PC/DCI, deals with HTAUTOMAT facilities and staffing. A first point answers a referenced paragraph: an HTAUTOMAT 3 facility should sit within the present restricted area if at all possible. Headquarters' main responsibility for backup of two named units will rest with HTAUTOMAT 1. The intended relationship between the chief of each field component and HTAUTOMAT 1 is set parallel to that between the supervisor of each contractor group and that contractor's home office.

A second point fixes the starting staff. The initial complement of HTAUTOMAT 3 will comprise six to eight people, most of them now in a named status redacted in the scan. Later paragraphs cover planning of layout and bar any additions to HTAUTOMAT 2 or 3 until after full AQUATONE automation steps are complete. Names and places throughout are redacted.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000400100009-6:
Top Secret CHESS report in the Agency's files, cite MSG Whiskey-0148, carries reporting on four countries: Egypt, Syria, Jordan, and Lebanon. A header note orders the top portion deleted before lateral dissemination. Egypt items come first. Abu Suweir Airfield showed 43 Fagots. Alexandria Airfield had 1 C-45 and 1 liaison type, runways serviceable. Amriya and Amriya South were abandoned, and Ballah, unserviceable, showed 60 trucks. Bilbeis Airfield showed 35 T-6 aircraft and 46 probable MiG crates. Cairo Almaza Airfield showed 9 Beagle, 6 C-47 type, 26 Coach and Crate, 3 unidentified single-engine aircraft, and 2 helicopters.

Egypt items turn to sites. An Ismailia camp east showed 10 vehicles, possibly 6 tanks. An ammunition area northeast of Ismailia showed 101 trucks and 24 trailers. The Jabal Umm Tabaq installation showed 110 vehicles, with large amounts of equipment and supplies in open storage. Kasfareet installation showed 180 trucks, 16 tanks, and 6 field artillery pieces. Mahattat al-Ballah showed 46 trucks, possibly 6 tanks and 10 field artillery pieces.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000400100036-6:
Untitled Agency photo report on Syria alone gives airfield returns in full counts. Aleppo Airfield showed 3 Meteor, probably derelict, 1 C-47 type, 4 T-6 type, and 24 single engine piston type, for a total of 32 aircraft. Damascus Airfield showed 9 Fresco type, 2 Fagot type, 12 Meteor type, 6 C-47 type, 1 C-54 type, 4 T-6 type, 1 liaison, and 26 derelict aircraft, with 47 trucks.

Hama Airfield showed 5 Fresco aircraft, an aircraft on a parallel taxiway, 15 aircraft crates, and 16 probable aircraft engine crates, with construction put at 30 percent in the garbled line. Bab el Haoua was unserviceable with no aircraft, Deir ez Zor and Djerah showed none, and Dumier showed no aircraft but continuing construction and extensive trenching near the field. Hums military camps close the report, each estimated at about 60 vehicles.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000400100072-6:
Operational Immediate message in the Agency's files, cite Whiskey-0079, carries photo report No. 1375. Its date of information is 21 May 1957. It covers Jordan, Lebanon, and Syria. Its heading holds a dispute: the report was classified Top Secret CHESS on a commander's instructions, resting on a paragraph of a standing operating procedure. That conflicts with instructions issued by project headquarters, and clarification is requested.

The reporting opens with Jordan. Mafraq New Airfield showed no aircraft, and 100 vehicles. It showed large amounts of unidentified open storage and many probable POL drums. Mafraq Old Airfield showed no aircraft, about 360 tents, 42 possible field artillery weapons, and 28 possible tanks. Later Syria items are mostly negative. Palmyra, Sal es Sahra, and Tango-2 showed no aircraft. Tango-3 gave no information, and Tango-4 showed no aircraft. The run ends with Baniyas Harbor: no shipping reported, with about 20 vehicles at a POL storage area.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000600030005-6:
An Intelligence Advisory Committee paper dated 22 August 1955 takes up intelligence on international communism. It submits two items for the meeting set for 30 August. Tab A holds an Army G-2 memorandum to the committee chairman. That memo voices concern about how intelligence on this subject was produced and handled across agencies. Tab B reports on talks between CIA and the State Department about where wider production should sit.

Those talks ended with an approved finding. Centralising all collation and upkeep of such intelligence in one agency was not practical. Instead, the State Department would expand its production, and CIA would expand work tied to its own operational needs. Together, the two expansions were expected to ease gaps the survey of USIA needs had shown. The G-2 proposal and the joint report both went onto the committee agenda.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700020023-6:
A secret paper on services of common concern runs long, and shares its opening ground with a companion piece. Pearl Harbor exposed a broken intelligence setup. The National Security Act of 1947 could have answered with one agency for every need. Its drafters held back, judging that special units must stay close to service and political planning.

Leadership, not merger, was their answer. One chief would link the bodies, answer upward, and let shared work grow over time. Later pages ask why some tasks landed at the centre at all. Such services sat at the edge of each department's needs, yet held real value for the whole system. Being marginal, they suffered first when department budgets were cut. Split effort also bred waste and raised the risk of security breaches. Those three facts, the paper argues, made a central home the safer course.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700030004-6:
A draft Inspector General report takes up one charge: bias in how raw information gets handled. Critics held that an agency cannot fairly both coordinate and operate. The same body, judging work it also performs, would act as prosecutor and judge at once. Early pages quote that Senate era objection at length. It warned that a coordinator drawn into operations would favour his own shop with the best tasks.

The draft then pushes back with practice. Judging offices inside CIA sit apart from the field arm that gathers the reports. Staff insist those judges feel no loyalty toward home product. If anything, they grade it more harshly than outside agencies do. Other consumers of field reporting sit behind walls of their own, the draft adds. The result, it argues, is review free of the lean the critics feared.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700050039-6:
A progress report dated 5 March 1951 lists interagency problems engaging the coordination office. It is marked as the second such report. Headings name the Agency parts chiefly concerned. First item: biographic intelligence. Agencies were asked on 29 January to answer a survey on the best shared biographic facility for the federal system. Most have replied, and joint advice on improving current practice will follow once answers are sorted.

Other entries move fast. Managers have agreed a rewrite of an administrative instruction, bound for the Director. Defence directives sent for committee views were put off at the 8 February meeting. They would place CIA voices at centre directing levels, speaking for civilian agencies. A separate entry covers papers for defectors and other aliens of value: a letter went to Deputy Attorney General Ford on 23 February. Later items include psychological warfare support, where present terms leave the lead with the State Department.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700070055-6:
A first yearly report of the Intelligence Working Group, dated 18 September 1953, covers August 1952 to July 1953. The group backs the Economic Defense Advisory Committee with intelligence support. Its birth came from a joint proposal by the Director for Mutual Security and the Secretary of State, backed by the Secretary of Defense. Terms were cleared on 29 July 1952 and revised in February 1953.

Seats are spread wide. Intelligence arms of State, Army, Navy, Air Force, and CIA hold full places. Associate seats go to aid, defence, commerce, and treasury offices tied to economic defence. CIA supplies both chair and executive secretary through its research arm. Later pages describe how action bodies may call on the group for direct help. Set channels let work groups draw on its files and skill. CIA now routes most of its own economic defence material through the group for review and joining up, the report notes.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100160003-6:
An Air Intelligence Information Report from the Air Attache in London, dated 11 June 1958, passes on a Soviet press piece. Captain Clinton Adams signed the report. Its subject is the same Tumanov piece on synthetic materials in aircraft construction, from Sovetskaya Aviatsiya of 25 May 1956. An abridged translation came with the report, in four copies.

The summary names four aircraft the piece touches: the TU-104, TU-114, IL-18, and AN-10. Glass fibre worked into foam plastic gives structural strength. Glass cloth plastic serves for soft fuel tanks. Perspex makes aircraft windows, and synthetic glues bond metal to metal or to other stuff. An epoxide resin coats metal. The attache's own verdict is cool: the piece stays very general. It may still serve as background reading on how Soviet builders used new materials in airframes.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100480071-6:
A third copy of the second yearly report of the Intelligence Working Group fills the file, dated August 1954. Coverage runs from 1 July 1953 to 30 June 1954. The opening restates the group's three duties for the Economic Defense Advisory Committee. It musters data, flags gaps for collection, and supplies reports and current facts. A wide list of cases shows how broad its work ran.

One early case gets depth: Soviet financial operations. A subgroup under a Treasury chairman was formed to study the bloc's external financial dealings. It judged both the need for facts in that field and how good the stock was. The report is candid about missed chances too. In a case on differing controls for the European bloc and Communist China, the group could have helped yet was bypassed. A Far Eastern working group called on CIA direct instead.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100490007-6:
A list of papers on economic defence is sent under a short memo dated 10 June 1955. It answers a request made the day before. The list gathers papers from one office that touch the policy side of economic defence. A warning comes with it: some entries were turned down, or meant for Agency use only. They stay on the list all the same.

Titles and dates then run for pages, from early 1953 into 1955. Many are feeds into bigger estimates. One weighs factors shaping bloc strength at mid-1955. Others cover Soviet bloc powers, Communist China's economy since 1949, and bloc trade returns. Some treat controls at home and abroad, and their likely effect on the West. Later rows turn to Soviet output, trade, and a 1957 forecast. Read whole, the list maps what one research office fed into economic defence debates across two busy years.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100490034-6:
Minutes of the eighth meeting of the Economic Defense Intelligence Committee cover a session held on 14 April 1955. They are dated 15 April. Watching freed goods opens the record. A joint body memo, sent round before the meeting, listed goods to place under intelligence watch. Two Paris cables framed the method: facts could best come through quiet bilateral asks to exporting lands, or from allied control trade figures.

The acting chairman called the talk exploratory. It should not spawn action past what the cables already urged. If CIA took the task on, one desk would bear it as added work. A member warned that desk's facts were fragmentary. Long debate followed on other ways to win the data. A status item then recalled that an East-West trade collection subgroup had been folded at the prior meeting.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100500014-6:
Procedures for the Intelligence Working Group go out to the whole Economic Defense Advisory Committee structure. A cover note states the pack was reviewed and cleared by the group and the Executive Committee. It goes to all parent body members and working group chairmen for their guidance. One set of rules draws special notice: how to ask for intelligence support. Those rules bind the whole structure.

The first attachment is an operating procedure. Its aim is to show new working group chairs what help the group can give. It also fixes how the parent body and the group work side by side. Terms of reference and an office procedure memo ride along. Roots are traced to letters swapped among the Director for Mutual Security, the Secretary of State, and the Director of Central Intelligence.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100510013-6:
A CIA study of the Sino-Soviet bloc nickel position in 1957 goes out under a memo dated 29 July 1958. Commerce opened the case. Members had till 8 August to call for debate, or the study would stand approved and the case close. Its findings open the text. Bloc nickel supply in 1957 met the stated needs of direct military use.

It also left room for a fairly low level of civil use. Total supply is put at 59,600 short tons. Output made up about 59,500 tons of that, and net imports from the free world only about 100 tons. All bloc output save a small East German share, under 200 tons, came from the USSR. Priority military demands ate nearly sixty-five percent of Soviet supply, the study adds. To match American levels of nickel in hand, the bloc would have needed about 29,000 tons more, a rise of some thirty-five percent.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100510022-6:
A CIA summary on the glass fiber industry in the Sino-Soviet bloc is dated 9 April 1958. It answers a case opened by member agencies. Findings are numbered and blunt. Bloc output of glass fibers is tiny beside free world output. It also trails the bloc's own plans for wider output of protective goods. Demand from industry and the military will grow faster still.

So the bloc should stay in deficit on this material, the summary judges. Research tells the same story of lag. The bloc sits behind Western Europe and the United States in glass work, optical glass and fibers among it. Yet its research push is strong, above all on superfine fibers to stiffen plastics. Little is printed on exact uses, perhaps for security reasons. Output centres are named: the biggest plant stands at Tallinn. New plants were set for Chernikovsk, Astrakhan, and Gus-Khrustalnyy.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100530002-6:
A tab dated 18 February 1954 lists Intelligence Working Group work for July to December 1953. Finished studies lead. Titles run from a Soviet bloc kyanite study of July to an October appraisal of Soviet offers of chrome, manganese, platinum, and palladium to the United States. A study of the bloc tractor scene runs to twenty-nine pages. A scrap metal study, on Middle East flows in 1952, runs to sixty-four.

Shorter pieces fill gaps: Soviet banks and East-West trade finance, magnetic recorders, and steel wire, strand, cable, and rope. The group's first yearly report sits in the same list. Other entries cover allied review of chemical list items, and signs of bloc weakness under controls on boron compounds. Work in hand follows: Soviet bloc financial operations, and diversions of strategic metals. Tin, lead, zinc, and antimony from four Latin American lands form one part of that diversion study, dated to 1952 and 1953.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000200050040-6:
A business letter dated 6 June 1956 makes final plans for a propellants seminar. It comes from the chief of chemical engineering research at Battelle Memorial Institute in Columbus, Ohio. The reader is a woman at 2430 E Street in Washington. Four Battelle staff need security clearance for the seminar, set for 13 and 14 June. Their names have gone to the Battelle security office for passing on.

Needs for the talk are modest. A projector for standard slides will do, with a blackboard if one can be had. Printed matter will be brought for handing out. The writer asks in return for word on the meeting place and the day's times: start, breaks, and close. A copy went to a Colonel Brewer. A second paper in the file, dated 12 July 1956, is too garbled in this scan to follow in full. It seems to deal with the seminar record after the event.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000200050059-6:
Sets of questions for a propellants seminar fill the file, built by a working group after its 16 December 1955 meeting. A note dated 9 May 1956 sends six copies on to a Battelle expert, by way of a colleague. The aim is stated up front: export control policy on single goods needs facts, and these questions hunt them.

Early questions are broad. Are propellants mainly for war use, and what else are they for? Who, by land or firm, knows how to make them? Could output be curbed by barring the machines that make them, or growth curbed by holding raw stocks? Is there one key material whose control would bite hardest? Supply gets the same test, for made goods and raw stocks, in the free world and the bloc. Later sections drill into boron compounds, asking for their source and the bloc's skill in the field.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000200050068-6:
Question sets for a fuel and propellant symposium fill the file, passed on by a CIA export policy staffer to a colonel. Set I opens broad. What does a propellant do under shifting height and air density, or under shifting needs of speed and range? When does a propellant fall under the munitions list, and thus under world control as a weapon good?

A survey follows by use: aircraft, missiles, rockets, and torpedoes. Needs differ by field, and cases are asked for. Magnesium and boron get a special probe: where do they, or their compounds, fit best, and what other metals were tried, with what results? Hydrazine, cellulose nitrate, and perchlorates are each placed in turn. Set II drills into cellulose nitrate alone. It asks what marks split propellant grades from other grades: nitrogen count, thickness, softening.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000200080010-6:
An explainer on the allied export control system fills the file, though parts of the scan read poorly. It defines two Paris bodies. The Consultative Group joins the taking part lands at senior level. Under it sits COCOM, the coordinating committee. COCOM is a standing, informal body, not backed by any treaty. Its member lands pledge to curb strategic goods to the Soviet bloc, yet each land runs its own controls and its own enforcement gear.

Twelve lands are listed as taking part, among them Britain, France, the Low Countries, Norway, West Germany, Italy, Portugal, Denmark, the United States, and Canada. Greece, Turkey, and Japan are weighed for seats. Lists sort the goods: the first international list holds goods agreed for full embargo. Later pages turn to American law. The Battle Act presses lands that take American aid to bar set goods to bloc buyers.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000200170001-6:
A Periodic Requirements List for the Far East, issued by the Office of Current Intelligence, covers 1 October 1959 to 31 January 1960. It is Guide No. 164, and it runs very long. Opening pages explain the series. Each list flags the facts needed for current coverage of big moves across a four month span. 

Needs come from State's intelligence and regional arms and from three CIA offices. Gaps flagged in post-mortems on national estimates also feed in. The lists go out to collection arms of every board agency. In total they may outrun any one collector's reach, the intro admits. Sample needs deep in the file seek life details on men in a political party and its linked bodies. Moves by pro-Communist hands to seize that party draw keen interest, as do bids to spread its work into Borneo.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000200010022-6:
A fat file presses the case for giving CIA power to apply patent secrecy orders itself. A memo dated 21 June 1957, to the Office of General Counsel, opens it. Finds from the technical services research program have already led to patent bids, it states. Secrecy orders must in time fall on those bids. Counsel has been sounding out the steps to win that power, after informal talks with the research staff.

The memo confirms the ask in firm terms. Such orders might run from three to ten a year from that one program alone. Other Agency arms would add more. Without the power, CIA must beg a named agency to act for it. Defence might help at times, it concedes, but not always. Acting for another also brings money risk: an inventor can claim pay for harm a secrecy order causes. Statute text rides in the file, sections 181 and 182 in full.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300070007-6:
A legal memo dated 7 January 1958 weighs a Comptroller General ruling for Agency training. The comptroller had asked what limit ruling B-134318, of 15 November 1957, sets on training spend. The ruling ties meeting costs to work close to an agency's own statutory tasks. Broad topics shared by all agencies, management among them, fall outside that line.

The case behind the ruling came from Commerce. Its act let salary funds pay for meetings of bodies tied to the work the funds serve. The Comptroller held that wording could not pay for a management conference. Counsel's memo works through whether a bar built on that wording reaches CIA's own courses and conferences. General subjects such as management draw the closest look. A second memo to the General Counsel rides in the file, on the same question, showing the point was weighed at two levels before the Agency settled its course.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300070016-6:
A short memo dated 17 January 1957 moves a language awards plan toward a formal ask. It goes to the deputy director for support, from an assistant general counsel. Counsel held doubts on the law behind paying incentive awards under the planned Language Resources Program. Loose talks with audit staff hint a kind view might be won from the Comptroller General. Still, a formal filing is needed, the memo holds.

A draft filing for the Director's signature rides along. One point of contrast is noted. The Foreign Service holds no like program yet. It may have to seek its power through fresh law instead. The draft plea itself, partly garbled in this scan, sets out why the Agency must keep staff skilled in many tongues. Judging skill fairly is hard, it argues, and standards must be set and held if the awards are to mean anything.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300150008-6:
A study of manpower control for the Clandestine Services goes forward in late November 1958. A cover note sends it to the Director ahead of a December meeting. Their concurrence is sought at this stage, before the plan hardens.

The study's core fear is age. Left alone, it warns, the Clandestine Services will be staffed by a mostly old group by 1974. Its first tab charts that drift. The cure has two parts: fix a fair spread of staff by age, and win the legal and office power to hold that spread. Tab B sets a target spread by age and by grade. Both differ sharply from today's shape. Men ill-suited to secret work would be picked out up to age thirty-five. Past fifty, a set share would face forced exit each year.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300200011-6:
A memo weighs two texts on how much Soviet science print the West can get. One is a law journal piece. Jennie and Herschel Clesner, staff to a Senate subcommittee on patents and copyright, wrote it for the Federal Bar Journal. 

Washington, they claim, sits on powers it has held for years and does not use. Commerce and the National Science Foundation take blame by name. A great flood of Soviet science print flows in, they say, then gathers dust in the Library of Congress and like stores. Working scientists and businessmen never learn it exists. The pair also claim the state hides its own paid work, and that no one office is trained to screen secret science for release. The memo then turns to a like piece from CIA's own hand, and sets the two side by side.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300200020-6:
A letter dated 14 November 1957 sends a cleaned text to the State Department. Lawrence Houston writes to Loftus E. Becker, the Department's legal adviser. The piece at stake is an Agency study of a hard point: how to hold back facts sought by courts or by Congress. Parts of it touched live Agency work that could not be shown.

Becker had asked, in July, if the secret parts could be cut and the rest shared. That has now been done. Two copies of the open text ride with the letter, and more sit ready if he wants them. One tip of Becker's is taken up with thanks. The study now cites the President's 1954 letter to the Defense Secretary, which carried a note for the Attorney General on the same point. The cite sits in Annex A, on page two, not in Annex B as Becker had urged.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00634a000100040015-6:
A staff study takes up area study for the secret side's staff. The point at stake is two-part. First, fix what area study should reach. Next, find the lean and cheap path to that reach. The study writes for the Office of Training, which owns the school house.

Its ground notes run wide. The Agency holds set lines on tongue and area study now. Fresh weight comes from the top of the state. The White House, through its boards, and the Hill both press for a higher grade of work by state men past the shores. A Senate text is quoted to the same end. Chiefs of post and their staffs, it says, should know the tongue, the ways, the past, and the frame of each land they serve in. Land skill, it holds too, should grow side by side with trade skill in a man's rise.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00634a000100050005-6:
A memo dated 16 March 1959 gives the first day of the War Planners Conference. It will close on Thursday, with a last word from General Cabell at ten. The crown of day one was a talk by Mr Bissell, then fresh at the helm of the secret side.

Bissell laid out five broad turns he sees in the wind. The group was told to keep them in mind as the small teams worked. One, spelled in the text, shifts the grip on secret work. Schemes will be run from the core with a firmer hand: set plans, tight counts, and a year-by-year check. At the same time, each piece of work in the field gains more free rein. A whole branch was struck from the chart. Two more were split and re-set.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00634a000100080066-6:
Personal Effectiveness Abroad is presented here as a seminar on the cultural and personal factors that shape how Agency staff work overseas. The course description compares the American in his own society with foreign nationals in theirs. Forces that govern behaviour, attitudes, and reactions sit behind that comparison, for both single persons and social groups.

Participants learn where their own habits match or differ from those of the society where they will serve. Physical, mental, and cultural factors in foreign contacts are covered, along with accepted forms of behaviour practised in staged situations. The schedule moves through topics such as interviews, language and gesture, social customs, and political climates, with lunch talks by visiting lecturers.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00634a000100110008-6:
Suggestions for improving the Administrative Procedures course fill this report, written after the writer monitored a running of the course from 30 November through 18 December 1959. The course acquainted staff with the functional organisation of the Agency's main staff elements. It also taught basic techniques for administrative support at headquarters and at field establishments overseas.

Because some students would soon serve as part of very small administrative groups at stations abroad, the report urges revised course aims. More repeated, hands-on practice in varied and complex duties is recommended over lecture alone. Later pages fault vague student comment sheets, asking that feedback state why a lecture worked or how it could be improved, so teaching can actually get better.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00647a000100160009-6:
Proposals from the United States delegation for the 1959 review of allied export-control lists fill a Coordinating Committee memorandum dated 1 October 1959, numbered 3700.5. Each entry pairs a proposed new definition with a short statement of why the change is sought. The aim throughout is to keep wording matched to machines and gear now in real military use.

Spin-forming machines open the list, redefined so the embargo catches metal-forming machines that shape nose cones and missile parts while sparing smaller machines. Aircraft-making machinery follows. Later items bring space vehicles into wording for telemetering and telecontrol gear, a change the delegation calls a modernising step. The memo shows export control being rewritten, line by line, for the missile and space age.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00647a000100200004-6:
International List I and a new watch list are issued together in French in document 3300, dated 19 December 1958, by the Coordinating Committee for allied export controls. A contents page maps the whole system by category. Metal-working machines come first, then chemical and petroleum gear, electrical equipment, general industrial gear, transport, electronics and precision instruments, metals, chemicals, rubber, and miscellaneous goods.

Each category gives the number range and page for both List I and the watch list. Annexes add administrative principles, explanatory notes, a munitions list, and an atomic energy list. The body of the volume then defines controlled items one by one, down to chemicals such as sodium nitride and synthetic hydraulic fluids with stated viscosity limits. It is the rulebook allied officials used to police trade with the Soviet bloc.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00680r000100280048-6:
An intelligence production program for United States Army, Pacific, issued from its headquarters office of the Assistant Chief of Staff, sets out what the command's intelligence division must produce. Its main mission is support for the commander, who supplies forces and logistics to United States Forces, Korea, and ground forces across the Pacific command area under current war plans.

Intelligence is required for conventional and unconventional plans in the Pacific area under cold war, limited war, and general war conditions, plus security and early warning against enemy attack. Long annex tables tie production to named operation plans, listing intelligence annexes for plans numbered in the thirties and beyond, an evacuation plan. The regions and headquarters responsible for each piece of work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-01094r000400020007-6:
Survey results for the Soviet Republics Division reach the Director of Central Intelligence from Inspector General Lyman B. Kirkpatrick. The main finding is stated plainly. The Soviet Union is the Agency's most vital target. Hitting it in every way calls for one single secret arm set aside for that task alone.

The division was found to chase its aims hard, though at times not well. Much of the fault is laid on outside curbs and limits placed on it. Set steps for fixing the faults are offered for the Director to approve. A draft letter is attached. It asks the deputy director for plans to send his comments on the survey by 1 September 1956.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-01094r000500040013-6:
Two Inspector General reports are summed up for the Director of Central Intelligence in a memorandum on the Office of Personnel and the Career Service Program. The career service review ran alongside a re-inspection of the personnel office and a wider study of personnel management across the Agency. The first inspection of that office had been made in 1953.

Career service, the memorandum warns, was still an extremely controversial subject inside the Agency. Inspectors had talked with all senior officers and a large number of working-level staff to prepare the report, which runs to thirty-seven pages. Later pages describe the personnel office's own machinery, including a records division with branches for transactions, statistical reporting, and central processing of staff paperwork.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200010105-6:
Choices facing Project AQUATONE are laid out in a decision memorandum whose surviving pages open mid-argument. Development work would run into the winter, with one electronics system not ready until late winter, and remaining development was to move to an Air Force base after the start of February. Against that backdrop, decisions were needed by 15 August.

Detachment A's future came first: resume work in Europe, redeploy at once to the Far East, or sit inactive at Wiesbaden. A second detachment at Adana faced the same kind of choice once ready. The writer warns that delay wastes money and ties up scarce technical staff. Well-informed technical opinion, it is noted, gave the U-2 less than a year before the chance of interception began to climb.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200040058-6:
A 6 February 1957 letter to General Nathan F. Twining, Air Force Chief of Staff, takes up the Air Force U-2 program and the move of Detachment C to Atsugi, Japan. Twining's approval of that deployment is thanked warmly. Once Admiral Burke granted access to the base, hangar changes would be pushed through quickly and the detachment moved in.

Space questions run through the letter. The Agency would free room for Air Force U-2 training as fast as it could, since Detachment C's presence limited that training. Only a small Agency group would stay behind after the move, finishing classified development work that could not be relocated. A closing worry concerns press talk linking the program with the Strategic Air Command, which could harm the case for continued overflights.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200110050-6:
A delicate supplier dispute reaches the project leadership in a 26 November 1958 memorandum numbered COR-0211. Richard Leghorn of ITEK had handed over a draft letter from Walter Levison on 20 November, still unsigned and marked as a draft. The letter criticised Eastman Kodak by implication, and Leghorn did not want it treated as an official paper or kept in the files.

The memorandum asks that the draft be handled with discretion by everyone concerned. The differences it aired pointed to a clear need: headquarters staff should study the Eastman and ITEK processors side by side and settle the conflict of opinion. A visit to Rochester to view Eastman's processor was planned. The writer warns that letting the two firms' quarrel fester would run directly against the project's own interest.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200130085-6:
Use of the CORONA product by the armed services is planned in a 16 January 1959 memorandum, COR-0314, to the Deputy Director for Plans. On 6 January a briefing had been held at a secure facility for authorised Air Force, Army, and Navy representatives. After a security briefing, Mr. Lundahl and his staff explained the equipment and procedures planned for processing and exploiting satellite photography.

Joint buying of equipment is stressed as a way to save money. Two clearance problems are foreseen, one immediate and one later. Service plans for secure exploitation centres are listed: the Air Force would build at Strategic Air Command headquarters and at its own headquarters, the Navy at its photographic centre at Suitland. The Army would join the central facility instead. A draft indoctrination text for a satellite reconnaissance clearance closes the paper.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200260144-6:
Project AQUATONE's approval and first build-up are recounted in a draft dated 19 November 1955. The Intelligence Advisory Committee had signed a memorandum on 23 November 1954 warning of serious gaps in intelligence on the Soviet bloc. Aerial reconnaissance and photography were named the most practicable way to close them, and the project was approved on 1 December.

Work began at unusual speed and on trust. Lockheed started designing an aircraft built throughout for maximum altitude and range on purely oral assurance. A top optical specialist, working with two other firms, began lenses and cameras meant to far surpass existing designs. Letter contracts were issued first and final contracts followed as fast as they could be drawn. By mid-February, specialised equipment was under development or manufacture at six companies, and a joint task force arrangement with the Air Force governed the operational phase.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100020051-6:
Economic intelligence work in the Office of Research and Reports is presented to a Clandestine Services review on 6 June 1958. The speaker opens on relationships: ties between the research office and the clandestine services were closer than ever before. Analysts understood collection capabilities better, requirements reached collectors in more useful form, and reporting coming back had improved in turn.

New work is highlighted. For the first time, a substantial research effort was being put on the economic side of Soviet guided missile programs, a subject of high national priority. The Office of National Estimates is named the office's largest single customer, taking thirty per cent of its research time. Joint work with the State Department produced reports every two weeks on Sino-Soviet bloc economic activity in underdeveloped areas.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100030005-6:
Change in the Czechoslovak aircraft industry is assessed in a short paper on its current status. In early 1958, production of the Farmer, the MiG-19, began to replace production of the Midget, the MiG-15, at Vodochody. A study of sightings of the factory area, though, shows the changeover stretching over a surprisingly long period.

Series production of the Farmer was probably delayed by manufacturing difficulties in Czechoslovakia, the paper judges. Two less likely explanations are also weighed: that the decision to build the Farmer was reversed, or that components were shipped away by rail to be assembled elsewhere. Only a few Farmers carrying Czechoslovak air force markings had been seen. Other planned changes include a new version of the Il-14 aircraft displayed at Prague in October.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100030078-6:
Soviet fighter aircraft shown at the 1956 Soviet air parade are assessed in an intelligence paper on new types entering production. At least one, probably three, and possibly four of the aircraft displayed at that show are believed to be in some stage of production. The spread of types marks a break from the earlier drive to standardise on a few models such as the MiG-15 and MiG-17.

Five new fighters capable of supersonic speed were seen and photographed by Western observers. Three are identified as Mikoyan designs, called Fishbed 'A', Fishbed 'B', and Faceplate, alongside Sukhoy designs called Fitter and Fishpot. Both Fishbed types are single-seat aircraft with one turbojet in the fuselage. A delta-wing Fishbed spotted on a factory field, with a second probable sighting, is linked to one of the Fishbed variants.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100040031-6:
Aims for an electronics session are set out in a paper dated 18 August 1958. The paper is numbered EIC/JTSC-D-2. The first day deals with the electronics gear industry. Its theme is fast growth since the war. The Soviet industry once set a hard limit on arms programs. It is now judged near the West in its power to reach big new steps in technique.

Making capacity can now carry science gains into real goods. Yet bulk measures hide the key point. Rival claims on special parts and goods may limit how many arms systems can be built. They may also narrow the choices open to Soviet planners. A closing paper is meant to sum up the views of those present. It would note where they differ. It would also frame a plan for the work left undone.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100060039-6: This declassified CIA general requirement covers military economic information. The war economy, tasked. The file holds the requirement. The record stays. Tomorrow's readers will find it. It retains its place in time. Kept for readers.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100110105-6:
Reviewer's notes on Project 36.2065, a paper on trends in the electronics industry of Communist China, question the draft page by page. Early notes press for consistency: if an estimate rests on barely met Chinese plans, the wording must say so. A flat question, 'Gross output?', recurs where figures are used. The summary is ordered cut down and recast around what the Chinese can and cannot do.

Definitions and dates are challenged too: one term must match the meaning used in a Soviet electronics paper, and one passage gives 1952-57 while another gives 1953-57. Tables and their text are said to be confused in places. Appendix notes suggest placing two joint public-private plants under their subordinate headings rather than under plants. Duplicate footnotes and weak transitions are marked further on.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100130086-6:
A gaps statement on the aircraft industry of Poland is forwarded for review on 2 February 1959. Knowledge of the Polish industry's scope, actual performance, and progress is called a matter of considerable strategic and economic importance. The effort and money Poland spends on aircraft production may indicate Polish and Soviet intentions in military matters and in free-world economic penetration.

Performance, above all in military production, is admitted to be imperfectly known. The statement summarises what is held on aircraft and engine categories and then turns to sources of information. Attaché sightings, one source type weighed, have not been frequent enough to keep a close check on production, because of surveillance and the locations of the aircraft factories. The gaps listed are meant to direct future collection at those blind spots.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100190044-6:
Gaps in information requirements for Communist China, focused on shipbuilding, are submitted on 28 May 1959 through the Shipbuilding Branch. Most basic shipbuilding requirements are already covered by naval intelligence requirements memoranda. The economic side of the industry, which the Office of Research and Reports needs, is not, and the gaps presented arise from that office's responsibility.

China's shipbuilding industry stands at an earlier stage than the other major bloc shipbuilders, such as Poland and East Germany, having begun about 1953. For naval construction, present estimates lean heavily on estimated order of battle because information on shipyards and building activity is lacking. To improve estimates of output and its value, the paper asks first for the rate of output of submarines, then for better reporting on plans and plan fulfilment across the industry.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100070003-6:
Terms dated 9 July 1959 frame a study of data machines. The terms come from the Central Reference Advisory Group of the Central Intelligence Agency. The study deals with the deputy directorate for spy work. Its aim is to judge what gains data machines would bring to set tasks in that area.

Cost drives the care taken. Machine use is very costly. It needs much planning in advance. This study is only a first step toward broad needs. Later steps would test whether the plan can work. They would cover coding, training, site works, fitting, and changeover. The study must still be deep enough to show the need for machine help. Fit tasks are spelled out. They include work already part-mechanised. They include large flows of routine clerical work. They include frequent checks of master files held in many places, with much copying. Steady inward flows of facts are included too.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090029-6:
Suggested revisions to the 29 November draft of the Director's speech to the National Association of Manufacturers are sent to the Director. The writer has marked the places concerned in the text. On page two, a boast called 'not likely to be realised in the foreseeable future' should read 'in the next decade.' That is more specific. Many people now believe the Soviets will overtake the United States in the foreseeable future.

A phrase about the Soviets having no atomic power should become 'they had no atomic weapons.' The first Soviet atomic bomb was not exploded until September 1949. 'Atomic power' might be read as industrial power from atomic energy. On the nuclear stalemate passage, the forward-looking point is Soviet spending on research to break the stalemate in their favour. A ranking of Russia among the states of the world should be cut as confusing. It refers to 1913, not 1928.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090038-6:
Asian studies and national security are joined in remarks by Dr. Otto E. Guthe of the Central Intelligence Agency. He spoke at the Asian Studies Conference at Indiana University, Bloomington, on 12 November 1959. He opens on the remarkable growth of Asian studies in American universities over the last decade. It arrived as American leadership in the free world, and involvement in Asia, called for fuller understanding of that region.

The nature of the challenge comes first. It begins with Communist China, whose influence in Asia cannot be escaped. The bloc's economic offensive across the region is tailored to local openings. It exploits an existing domestic tendency, a nationalistic ambition, or a source of dissension. The variation reflects opportunity, planning, and flexibility, not uncertainty or caprice. Guthe closes by turning to his audience. Colleges and universities, through Asian studies, can give further insight on Asian problems that bear on American security interests.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090047-6:
An address on some aspects of the Soviet economy was delivered by Gabriel Hauge, Special Assistant to the President, before the Economic Club of Worcester on 14 April 1958. The text is issued by White House press secretary James C. Hagerty. The Sputniks have brought a good deal of second-looking at the Soviet Union. Hauge chooses its economy.

His purpose is neither to bury the Russian economy nor to praise it. He weighs its strengths and weaknesses, and what they mean for the Russians, for newly developing countries, and for the American people. Since the First Five Year Plan of 1928, the Soviet Union has grown rapidly from the farming economy of the Tsars, by forced-draft industrialisation with its accent on heavy industry under Stalin. At the Twentieth Party Congress in 1956, Anastos Mikoyan complained that Soviet economists picked isolated facts for propaganda instead of truly judging economic activity abroad.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090056-6:
Communist Economic Penetration of West is a declassified Agency talk text on Soviet trade and aid under the banner of peaceful coexistence. It reports that Soviet trade with poorer free world nations had grown over 500 percent since early 1954. A working group from State, the Agency, and other offices had tracked that activity since February 1956.

The text calls Soviet economic strength large but notes that trade stayed small beside total output. It then turns to aid offers aimed at nations seen as open to pressure. Six nations, among them Egypt, India, and Yugoslavia, had drawn more than two billion dollars in credits. Terms, delays, and unused credit shares are spelled out case by case.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090119-6:
Soviet Economic Development is a declassified Agency briefing text on how fast the Soviet economy was growing and where its output went. Soviet gross national product is described as growing nearly twice as fast as that of the United States. It stood near 40 percent of the United States level, while consumer supply stood near 25 percent.

Military spending is put at about 170 to 180 billion rubles a year. Later sections look at metals and oil as future export earners. Petroleum goals set by Khrushchev for 1972 are examined in detail. The text suggests the Soviet Union could become a major supplier of such goods to Western Europe within ten years.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100100009-6:
The Soviet Economic Challenge is the text of an address to a Sixth Annual Conference on International Affairs in February 1960, kept in Agency files. The speaker calls the Soviet drive a total challenge, not a merely economic one. Fast forced industrial growth sits at the core of the Kremlin case to uncommitted nations.

The address then contrasts aid styles on each side. Bloc help is geared to industrial growth, and complete plants are a common form of it. It is rarely given for sanitation, public housing, public schools, or farm goods. Soviet lenders, the speaker adds, keep the choice of being tough or lenient as events unfold.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100100027-6:
Sino-Soviet Bloc Economic Offensive is a declassified Agency talk given on April 22, 1959 under the Foreign Policy Clearing House. It states that Bloc trade and aid had moved into high gear the year before. Over one billion dollars in new credits were extended in that single year.

The total of Bloc credits is put at about 2.5 billion dollars. In Afghanistan, Ceylon, Egypt, Syria, Iraq, and Indonesia, Bloc aid passed that of the United States. The talk closes on repayment. Yearly deliveries to poorer nations cost the Bloc far under one percent of its output. Imports from those nations ran mostly to foodstuffs and raw materials such as cotton.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100020008-6:
An untitled staff study in declassified Agency files sets out the basic aim of the economic defense program. That aim was to halt or impair the present and future military strength of the Communist Bloc. The means were controls on Bloc trade and other outside economic ties, used without undue harm to free world strength or unity.

A complete stop to trade is weighed first and set aside. It would deny the Bloc all imports, but it clashed with United States trade policy and could not be won from allies. Later pages weigh other control designs, among them curbs on what the West buys from the Bloc. Bloc exports earned the foreign exchange that paid for Bloc imports, so that flow drew close study.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100020026-6:
Analyses of Economic Defense Policy is a declassified Agency memorandum dated April 29, 1955. It takes up the different types and levels of COCOM and CHINCOM controls. The writer argues there is nothing illogical in such differences as such, and warns that forcing one level could raise a harder problem.

Grounds for stricter controls on Communist China and North Korea are set out at length. Fresh memories of Korea and of captive Americans lead the political case. Later pages describe how the drafting group worked: experts from several agencies met, framed sub-questions, and handed tasks to named people and offices.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100040006-6:
Foreign Attitudes Toward Economic Defense is Staff Study No. 3 in the CFEP Drafting Group's Economic Defense Policy Review, draft of June 6, 1955. It surveys how allied nations viewed curbs on trade with the Soviet Bloc. The study runs to 31 pages and was spread through the drafting group by its executive secretary.

Its Italy pages weigh press and industry pressure against controls. Italy's main newspapers, owned by large industrial firms, are described as hostile to East-West trade controls. Those firms wanted to sell their goods to the Soviet and China Bloc. The study also notes fights over Battle Act terms as a sore point in Italian debate. The study survives in the Agency's CREST files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100080002-6:
Uniformity of Participation in Free World Controls is Staff Study No. 7 in the CFEP Drafting Group's Economic Defense Policy Review, held here as a set of revised pages dated June 23, 1955. The packet lists which pages of the June 6 draft were replaced. Pages 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, and 10 through 14 were all changed.

Line level edits are spelled out for the rest of the draft. One swaps a stronger wording, there is reason to believe, for a weaker one on page 5. The study's subject is special latitude in trade controls. Its harms are listed plainly: blunted controls, harder talks, and pressure from other nations for equal freedom. The study survives in the Agency's CREST files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100090001-6:
Differentials Between U.S. and Multilateral Controls is a summary of Staff Study No. 8 in the CFEP Drafting Group's Economic Defense Policy Review, dated June 23, 1955. It lists the gaps between United States controls and the joint controls kept with allies. Goods, technical data, and licensing form the main heads.

The United States embargoed some goods that joint lists controlled lightly or not at all. It also controlled all unclassified technical data bound for the Bloc, bar what the public could already get. The summary defends the stricter line: joint controls set a floor, not a ceiling. Looser joint rules would otherwise invite leaks that defeat the tighter United States controls. The paper rests in the Agency's CREST release.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100170002-6:
East-West Trade in Embargoed Commodities is a declassified Agency study of the hardest part of East-West trade to track. Shipments of banned goods, it states, are typically absent from official statistics. Proof of them must come in the main from intelligence sources.

Shifting embargo lists add to the problem. The 1954 list revision left a much shorter list for the Soviet Bloc than for Communist China. Goods lawfully shipped to Soviet ports were then passed on against the China embargo, with no record of their true end point. Copper dominates the volume study: about 100,000 tons, valued at 75 million dollars, are estimated to have reached the Soviet Bloc in 1953.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100200008-6:
Political Impact of Free World Controls on Trade with the Sino-Soviet Bloc is Staff Study No. 20 of the CFEP Drafting Group, draft of June 17, 1955, contributed by the Defense Department. Marked for United States officials only, it weighs the costs that joint trade controls place on each camp. Its conclusions section opens the study.

Heavy source notes back the argument. One note points readers to a November 1953 EDAC background and position paper prepared for United States-United Kingdom talks. That paper, The Impact of Controls on the Soviet Bloc, ran to seven pages with two appendices. The study's frame treats higher controls as raising the strategic cost borne by the Bloc. The paper rests in the Agency's CREST release.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000200060021-6:
A clearance memorandum dated 27 May 1954, Control No. 2022, tells IWG members how far a named report may be shared. The report's information dates from March 1954. Copies could go to FOA/MDAC in Washington and USRO in Paris for information only, and to posts from Zurich to Istanbul for action, at stated secrecy levels.

Name notes fill the rest of the memo. A Zurich firm owner is tied to the firm Gebruder Engels, with its street address drawn from the city phone book. Another Zurich firm, TRACO, is listed with its director and manager named. A later note credits a Continental firm with diverting 348 tons of forging press material to the Bloc in 1951. The memo survives in the Agency's CREST files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000200100008-6:
Supplement 10 to Diversion Control Panel Case Inventory, dated May 10, 1957, lists suspected diversion cases in a tight table. Each row gives a case number, goods, route, firms, and the cables that support it. Case 424 covers motor vehicle parts bound for China through Macao, Hong Kong, and Japan.

Cobalt chloride, copper residue shipments from Bombay, and machine tools follow in order. Marine engines, copper and nickel deals, and a diamond smuggling case through Dakar and Lebanon fill later rows. Copper cases recur near the end, one routed through Switzerland, Iran, and Chile. The list's value lies in its map of routes and repeat names. The supplement survives in the Agency's CREST files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00309a000100010009-6:
Minutes of Planning Group Meeting, 24 November 1958, recorded in a memorandum dated 11 December 1958, open with the group's origin. In October 1957 the Acting Deputy Director (Plans) had called for overall planning. Separate offices were each pushing their own moves toward speedier communications and reporting, with no shared frame.

Two problems were set for study. The first asked what documents, and how many, should ride in the communications system. The second asked how those documents could be handled without delay. Later pages sample the work such a system served, from reading panels and analyst files to studies of East German electronics and Soviet tractor output for 1950 to 1957. The minutes survive in the Agency's CREST files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00309a000100020008-6:
A memorandum to the Deputy Director (Support) comments on the Inspector General's report on training in the Agency. The writer calls that report a valuable piece of work: full, well expressed, and thoughtful. Its recommendations touch the writer's own office only lightly, so the remarks are offered as personal reactions.

Clerical training draws a mild reply: a fresh look can do no harm. A proposed board of overseers for training is judged worth a trial, though not if it stops at briefings. One firm edit is urged on a hiring rule. Junior professional officers should enter through the JOT program normally, the writer argues, not without exception.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00309a000100040079-6:
Individual Instruction is a declassified Agency training paper on teaching built around the single learner. Such instruction, it explains, is planned for one person or shaped to single needs rather than to a group. Each learner can then move at his own best pace without holding others back.

Failure, the paper argues, can be all but removed by this method, except for the most deficient learners. Group teaching still wins where sameness is the goal, as in drill. For intelligence work, the paper prizes sharp, weighing thought as much as hand skill. Good assignments, it closes, should provoke thought and carry real meaning for the learner.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00309a000200020016-6:
Achievement Awards for Directed Language Study is a memorandum dated 28 June 1960 that reopens a pay question. The Agency's award system, first set out in January 1957, pays staff who reach set levels in named foreign languages. Skills gained through training earn awards twice the size of those for skills kept up without it.

Critics now argue that directed study is paid for twice: once in duty time, and again in the award. The memo calls that charge an old chestnut. It points to other incentive pay in the Agency, from hardship allowances to flight pay. Foreign practice is also cited: British, Canadian, and State Department plans place no bar on how the skill was gained.
cinq-mars-volume-6:
Alfred de Vigny opens the last stretch of his novel in Cinq-Mars, Volume 6 of the English edition. A defile through the Pyrenees carries the action toward Spain. Snow bridges and precipice paths slow the travelers crossing between kingdoms. The conspiracy's foreign errand, long whispered, here takes the road in person.

Papers bound for Spain tie Cinq-Mars openly to France's enemy. Discovery follows, and the favorite who charmed a court must answer as a traitor. De Thou, who shared the secret without sharing the ambition, stands beside him in the fall. Trial scenes at Lyon weigh the treaty and the king's withdrawal of favor. De Vigny gives both young men dignity as the scaffold nears. Readers closing the six volumes get the famous ending whole: ambition and loyalty punished together, in a France where Richelieu's power outlives even the men it destroys.
clarissa-harlowe-or-the-history-of-a-you:
Clarissa Harlowe — Volume 6 of Richardson's novel in letters is built on a long run of letters, over seventy in the volume's own count. Lovelace writes to Belford of his conditional promise to Tomlinson in the lady's favor. His whimsical contest with his conscience ends, the contents say, in his latest adieu to it.

A garden meeting gives Clarissa her great scene. Composed and noble in talk, she still will determine nothing in his favor. She resolves to go to church, but will not suffer him to accompany her. In his own letters Lovelace drops from proud victor to kneeling slave, begging that she forgive him and receive his vows at the altar at once.
dio-cassius-roman-history-cary-vol-6:
