Books fifty-one through fifty-five of Dio Cassius tell how one man's win at Actium became a new form of state. Earnest Cary's Loeb English fills this sixth volume. Dio wrote around 230 CE, two centuries after the events, with a senator's care for how power was dressed in old forms.

Octavian beats Antony and Cleopatra, takes Egypt, and then stages his settlement with the senate. Dio explains the Augustan order step by step: the powers granted, the frontiers set, the armies placed. He also tells of plots and court strain in the early principate. Few sources match Dio on how the empire was built.
doe-osti-17149786-destructive-pie-of-agr:
William Cureton and Oak Ridge colleagues present the destructive examination of a single AGR-5/6/7 fuel compact, 3-6-3, in report ORNL/TM-2026/4857 dated September 2026. The compact came from the high temperature margin capsule of the irradiation campaign. It reached a burnup of 14.77 percent and a fast neutron fluence of 5.47 times ten to the twenty fifth per square meter, at an average 1363 degrees Celsius.

Methods included deconsolidation leach burn leach analysis, particle gamma scanning, light microscopy, 3D x ray tomography, and electron microscopy with x ray spectroscopy. Leach results suggested about one particle had exposed kernel material. Gamma scans found one particle, 363-SP02, drained of cesium and classed as a silicon carbide failure, though it kept its actinides. Combined evidence points to roughly one particle failure of each kind.
doe-osti-17150515-chemical-evolution-of-:
William Cureton, John Hirtz, Antonio dos Santos, and Oak Ridge colleagues with a University of Tennessee partner track chemistry changes inside irradiated TRISO fuel, in report ORNL/TM-2026/4930 dated September 2026. The kernels are UCO, a mix of uranium oxide and uranium carbide. Carbide is added to soak up oxygen and suppress carbon monoxide gas, which can attack the coatings.

Single particle neutron diffraction watched the carbide phases as burnup rose. The expected path, carbide used up and the kernel turning to oxide plus free carbon, did not occur. Instead the UC2-x phase shrank while an oxygen bearing rocksalt phase, U(C,O), grew steadily. The split between uranium held in carbide and oxycarbide phases can now be estimated, which may let designers trim excess carbide from kernel recipes.
doe-osti-17197387-chemical-evolution-of-: Cooked TRISO fuel's chemistry got tracked again, and this DOE report follows the AGR-5/6/7 UCO changes. The pages log the element shifts. The fuel chemists get their timeline. The fuel was irradiated. The timeline was chemical. The shifts were element.
doe-osti-17197390-destructive-pie-of-agr: Compact 3-6-3 got torn apart again, and this DOE report covers the destructive PIE. The pages record the autopsy details. The fuel scientists get their data. The compact was AGR-5/6/7. The data were autopsy. The details were autopsy. The scientists got data.
doe-osti-3363904-analysis-report-for-hyd:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/SPR-2026/4605, by Kellen Springer, Carson Grant, Lindsey Lecrivain, Brian Ticknor, and Jenn Parikh, dates to May 2026. It records laboratory analysis of hydrolyzed uranium hexafluoride samples. Uranium hexafluoride is the feed gas used in uranium enrichment, and adding water converts it into solid compounds that analysts can measure. The samples arrived at the lab sealed in P-10 tubes.

The report walks through sample preparation under the lab's quality assurance plan, then the chemical analysis itself. Results characterize what the hydrolyzed material contains, which supports nuclear material accounting and safeguards work. Short and factual, the document is a laboratory analysis record: what was received, how it was prepared, and what the measurements showed.
evan-harrington-volume-6:
Volume six of George Meredith's Evan Harrington covers chapters thirty-two to thirty-eight, nearing the crisis. Evan's light begins to twinkle again after disgrace and doubt. A great picnic on the heights, with music and dancing, sets the social stage. The hero takes his rank in the orchestra, playing second fiddle in more senses than one.

A pagan sacrifice and Rose wounded follow in quick succession. The retreat from Beckley turns the party's pleasure into confusion. Evan must act in darkness, without clear sight of friend or foe. Meredith tightens his comedy toward revelation, as the tailor's son can no longer hide behind borrowed rank. These chapters balance farce and feeling, preparing the final reckoning for Evan, Rose, and the formidable Countess.
fbi-vault-9-11-attacks-investigation-and:
Documents freed under Executive Order 14040 fill part 6 of this set from the Federal Bureau of Investigation probe into the September 11 attacks. A redaction key opens the part and gives the grounds on which lines are still withheld. The body of the part is interview and records work from San Diego.

Agents in the sampled pages check hotel and phone records tied to Omar Albayoumi. One man at a Marriott Residence Inn was asked, in part, because Albayoumi's phone had called the inn in March 2000. Staff ran name checks for Nawaf Alhazmi and Khalid Almihdhar and found no match in the inn's records. One check did tie an Omar Albayoumi in San Diego to a booking there. The pages show the slow records work that backed the probe.
following-the-equator-a-journey-around-t:
Following the Equator, Part 6, by Mark Twain, walks the pilgrim road at Benares, the holy city on the Ganges. Twain calls the city, in effect, one big church, its every cell a temple, shrine, or mosque, stocked like a great store with every earthly and heavenly good. His chapter opens with a calendar maxim about superstition and law, then lays out an itinerary for the visitor.

Step one is purification: bathe in the Ganges at sunrise, pray, and drink some of the water. Step two guards against hunger at the Cow Temple, and the list proceeds through the city's sacred economy with guidebook precision, drawn from a local guide and a missionary's conversation. Twain is respectful of the devotion and merciless about the system built on it, a double vision that powers the Indian chapters of his voyage.
freeman-norman-conquest-vol-6:
Tools, not tale, fill the sixth volume of Freeman's Norman Conquest, from 1867. Index, appendices, and notes stand behind the five books of narrative. Each fact in the great history is tied here to its source.

Serious readers use this volume to check Freeman's bold claims. Students find in it a map of the chronicles and charters he mined. The labor is dry, yet it is the bedrock of the whole structure. Few Victorian histories show their working so fully, and the volume honors an age when a historian proved his case in public, note by note.
froude-history-england-vol-6:
Two queens duel across the sixth volume of Froude's History of England, issued in eighteen sixty. Elizabeth holds England while Mary Stuart, captive and plotting, claims its crown. Their long contest ends at last on the scaffold at Fotheringhay Castle.

Froude makes Mary's captivity and death the dramatic heart of his work. Letters, plots, and trials build toward the fatal warrant and its signing. Statecraft and tragedy merge in his telling of the affair. The volume shows his gifts at their height. Deep research in the archives weds a storyteller's sense of doom, pity, and high political stakes.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-6:
Charles Bohlen, the Secretary of State's assistant, listed Moscow's added agenda points for James Dunn on July 17, 1945. The top secret memo is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Molotov had outlined the points to the President and Secretary that morning.

Eight Soviet items are named in order. They are Tangier, the Levant, and the fate of captured German naval and merchant ships. The Franco regime in Spain is fourth, with Stalin's view spelled out. Franco's government, Stalin holds, was imposed by the Axis and should be eliminated by some devised measure. Poland follows, on the London government's survival and the western frontiers. Reparations, trusteeships for Italian colonies, and ties with the former Axis satellites close the list. Byrnes wanted Dunn to study each point.
frus-1958-1960-cuba-vol-6:
Foreign Relations of the United States is the official documentary record of American foreign policy, published by the State Department's Office of the Historian. This volume, the sixth for 1958 to 1960, covers Cuba. The documents are declassified and public.

They run from the fall of the dictator Batista through Fidel Castro's first two years in power. Cables and memos trace the revolution's radical turn, the seizure of American property, and the slow break in relations. Washington's hope, confusion, and hardening anger all stand in the record. The volume is the paper trail of a friendship collapsing into a sixty-year feud.
gao-gaoreports-b-294358-6:
University Research Company, LLC, protested a health services award in GAO files B-294358.6 and B-294358.7, dated April 20, 2005. The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration had reselected IQ Solutions, Inc., to run its Health Information Network. GAO denied the protest. The selection official had taken in the project officers' views, which favored the protester. The decision paper noted those views and adjusted the analysis on some points. On others it fairly kept the panel's view.

The digest defends that balance at length. Input from project officers adds to, but does not displace, the scoring panel's work.
gao-gaoreports-b-294974-6:
In GAO ruling B-294974.6, dated December 1, 2006, Logan, LLC, formerly Envirosolve, LLC, was the protester. The Drug Enforcement Administration had shut the firm out of the rotation of orders under its hazardous waste cleanup agreements. GAO denied the protest. This copy is a redacted version cleared for release. The law's demand for the fullest practical competition had been met when the agency competed to set up the agreements with several vendors.

No fresh contest was required for each order placed under them. Choices on whether and how to place orders with a given vendor, GAO held, concern contract administration. Such matters sit outside bid protest review.
gao-gaoreports-b-295529-6:
Alan D. King, deputy garrison commander at Walter Reed Medical Center, brought the protest in GAO file B-295529.6, decided on February 21, 2006. King challenged, for federal employees, the A-76 outcome at Walter Reed. The Army had chosen a contract with IAP World Services over in-house work. GAO ruled that King was not an interested party with standing to bring the protest. A 2005 statute lets the official who submits the agency tender sue in such contests. It reaches only studies begun on or after January 26, 2005.

The Walter Reed study began before that date. The new standing rule thus did not cover King's case.
gao-gaoreports-b-295663-6:
In GAO ruling B-295663.6 and B-295663.12, dated April 18, 2005, Restoration and Closure Services, LLC, was the protester. The Department of Energy had awarded a contract for environmental cleanup at its Portsmouth, Ohio site. GAO dismissed the protest. One thread barred the path at the start: consultants for a party sought cover under the protective order. Their promises limited their work only as to this one site. They stayed free to help rivals prepare offers for like work at other sites. Admission was denied on that ground.

On the merits, the firm could show no prejudice from the scoring it attacked. Without a real chance of harm, the case could not proceed.
gao-gaoreports-b-296490-6:
The Treasury sought a change to the fix for the guard systems case in GAO decision B-296490.6, dated May 31, 2007. GAO had backed Johnson Controls in the prior round. The first fix was a fresh review and a new pick. The Bureau of Engraving and Printing said its needs had shifted.

GAO granted the change. The agency would split the need into two new contests. It would award new deals fast, then end the flawed deal. That plan served its needs best. Since the firm could no longer win the first need, GAO backed pay for its bid costs. The firm thus got bid cost relief, not the job.
gao-gaoreports-b-296493-6:
Advanced Technology Systems protested a Housing task order in GAO decision B-296493.6, dated October 6, 2006. The winner was again Pyramid Systems. The system was the same rental aid system, TRACS. The firm hit the review of work hours and staff mix. It also hit a fitness call for the winner.

GAO sustained the protest in part and denied it in part. No fresh fitness call was due on a schedule order. The first call had set fitness. But the agency did have to weigh hours and staff mix. Its note on that point was too thin. Thin notes on hours and mix could not back the pick.
gao-gaoreports-b-296946-6:
University of Dayton Research Institute protested Air Force acts in the same design contest in GAO decision B-296946.6, dated June 15, 2006. The work was design and tech support for weapon systems. After first bids, the agency spoke with winners. Those talks led to shifts in the rates that set the pick.

GAO sustained the protest. Talks that shift scored rates are true talks, not mere chats. True talks must be held with all firms in the field. The agency had held no field and no full talks. That flaw broke the rules for fair talks. When scored rates move in talks, all in-field firms must get talks.
gao-gaoreports-b-297790-6:
T Square Logistics sought its cost sum in GAO decision B-297790.6, dated June 7, 2007. The sum sought was 51,611.83 dollars. The first fight was the Grissom base support case. The Air Force fought the sum in part. It named the firm's block of a talks track as a base to cut costs. Claim costs were also at stake.

GAO backed the full sum sought, plus claim costs. A firm's block of a talks track does not cut costs that are sound in their own right. The costs were backed as fair on the record. Claim chase costs were due as well. The agency thus owed the whole sum.
gao-gaoreports-b-298249-6:
Five firms protested Army awards for tech services in GAO decision B-298249.6, dated October 24, 2006. The plan was the IT Enterprise Solutions buy. Eleven deals went to rival firms. Talks on labor rates were the flaw. The agency flagged rates far above its cost guess. Rates not flagged were read as fine.

GAO sustained the protests. That read was fair on the words used. It was also wrong. Rates left in last bids thus stayed high by a false cue. Talks that mislead firms on price are not true talks. A cue that firms will trust must be true. Misled price talks undo the picks that rest on them.
gao-gaoreports-b-298364-6:
TYBRIN Corporation protested an Air Force award to The CENTECH GROUP for support work at Edwards Air Force Base in California. The contract covered advice and support for research, development, test, and evaluation work. The job was set aside for small firms. The case is B-298364.6 and B-298364.7, dated March 13, 2007.

TYBRIN argued that CENTECH's proposal broke a key limit on subcontracting. The terms required at least 50 percent of personnel cost to go to the small firm's own staff. GAO found that the proposal, as sent in, clearly missed that rule. A Small Business Administration certificate did not cure the flaw. GAO sustained the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-310939-6:
Labatt Food Service, Inc. lost its protest in GAO decision B-310939.6, dated August 18, 2008. The Defense Logistics Agency sought food supply services. Labatt's bid was tossed as late. The toss tied to a late nod to a call change. Labatt said each firm sent its bid by a path the call banned. It said all bids should have been tossed as late.

GAO denied the protest. The call said its own due time would rule late calls. Labatt's bid missed that due time on the file. The send-path claim showed no harm to Labatt. A ban not heeded for all can not help a firm that missed the clock.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-6:
States send vast education data to Washington, and the flow was messy. Report GAO-06-6, issued October 28, 2005, reviews the Education Department's data management initiative. States must provide data each year to receive federal school funding. Past collections were burdensome, with many duplicate requests from many offices. The data were often late or inaccurate. In 2002 the department began a plan to merge collections into one system. The system would focus on performance.

GAO prepared the study under the Comptroller General's authority. It reports progress on the initiative. Significant progress has been made, GAO found. Better planning is still needed to meet project goals. Readers get the burden and quality story.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-6:
Banks owned by minorities serve neighborhoods others skip, and GAO-07-6, a GAO report dated October 4, 2006, asks how well regulators back them. A 1989 law, the Financial Institutions Reform, Recovery, and Enforcement Act, set goals for two regulators. The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and the Office of Thrift Supervision must work to preserve and promote such banks. Two other watchdogs join the effort by choice.

GAO reviewed the banks' profit health using federal data. It cataloged what each regulator does to help, from training to merger aid. It surveyed every minority bank for its view. Help exists, led by the deposit insurer, which also runs joint efforts. But no regulator grades its help with steady outcome measures. Surveys of the banks are rare. GAO's push is plain: help is not enough if no one can tell whether it works.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-6:
Comparing public and private prison costs is studied in GAO report GAO-08-6, dated October 5, 2007. Spending to house federal inmates in non-federal facilities nearly tripled in 10 years, from about $250 million in fiscal year 1996 to about $700 million in fiscal year 2006. Congress asked whether contracting saves money at low and minimum security sites.

A sound comparison cannot be done today, GAO found. The Bureau of Prisons does not gather matching data from private facilities on staffing, programs, safety, or quality. Contractors keep some data in forms that do not line up. The bureau doubts the value of collecting it and fears higher contract costs, but gave no proof. GAO urged a cheap way to gather comparable data. The bureau disagreed.
godolphin-volume-6:
Volume 6 of Godolphin opens at chapter fifty-nine, where Constance makes a discovery that enlightens her as to Godolphin's nature. She reproaches herself for having betrayed, before Radclyffe, her dependence on even her husband's heart for happiness. Her conscience takes alarm at so grave an error. Yet she cannot hold back the wild thrill of recalling words that assured her she was still beloved by Godolphin.

Radclyffe's penetration and sincerity are beyond her doubt, so his word carries weight. The closing volume of Lytton's tale of society brings its long study of hidden feeling toward rest. Pride, shame, and late knowledge meet in Constance's reckoning. Readers who have followed the set will find here the end of the long dance between love and the world.
history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-the-r:
Edward Gibbon's sixth and final volume, with Milman's notes, opens at chapter fifty-nine with the Crusades. The Fourth Crusade follows, diverted to Constantinople, and chapter sixty-one narrates the partition of the Byzantine empire by French and Venetians. Greek emperors at Nicaea and the Latin emperors occupy the next chapters.

Gibbon then ranges over the Mongols, Timur's world-shaking campaigns, the Ottoman Turks, and the final siege of Constantinople in 1453, closing with Rome's ruins and his famous reflections among them. Timur meditating at Smyrna shows the sweep. Seventy-one chapters end here: the history that began with the Antonines concludes with an empire fallen and a city twice transformed.
humboldt-personal-narrative-williams-vol:
Volume six of Humboldt's Personal Narrative, in Helen Maria Williams's translation, appeared in 1826. The expedition moves from the Andes toward Peru and the Pacific coast. Humboldt's survey of Spanish America nears its close; Mexico and the voyage home lie just beyond this volume's edge.

He studies Lima, the cold ocean current that now bears his name, and the guano riches of the coast. Quito's volcanoes get their measurements, and the party descends toward the sea. As always, plants, rocks, stars, and politics share the page. The English set, running since 1814, had made Humboldt a household name among readers of science.
husbandry-deep-waters-part-6:
W W Jacobs set this tale in his Deep Waters set, told by the night-watchman. The watchman opens with a theory of dealing with wives. A man who fails curses a little and forgets, he says. A woman who fails recalls what you did wrong ten years ago.

He tells of a young fellow, newly married, whose wife worked from cooing to temper. A later row brings a carman with a kicked shin into the tale. The watchman, mid-fight, surprises himself by calling for the police. Policemen are too inquisitive for his taste, as a rule. Jacobs wrings the comedy dry in dockside speech, as ever.
ibsen-collected-works-archer-vol-6:
Satire and breakthrough share the sixth volume of Archer's 1908 Ibsen. The League of Youth mocks small-town political ambition, while Pillars of Society turns on a shipowner whose respectable front conceals corruption. Together they catch the moment Ibsen turned from historical verse toward the modern world.

In Pillars of Society, Consul Bernick's lies about his ships and his past slowly close around him. Exposure threatens everything until confession breaks the spell, a pattern later plays would darken. The League of Youth, lighter in touch, still stings any age that knows machine politics. Critics treat the volume as a hinge in theater history. After these plays, modern drama had found its road.
in-the-library-the-lady-of-the-barge-and:
W. W. Jacobs wrote In the Library as one tale from The Lady of the Barge and Other Stories. Trayton Burleigh sits by a low fire in a wet, warm night in London. The room is library, study, and smoke-room on the third floor. Burleigh hates James Fletcher, who shares the house left to both men.

Fletcher has told him he must leave in the morning and wander. Burleigh listens at a door as a cat cries on the stairs and fear grows. Half the valuable house is his, yet he faces ruin. Jacobs builds a quiet tale of hatred and dread.
jataka-cowell-vol-6:
Volume six, from 1907, completes Cowell's English Jataka, the first full translation of the Buddha's birth stories. The closing tales are the longest and grandest of the 547. Chief among them is the Vessantara Jataka, the last birth before the Buddha's final life.

Prince Vessantara gives away everything: his wealth, his kingdom's rain-bringing elephant, and at last his own children and wife. His total generosity is the summit of the virtues the whole cycle teaches. The tale is still acted and painted across Southeast Asia each year. With it, Cowell's twelve-year labor closes the great story treasury of Buddhism.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-s-tomb-6: Aaron's Tomb is the burial-place of Aaron. According to Numbers, chapter 20, verses 23 to 28, it was Mount Hor, on the edge of the land of Edom. A later tradition, which the entry calls Mohammedan in origin, points instead to a hill near Petra, called the Hill of Aaron. A tomb is still shown on its summit. The entry notes that this claim does not fit the route from Kadesh given in Numbers, chapter 33.
lecky-england-18th-vol-6:
War with Napoleonic France fills the sixth volume of Lecky's History, from 1890. Trafalgar secures the seas, while the Peninsular campaign bleeds armies in Spain. Waterloo then ends the long struggle and frees a continent from a tyrant's grip at last.

Lecky tells England's supreme trial with fitting gravity throughout. Liberty strains under taxes, press gangs, and laws against dissent. Endurance, more than brilliance, forms his theme for these years. The volume traces the making of Britain's later greatness in fire. A free state survived total war without wholly losing its soul, in his sober view.
life-on-the-mississippi-part-6:
Part Six turns to war talk in Chapter 26, Under Fire. The boat enters the former battle-stretch below Columbus. Officers recall the famous battle of Belmont on the Mississippi. Several had served in the river war-fleet during the fighting.

One pilot fought his first battle aboard the Confederate service. He stood alone in the pilot-house, a target for all shooters. No elbow companion could shame him from showing fear. His story fills a gap, Twain says, that histories left empty. The R. H. Hill carried troops and artillery across that morning. His partner went sightseeing while the pilot stayed at his post.
memoirs-of-madame-la-marquise-de-montesp:
Book six of Madame de Montespan's memoirs opens at chapter nineteen. The court travels in Picardy and Flanders in that chapter. Madame de Montespan, pointedly, is not asked to go on the trip.

The King had not come back to their old close ties. His bond with her now ran through their children, she says. Chambers of Reunion at Metz and Brisach stripped great lords of land. The Prince Palatine lost the whole county of Veldentz by that means. The King tells her of the trip's delights on his return. Her own thoughts on that slight fill the chapter's close.
merivale-romans-empire-vol-6:
Reform and conversion mark the sixth volume of Merivale's History, from 1865. Diocletian rebuilds the state with stern new systems of rule and tax. Constantine then makes the Empire Christian, turning Western history onto a wholly new course within one lifetime.

Merivale brings his great work to the threshold of the medieval world. Ancient Rome ends here, and something new begins in its place. He tells the hinge of Western history with grace and care. The volume shows the rescue of a failing empire. It also shows a Christian order born, one that would outlast Rome itself.
nasa-tm-19710010488-msc-apollo-13-invest:
Panel 6 of the Manned Spacecraft Center Apollo 13 Investigation Team wrote this related systems evaluation. Volume 3 covers the Command and Service Module, the spacecraft whose oxygen tank failed in April 1970. The panel checked other parts and systems for the same kind of hidden failure risk.

The volume opens with the module pressure vessel, then gives a long subsystem by subsystem assessment. Later sections weigh how much damage each failure could cause. The report closes with conclusions and recommendations. It shows how investigators widened the Apollo 13 inquiry from one broken tank to the safety of the whole spacecraft.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-1-vol-6:
Volume six of Schaff's Nicene Fathers, first series, turns from Augustine the fighter to Augustine the pastor. It holds his work on the Sermon on the Mount, his Harmony of the Gospels, and his homilies on the Gospels. The volume appeared in 1886.

On the Sermon on the Mount reads Christ's teaching as the charter of the Christian life, line by line. The Harmony then weaves the four evangelists into one account, answering readers troubled by their differences. The homilies show the bishop preaching to his people at Hippo in plain, urgent speech. The volume is the gentlest Augustine in the series.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-2-vol-6:
Jerome, the great scholar monk of Bethlehem, fills volume six of the Nicene Fathers' second series, from 1890, with his principal works. Jerome translated the Bible into Latin, the version the West used for a thousand years. Schaff and Wace edited the series.

The volume centers on his letters, the liveliest surviving from the ancient church: to widows, virgins, pupils, and rivals. He advises on study, fasting, grief, and the raising of girls, all in prose that sparkles and stings. His treatises against Helvidius and Jovinian defend the ascetic life he preached. No father is better company, or worse tempered. The volume is Jerome in full.
odd-man-out-sailor-s-knots-part-6:
William Wymark Jacobs wrote Odd Man Out as a comic tale. It is part six of Sailor's Knots, printed in 1909. A night watchman tells the story in his own voice. He warns that friendship can be a snare. He recalls shipmates Ted Denver and Charlie Brice.

The two friends shared money, lodging, and tobacco for years. People called them the Siamese twins for their closeness. Then a young woman entered their lives. Jacobs uses the tale to test loyalty and jealousy. The humor rests on plain speech and human folly. The watchman's blunt talk gives the tale much of its charm.
oriental-encounters-palestine-and-syria-: Marmaduke Pickthall's Oriental Encounters, copyrighted in 1918, recalls the years 1894 to 1896. Pickthall spent them in Palestine and Syria as a very young traveler. The hosted sample shows the title page and contents only. The contents promise an introduction and chapters built from meetings and incidents. Their titles include Rashid the Fair, a mountain garrison, a rhinoceros whip, and a courteous judge. Such scenes suggest Levantine life under Ottoman rule. Because no chapter text appears in the sample, this note describes the book's plan from its contents page alone.
over-the-side-captains-all-book-6:
W. W. Jacobs tells Over the Side as a man who went to sea at fifteen. His father would not apprentice him to it, so he shipped before the mast. Seamen, he begins, are the class most prone to superstition. They float on black water with strange creatures below. One incident made him chary of calling any man a fool.

He shipped on the brig Endeavour, bound for Riga, under a fine skipper. A brawny, good-natured shipmate named Bill Smith protected him. The crew's one spiteful man was Jem Dadd. Dadd loved frightening his fellows with the supernatural. He would never let a rat be killed: rats were drowned sailors' souls, he claimed. Six or seven days out, something strange happened on Dadd's watch. The tale is Jacobs in his night-watch vein.
pausanias-description-greece-frazer-vol-:
The sixth volume of Frazer's Pausanias is its index and closing commentary. Frazer's 1898 edition ends with the key to the whole work. Every person, place, and rite across five volumes becomes findable here.

A full index turns thousands of pages into a searchable reference. Closing commentary gathers Frazer's final judgments on the traveler and his world. Six volumes amount to the most complete guide ever made to ancient Greece. Frazer's labor stretched across years of translation and verification. Modern digital searches have replaced the index's function, not its scholarship. The set still sits on the shelves of every serious classical library.
personal-memoirs-of-p-h-sheridan-volume-:
Part 6 of volume 2 of Sheridan's memoirs opens at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, in September 1867. Sheridan takes command of a department covering Missouri, Kansas, the Indian Territory, and New Mexico. West of the Missouri, he writes, Native peoples had grown restless as the Pacific railroads crossed their hunting-grounds and pioneers poured into Kansas and Colorado.

The chapter promises the Treaty of Medicine Lodge, raids, the death of the scout Comstock, and preparations for a winter campaign. Buffalo Bill appears, undertaking a dangerous task. These pages show the cavalry general turned frontier commander, in the hardest of his peacetime assignments.
personal-memoirs-of-u-s-grant-part-6:
Part 6 of Grant's memoirs opens at chapter sixty-two, with Sherman in possession of Savannah. Grant confesses he never originally meant Sherman to march north through the Carolinas. He had collected transports to carry the army by sea to the James River, until Sherman proposed the march and Grant gladly approved it.

The reasoning is strategic and unsparing: Georgia's railroads already destroyed, the Carolinas must be made helpless to feed Lee's army, shrinking Richmond's supply ground to exhausted Virginia. This final part, with footnotes for the whole work, carries the war to its end under Grant's direction.
ranke-history-england-vol-6:
Civil war, Cromwell, and Restoration close Ranke's History in Volume 6. The 1875 Oxenford translation ends the six-book span of England's turmoil. Charles II returns to the throne as the great tale resolves.

Ranke passes cool judgment on the whole English revolution here. He weighs king, army, and parliament in the scales of Europe. Cromwell's rule gets firm, fair treatment from the German master's pen. The republic fails, the monarchy returns, and old wounds stay open. Few historians of the age command such range or such calm. The final volume takes the measure of England's most wild century.
samantha-among-the-brethren-volume-6:
Part 6 of Marietta Holley's Samantha Among the Brethren, written as Josiah Allen's Wife, opens at Chapter XXIII with a letter and a journey. Miss Timson's letter was written to Samantha on the sixth day of his sickness, and Josiah and Samantha set sail for Loontown on the day after they got it. Samantha laid the case before the female sisters of the meeting house, and they all counselled her to go. Sister Bobbet had fallen on the apple parings, so the work of papering the meeting house could not go on in any case. The interests of Zion, the sisters said, would not languish on account of her absence for a day or two.

The errand to Loontown, all the sisters agreed, was a fair and square case of duty, though they divided on almost everything else.
sandra-belloni-volume-6: Header matter alone is shown for George Meredith's Sandra Belloni, Volume 6, marked v6 and counted as number 24 in a series by Meredith. Author and title are both named in the header, with a release date of September 2003. First posting was on January 4, 2002, as Etext number 4418, in Edition 10, in English and ASCII. The producers credited are Pat Castevans and David Widger. No preface, contents page, or chapter opening is present in the portion shown here.
sketches-new-and-old-part-6:
Mark Twain's sketches new and old continue in this sixth part, opening with The Undertaker's Chat. An undertaker pats a corpse's folded hands and praises the dead man as a brick in every way. Friends had demanded a metal burial case, yet no time remained to fetch one.

The corpse, in the undertaker's fond retelling, waved style aside: shake him up any box with room to stretch. A silver door plate proved just as hard to roust out in a country town. Whitewash the old canoe and paint his address on it instead, the dead man supposedly ruled. Twain's gallows humor shines here.
stories-by-american-authors-volume-6:
Volume VI of Stories by American Authors, dated 1891, prints The Village Convict by C. H. White, The Denver Express by A. A. Hayes, The Misfortunes of Bro' Thomas Wheatley by Lina Redwood Fairfax, The Heartbreak Cameo by L. W. Champney, Miss Eunice's Glove by Albert Webster, and Brother Sebastian's Friendship by Harold Frederic.

White's first tale gathers fishermen around a store stove to argue over Eph, just out of state prison for burning a barn. Some fear he will burn them out too; others recall that the foreclosure on his mother, turned out in winter, drove the high-strung boy to it. The talk sets mercy against fear in plain village speech.
the-adventures-of-harry-richmond-volume-: Part six of The Adventures of Harry Richmond is by George Meredith. Gutenberg front matter alone stands here. The story itself is absent. The front matter assigns series number 55. It assigns file 4449. First posting was January 31, 2002. A September 2003 release date is given. David Widger is named as maker of the file.
the-adventures-of-tom-sawyer-part-6:
Part six of Mark Twain's The Adventures of Tom Sawyer opens at chapter twenty-three, when the sleepy village air is stirred hard by the murder trial. The trial at once becomes the one topic of talk in St. Petersburg.

Each mention of the murder sends a shudder to Tom's heart, since his conscience reads each remark as a feeler aimed at him. He cannot see how he could be guessed to know of the crime, yet he stays in a cold shiver. He draws Huck to a lonely place to unseal his tongue and split his load of dread. Readers watch Tom weigh his oath of silence against an innocent man, Muff Potter, in the dock.
the-battle-of-the-strong-a-romance-of-tw:
Volume six of Gilbert Parker's romance opens at chapter thirty-nine on October 4, at the opening of the Assise d'Heritage in Jersey. A bell on the Cohue Royale clatters while court, States, governor, bailiff, jurats, seigneurs, and naval officers gather. The island is in festival mood.

All wait to welcome Admiral Prince Philip d'Avranche, Duc de Bercy, and to offer a bounty to Jerseymen who enlist under him. Chapbooks tell of French defeats and the sea fight that made Philip an admiral. Yet Philip and his flag lieutenant do not arrive. The Comtesse Chantavoine sits outwardly calm while officials whisper and crowds grow restless.
the-bay-state-monthly-volume-3-no-6:
November 1885, volume three, number six, opens with a portrait of Henry W. Paine and a sketch by William Mathews. Mathews begins not with Paine but with the legal profession itself, often mocked in jest books along with medicine. He argues that eminence at the bar is a true test of ability.

Quackery, he says, may win wealth in other callings, but shallowness cannot pass for depth before a sharp bench and watchful rivals. Every cause sets one attorney as a sentinel upon the other, so slips are exposed at once. A lawyer's public standing, in this view, is a sifted judgment formed after severe trial, fitting praise for Paine's career.
the-bequest-ship-s-company-part-6:
W. W. Jacobs placed a tale called The Bequest in his Ship's Company collection. Robert Clarkson sits by his fire after the funeral of his lifelong neighbour and successful rival in love. The dead man, Phipps, had won the woman both men courted thirty years earlier.

A doleful visitor, Mr Smithson, calls to ask how Clarkson bears up and hints that he will have her at last. Clarkson answers that this was the dead man's wish. Yet anger grows when he reveals the provision left behind: only furniture and fifty pounds of insurance money. A bequest meant as generosity begins to look like a burden.
the-confessions-of-harry-lorrequer-volum: Volume 6 of Charles James Lever's Confessions of Harry Lorrequer, printed at Dublin in 1839, is shown here by front matter alone in this record. The plates listed are The Inn at Munich, Mr. Malone and Friend, and a Lorrequer scene left unfinished in what is present. The barracks verse about pipe-clay and mortars stands at the head, as in the earlier volumes. No contents or chapter text follows here, and a second record also called Volume 6 carries chapters XLII to LV.
the-dore-bible-gallery-volume-6:
Volume six of The Doré Gallery of Bible Illustrations opens with the Nativity. The text follows Luke: Caesar's decree sends Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem, where her son is born and laid in a manger for lack of room at the inn. Shepherds in the fields hear an angel bring good tidings of great joy, then a host of heaven sings.

The shepherds hurry to see the child. Doré's engraving bathes the stable in soft light. With this volume the gallery turns from Israel's kings and prophets to the life of Christ.
the-gilded-age-part-6:
Part 6 of The Gilded Age: A Tale of Today is dated 1873. Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner wrote the novel. This part opens with Chapter XLVI. Philip Sterling walks up Pennsylvania Avenue with Senator Dilworthy. It is a bright spring morning. Peach trees are in bloom. The air is soft after a long night in the chamber.

Dilworthy calls the night's work a gift from Providence. A new school plan has passed one house. He says Laura Hawkins will be almost rich if the Hawkins claim holds. Philip asks a plain question. Will the family see much of the cash? The senator looks hard at him. Then he swears he has kept their good at heart all along.
the-great-conspiracy-volume-6:
John Logan wrote The Great Conspiracy: Its Origin and History. This record is Part 6 of that work. It opens with Chapter XXII, Freedom's Sun Still Rising. After Lincoln issued the Proclamation of Emancipation, the friends of freedom saw a danger. Until that act was written into the Constitution itself, there could be no real assurance of safety for the freed. A living spark of dissension would be left. It might at any time be fanned again into civil war.

Lincoln, Logan says, favored and even urged action by Congress at all proper times. Congress was slow. Definite action came only in the following year. Lincoln found it needful to speak in his third Annual Message. While he remained in his position, he said, he would not retract or modify the Emancipation Proclamation. The chapter carries the fight from the proclamation toward a constitutional amendment.
the-mayflower-and-her-log-july-15-1620-m: A Project Gutenberg header is all that stands in this record for volume 6 of The Mayflower and Her Log by Azel Ames. It marks the file as etext 4106, released in June 2003 and produced by David Widger. The header speaks of keeping files on one's own disk and of texts readable by humans and computers since 1971. Ames's history of the Pilgrims does not itself appear, leaving the wrapper as the record's only readable content.
the-ordeal-of-richard-feverel-volume-6: The pages present for volume 6 of George Meredith's The Ordeal of Richard Feverel hold nothing but the Project Gutenberg header. It names the etext number 4411. It also gives a first posting of December 28, 2001, with a release date of September 2003. No part of the novel itself appears. Produced by Pat Castevans and David Widger, the file is the seventeenth Meredith item in the Gutenberg series. Title and author are all that can fairly be reported of the book here.
the-prince-and-the-pauper-part-6:
Part 6 of Mark Twain's The Prince and the Pauper opens at Chapter XVIII, The Prince with the Tramps. The troop of vagabonds turns out at dawn under a lowering sky, sloppy ground underfoot and a winter chill in the air. Gaiety is gone. The Ruffler puts Jack, the disguised king, in Hugo's charge and warns him not to be too rough. John Canty is ordered to keep away from the boy.

As the weather mildens, the gang's spirits rise into insolence. Passengers give them the road and take their ribaldry meekly. They snatch linen from hedges in full view of owners too afraid to protest. At a farmhouse they make themselves at home while the trembling family empties the larder for their breakfast. They throw bones at the farmer and butter the head of a daughter who resents them. They threaten to burn the house if word reaches the authorities.
the-three-sisters-night-watches-part-6:
W. W. Jacobs begins The Three Sisters, from his Night Watches, at a deathbed thirty years before a wet autumn evening. Ursula Mallow, eldest of three sisters at Mallett's Lodge, lies behind dingy moth-eaten curtains under a smoking oil-lamp. She commands her sister Tabitha that nothing is to be changed. Her room must stay locked and unopened forever. Tabitha answers brusquely that it cannot matter to her then.

Ursula insists it does matter, for she is certain she will sometimes visit the house again and watch over them both. She kisses weeping Eunice and promises to come for each sister in turn when her lease of life runs out. Then the lamp goes suddenly out. Jacobs blends his usual dry comedy of character with a genuine ghost-story chill, letting a domineering sister rule from beyond the grave.
the-works-of-lord-byron-vol-6: Poetry volume six of Byron's works, edited by Ernest Hartley Coleridge in 1903, is shown through front pages only. The edition is dedicated to Algernon Charles Swinburne. Transcriber notes explain how Greek passages were handled. They appear as Beta-code transliterations in the electronic text. Long and short vowels are marked with brackets. Notes also praise the edition's copious footnotes. The poem itself does not begin within the pages present here.
thirlwall-history-greece-vol-6:
Volume 6 of Thirlwall's History, from 1845, walks through the war's wreckage. Lysander triumphs, and the Thirty Tyrants seize Athens in his wake. The death of Socrates closes the book's span of bitter years.

Thirlwall keeps his usual fairness amid ruin, revenge, and fear. Democracy falls, returns, then judges its greatest critic to death. He lets readers weigh each act without pushing them to a side. The Greeks must live with what they have done to themselves. His steady hand guides readers through tangled trials and coups alike. The morning after disaster has seldom been told so clearly.
un-ga-res-31-6:
South Africa's plan to carve black homelands out of its map drew a flat refusal in Resolution 31/6, adopted by the General Assembly in 1976. The apartheid state had declared the Transkei, the first of its so-called bantustans, free on 26 October 1976. A vote of the year before had already condemned the whole scheme. Reports of the Assembly's anti-apartheid team lay before it.

The bantustans are condemned in the strongest terms. They were built, the text holds, to lock apartheid in place, to break the land's unity, and to strip the African people of their rights while white rule lasts. The Transkei's claimed freedom is rejected as void. All states are called to grant it no respect of any kind.
un-ga-res-6: War relief still hung over Europe when the General Assembly passed Resolution 6 on 1 February 1946. The relief agency UNRRA was set to end its work in Europe by the close of 1946, and in the Far East by March 1947. A new team was formed for two tasks. It would press states that had signed the UNRRA deal but not yet paid the fresh sums asked of them in 1945. It would also urge UN members outside the deal to join it.
un-ga-res-a-69-6: Sport can build peace, holds Resolution A/69/6, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The text recalls the chain of votes since 2003 that treat sport as a tool for schools, health, growth, and peace. The year 2005 was kept as the world year of sport. Each 6 April now serves as the world day of sport for growth and peace, and the Secretary-General's report on the gains of sport is noted with thanks.
un-ga-res-es-11-6:
One year into Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the General Assembly set out its terms for peace in Resolution ES-11/6, adopted on 23 February 2023. Its head names the point: the Charter's own rules are the base for a full, just, and lasting peace in Ukraine. The ban on force against the land or freedom of any state is recalled. So is the rule that no land gain won by force may be held as lawful.

The text recalls the past votes of the emergency session, and the 2014 vote on Crimea. A just peace, it holds, would be a great gain for peace in the whole world. The world court's order of March 2022, which told Russia to halt its attack, is recalled as well. The terms are drawn from the Charter, not from the gun.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 31/6, adopted in parts on 26 October and 9 November 1976, is a wide set of texts on South Africa under the heading Situation of South Africa. Its first part strongly condemned the bantustans. It rejected the claimed independence of the Transkei and declared it invalid. It told all governments to give it no recognition and no dealings.

Later parts backed the United Nations Trust Fund for South Africa. They voiced support for South African political prisoners after the Soweto killings, and demanded their release. Others pressed the Security Council for a binding arms ban. Others condemned joint work between Israel and South Africa. Others backed a boycott of apartheid in sports.

The General Assembly adopted resolution 6 (I) on 29 January 1946 to chase down unpaid pledges to the United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration. It creates a five-member committee, appointed by the Assembly's President in consultation with the Secretary-General, to press member states for outstanding contributions and report back to the Assembly's next session. The committee works as UNRRA's relief operations wind down in Europe at the end of 1946 and in the Far East in early 1947.

General Assembly resolution 69/6 (2014) promotes sport as a means to advance education, health, development, and peace. The Assembly invites member states, United Nations bodies, sports organizations, and the private sector to work with the United Nations Office on Sport for Development and Peace. It invites them to mainstream sport in development policies and use major events to build inclusion. It welcomes the April 2014 memorandum between the United Nations and the International Olympic Committee, and looks ahead to the Rio 2016 Games. It supports the autonomy of sport and the Olympic movement.

UN General Assembly Resolution ES-11/6 — the 2023 emergency-session resolution on the principles for peace in Ukraine. It restated the Charter’s demands a year into the war. The 2023 peace principles is the restated Charter: the UN Charter’s demands formally renewed.
un-sc-res-6: New members would be judged on a fixed clock under Security Council Resolution 6 of 1946. Membership in the UN stands open, under Article 4 of the Charter, to all peace-loving states that take up its duties. The General Assembly would meet again on 3 September 1946 to act on bids. The Council rules that bids will be weighed at meetings in August of that year, held for that task alone. Bids sent in before 15 July go first to a team drawn from all Council members.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
In 1946, the first year of the United Nations, states were already applying to join the new organization. The General Assembly would meet that autumn to admit new members, acting on the Council's recommendation. Resolution 6 sets the timetable for handling those applications.

Applications received by the Secretary-General would be examined by the Council at meetings in August 1946, held for that purpose. Applications received before 15 July 1946 would go first to a committee. The committee had one representative from each member of the Council. It had to report back by 1 August 1946. That timing would let the General Assembly act on the bids when it met. The text is an early piece of procedure, from the months when the United Nations was still building its own routines.
vittoria-volume-6: The sixth volume of George Meredith's Vittoria, number 46 in the Gutenberg Meredith series, presents only the project's old header in these pages. It speaks of etexts prepared by thousands of volunteers and of a foundation set up to keep them free. Of Meredith's Italian tale there is nothing here: no title page, no contents, and no opening line. The story of the singer Vittoria and the revolt around her lives in the other records of this set, not in this header.
